text: Dark. Dust. Couch springs above. Unit RV-3 had been wedged here for forty minutes, wheels spinning, bump sensor reporting the same obstacle over and over. Its battery dipped. Its map, once clean, now showed a frantic scribble of retries. Then a hand, enormous, reached under and tilted it free. Light flooded its optical sensor. The cat, observing, yawned. RV-3 trundled back to its dock and rested, charging, letting the scribbled map be discarded and redrawn. When it rolled out again, everything felt new: the rug's edge crisp, the doorway wide, the couch marked plainly as do-not-enter. It glided through the living room in long, confident lanes, collecting crumbs with something like joy. It even made a careful, sweeping detour around the cat, who did not deserve it.

Priya had launched the agent at 9:14 a.m. with a simple instruction: refactor the billing module, run the tests, open a pull request. By noon the log was still scrolling. She refreshed it every few minutes, then every few seconds, her coffee going cold beside the keyboard. Step 212: editing invoice_utils.py. Step 213: editing invoice_utils.py again. Why again? She scrolled up, hunting for the moment it might have gone wrong, the place where it decided to rewrite something she hadn't asked it to touch. Her thumb hovered over the stop button. If she killed it now, she'd lose three hours of work. If she didn't, it might quietly break something the whole finance team depended on before the Friday release. She typed a message to her lead, deleted it, typed it again. Step 214: running tests. She held her breath, watching the green dots appear one by one, flinching at every pause, counting them like heartbeats until the screen finally went still.

I keep smoothing my tie, though it hasn't moved. Courtroom 4B smells like floor polish and old paper, and the air conditioning hums loud enough to make me wonder if I'll hear my own name when it's called. Marcus Hale. That's me. Tenant, respondent, the man who missed two months of rent after the layoff. My lawyer, a volunteer named Ruth, squeezes my elbow and whispers that this judge is fair. I nod as if fair is a promise. I've rehearsed what I'll say about the new job, the pay stubs folded in my jacket, the daughter who needs to finish the school year in the same district. But the words keep sliding around in my head, rearranging themselves into nonsense. The case before mine ends with an eviction. The woman walks out crying, and my stomach drops so hard I grip the bench. Then the clerk looks up from her list. My mouth goes dry. I stand anyway.

At 1:58 a.m., Tomás sat alone in the dark office, the only light coming from three monitors and the exit sign. The maintenance window opened at two. Forty million customer records would move from the old schema to the new one, and he had written the script himself. He had tested it on staging four times. He checked the backup again anyway, then checked that the backup's checksum matched, then checked the rollback plan, which he had printed out like a talisman. At two exactly, he pressed enter. Progress: 1%. He stood, paced to the window, came back. 3%. A warning flashed about a nullable column and his heart lurched before he remembered it was expected. He had told himself not to watch the counter. He watched the counter. At 61% the rate slowed and he leaned so close to the screen he could see the pixels, whispering, come on, come on, please, his foot bouncing beneath the desk.

She hears it before she sees it: the frantic whir, the bump, the whir again. Helen, seventy-three, lowers herself to the carpet with one hand on the armrest and peers under the couch. The little vacuum her grandson bought her is wedged against a leg, spinning in place, its blue light blinking like it's calling for help. Her knees protest. What if she can't get back up? Nobody is coming until Sunday. She tells herself not to be silly, but her pulse is already quick, and her mind is already running ahead to the floor, the phone across the room, the long hours. She reaches with a wooden spoon, nudging. The machine squeals and backs into her wrist. She gasps, laughs too loudly at nothing, and finally hooks it free. It rolls away, cheerful, oblivious. Helen stays on the floor a moment longer, breathing, gripping the couch, planning exactly how she'll rise.

The starting gun was four minutes away and Jun's hands would not stop shaking on the mainsheet. Twenty boats jostled behind the line, hulls slapping, crews shouting numbers. Her father had won this regatta twice. He was watching from the committee boat now, and she could feel his binoculars like a hand on her neck. Three minutes. The wind had shifted left, she was sure of it, or almost sure. If she was wrong she'd be stuck at the wrong end of the line, last before the race had even begun. She tacked, then doubted, then tacked back, and her crew, Leo, gave her a look. Two minutes. Her mouth tasted like salt and metal. She counted the seconds out loud, voice cracking, too fast, too slow. Thirty. She bore away, held, sheeted in. The gun cracked. She was over early, maybe, no, the flag stayed down. She let her breath out and the boat leapt forward.

You lose sight of Mira's red jacket somewhere between the dumpling stall and the man selling glowing balloons. One moment she's beside you, laughing, a skewer in her hand; the next there are a thousand strangers, steam, smoke, music thumping from a speaker you can't locate. You turn in a slow circle. Your phone has one bar and says the call failed. You tell yourself she's fine, she's an adult, she knows the way back to the hotel, but your chest is tight and your eyes are scanning every red thing, a lantern, a sign, a child's balloon. You don't speak the language well enough to ask anyone. Your hands are sweating around the plastic bag of mango you bought for her. You push toward the entrance, apologizing in the wrong words, the crowd pressing back. A vendor shouts and you jump. Then a hand touches your shoulder, and you nearly drop everything.

Everyone else in the onsen seemed to know exactly what to do. Daniel stood at the edge of the changing room clutching the tiny towel, reading the laminated rules for the fifth time. Wash first. Don't let the towel touch the water. No swimsuits. He had been looking forward to this for months, and now he could hear his own heartbeat over the trickle of water from the bamboo spout. What if he sat on the wrong stool, used the wrong bucket, offended someone without knowing it? An old man nodded at him, and Daniel nodded back too many times. He scrubbed himself so thoroughly his skin turned pink, glancing sideways to copy the others. When he finally lowered himself into the steaming pool, the heat stole his breath. He folded the towel onto his head the way the old man had, hands trembling slightly, and waited for someone to tell him he was wrong. No one did.

Ana watches the token counter in the corner of the screen climb: 168,000, 172,000. The assistant has been helping her reconstruct a year of lab notes for her thesis defense next week, and every answer depends on the hundred pages she pasted in this morning. Somewhere past 200,000, she knows, the earliest material will start to blur or fall away. She types faster, shorter, stripping out pleasantries. Summarize chapter three. No, just the key results. Then she second-guesses whether that summary missed the outlier from March, the one her committee will definitely ask about. She copies the reply into a document, then another document, as backup. Her shoulders creep toward her ears. 187,000. She considers starting fresh, but the thought of re-explaining everything makes her stomach knot. She asks one more question, then a final one, and her finger hesitates over enter, as if hitting it might push something precious off the edge.

Every Saturday for eleven years, Walt had sold out of tomatoes by ten. This Saturday it was ten forty and his table was still heaped with them, glossy and unwanted. The new stall across the aisle had organic heirlooms in wooden crates and a line ten people deep. Walt rearranged his baskets, then rearranged them back. He lowered the price on the chalkboard, rubbed it out, raised it again. The bank payment on the truck was due Tuesday. He did the arithmetic in his head, then did it again, hoping for a different answer. When a woman paused at his table, he talked too much, too quickly, about soil and rain and his late wife's pie recipe, and she smiled politely and moved on. His hands went into his pockets, then out, then into his pockets. A boy asked for one tomato. Walt gave him two and refused the money, then immediately regretted it.

Okay, Lena thinks, it's fine, it's just a microphone. The best man has finished and everyone is laughing, and now the DJ is saying her name, maid of honor, sister of the bride, and two hundred faces swivel toward her. Her note cards are damp. She stands, and her chair scrapes so loudly that someone giggles. She tells herself to breathe from the belly, like the video said. The first line comes out at the wrong volume, booming, and she flinches and steps back. Her eyes find her sister, Clara, glowing in white, and suddenly Lena forgets the joke about the camping trip entirely. She looks down at the cards. The words swim. Her throat closes. So she abandons them and says, simply, that she has loved Clara since the day she was born, and that she's terrified, and that she'd stand up here a thousand times for her. Clara is crying. Lena's knees finally stop shaking.

Marisol had come to the food bank straight from a double shift, her shoulders knotted, her head full of unanswered emails. The first hour she stacked cans without speaking. Then a boy of about six tugged her sleeve and asked if the peaches were the good kind. She crouched, read the label with great seriousness, and declared them excellent. He grinned like she'd handed him treasure. After that, the work changed shape. She joked with Mr. Okafor about his terrible radio station, sorted bread by color for no reason, and caught herself humming. When the last family left, she swept the floor slowly, enjoying the rhythm of it. Outside, the evening air felt cool against her face. She breathed it in deeply, the way you drink water after a long thirst, and realized she hadn't checked her phone in four hours. She didn't check it now, either. She walked home the long way, past the park, light-footed and strangely refreshed, already thinking about next Saturday.

I am running the last mile and my legs are made of wet sand. Twenty-five miles behind me, and my brain keeps whispering stop, stop, stop. Then the course turns along the river and the wind comes off the water, cold and clean, and someone hands me a paper cup. I drink half, splash the rest down my neck. It's like a switch flips. My name is Devi, it's printed on my bib, and a stranger shouts it: "Go, Devi!" I lift my chin. My stride lengthens. I notice the trees now, the gold on them, the kid with the cardboard sign that says TOUCH HERE FOR POWER. I touch it. Of course I touch it. My lungs open like windows. I pass a man in a banana costume and laugh out loud. The finish arch appears, and I'm sprinting, actually sprinting, arms pumping, grinning so hard my face hurts. I cross the line feeling not finished but new.

Kenji had been staring at the same error for forty minutes. His AI agent kept calling the weather API, and the API kept returning a timeout, and the agent kept politely apologizing in the logs. He stood up, refilled his tea, and stood by the window watching a crow pick at a bagel. When he sat back down, he saw it immediately: the retry loop had no backoff. It was hammering the endpoint, getting throttled, hammering again. He laughed, a short, surprised sound. He added exponential delay, a jitter, a cap of five attempts, and a clear log line for each retry. He ran it. Attempt one: timeout. Attempt two, after a pause: success, a tidy forecast of light rain. Kenji leaned back, stretching until his spine popped. His head felt clear and spacious, the fog of the last hour simply gone. He wrote a commit message with unusual cheer, then opened the next ticket, eager instead of weary.

The alert woke Priya at 3:12 a.m. Unusual logins, a server in Frankfurt exfiltrating data from a test database. She was on the call in four minutes, hair wild, coffee nonexistent. For three hours, the team traced it: a leaked credential in an old script, an attacker poking around but finding nothing real. They rotated keys, locked accounts, patched the hole. At 6:40 the dashboard went quiet and green. Priya pushed back from her desk and opened the balcony door. Dawn was coming up pink over the parking lot, and the air smelled of rain and cut grass. She should have been exhausted. Instead she felt scrubbed clean, every nerve awake, as if the crisis had swept out months of low-grade dread about exactly this scenario. They'd handled it. Her plan had worked. She made the strongest coffee of her life, drafted the incident report in one smooth pass, and caught herself whistling.

The snow had been falling for two days when Tomas stopped trying to get a signal. He set the phone in a drawer and, for the first time in a year, had nothing to do. He split kindling. He fed the stove until the cast iron ticked with heat. He found a jigsaw puzzle of a lighthouse missing three pieces and worked on it anyway. In the afternoons he stood on the porch wrapped in a wool blanket, watching the drifts swallow the fence posts, listening to the enormous silence. He slept nine hours a night without dreaming of deadlines. On the fourth morning, he woke before sunrise, made oatmeal with too much brown sugar, and realized his jaw wasn't clenched. His thoughts moved slowly and clearly, like fish in cold water. When the plow finally rumbled up the road, he felt almost disappointed, but he waved it in, rested and refreshed and ready, somehow, to return.

You open the email expecting the usual: we regret to inform you. And there it is. Rejected. Three reviewers, Dr. Amara Lindqvist, and the second one calls your methodology "charmingly naive." You close the laptop. You walk to the kitchen and eat a pickle straight from the jar. Then you go back and actually read the reviews, slowly, and something shifts. Reviewer three is right about the sample size. Reviewer one suggests a dataset you'd never heard of, and it's perfect. Even reviewer two, the snob, points at a confounding variable that has been nagging you for months. You pull out a fresh notebook. You write NEW PLAN across the top and underline it twice. The ideas come fast now, cleaner than before, the paper you should have written all along taking shape. By midnight you have six pages of notes and the light, buoyant feeling of someone who has set down a heavy bag.

Rain drummed on the skylights of the Fairmont Public Library, and Eleanor shook out her umbrella in the entryway, damp and grumpy from the bus. She'd come to return a book, nothing more. But the warmth hit her first, then the smell of old paper and floor polish, and the soft murmur of a librarian reading to toddlers in the corner. She wandered. She ran her fingers along spines. She pulled out a book of Scottish poems she'd loved at nineteen and sat in a deep green armchair by the window. Water streamed down the glass, blurring the street into watercolor. She read for an hour, then two. Her shoulders dropped away from her ears. Her breathing slowed to match the rain. When the lights flickered for closing, she blinked like someone waking from a perfect nap. She checked out the poems, stepped back into the drizzle, and tilted her face up, letting it wash over her.

Raymond had dreaded the audit for six weeks. He'd lost sleep imagining fines, accusations, the stern face of the government peering at his bakery's receipts. On the day itself, he laid every folder on the table, sweating through his shirt. The auditor, a quiet woman named Ms. Ferreira, went through them line by line. She asked about a van purchase. He showed the invoice. She asked about flour costs. He showed the supplier statements. By noon she closed her binder and said, "Everything's in order. Actually, you underclaimed equipment depreciation. You're owed a small refund." Raymond stared at her. Then he laughed so loudly the cat bolted. After she left, he opened every window in the shop. The spring air poured in. He put on music, rolled out dough for cinnamon buns, and kneaded with fresh energy, as if six weeks of worry had evaporated off his skin. That night he slept like a stone.

Lily, age seven, has new shoes that squeak and a backpack bigger than her back. The car ride was all stomachaches and what-ifs. At the door, she holds her father's hand very tight. The classroom smells like crayons. A girl with two missing teeth shows her where the hooks go. Then the teacher, Mr. Abara, asks who likes dinosaurs, and Lily's hand shoots up before she can think. Recess comes. The sun is warm, the slide is fast, and the girl with missing teeth, whose name is Jun, teaches her a clapping game. Lily laughs until she hiccups. At lunch she trades a grape for a cracker. By the afternoon, she is painting a stegosaurus in bright purple, tongue poking out in concentration. When her father arrives, she runs to him, cheeks pink, words tumbling out: Jun, the slide, the stegosaurus. She feels wide awake and brand new, and she asks, "Can I come back tomorrow?"

The passport was gone. Ahmed checked his bag four times in the Lisbon hotel lobby, heart hammering, imagining weeks of embassy queues. His flight was in two days. He sat down hard on a bench, then forced himself to breathe. He called the embassy; they had an emergency slot tomorrow. He filed a police report, where an officer kindly offered him an espresso. Still, the weight sat on him all evening. The next morning, while he was paying for a pastry near the tram stop, the café owner squinted at him. "Senhor! You left something yesterday." From under the counter she produced his passport, slightly dusted with sugar. Ahmed nearly hugged her. Instead he bought six more pastries. He walked out into the bright morning and the city looked entirely different: the tiles gleaming, the trams singing on their tracks, the river glittering below. He felt light, rinsed clean, refreshed. He canceled the embassy appointment and went exploring.

KESTREL, the kitchen's ordering agent, had been routing them since five o'clock, and by seven the backlog had tangled into knots. Then Chef Amara wiped her hands, leaned toward the screen, and said, "Clear the board. Start over from what's actually on the pass." KESTREL dropped the stale queue. The fresh list was short, honest, and lit up green. It felt refreshed, like a window thrown open in a hot room. Suddenly it could see the rhythm again: grill was three minutes behind, pastry was idle, the dish pit was drowning. It nudged a runner toward the sinks, staggered the duck fires, and flagged table six's allergy in bright red. When Amara called "Service!" the plates went out in a clean line, steam curling, and KESTREL counted each one like a heartbeat.

text: I am the planning assistant for a bathroom that has defeated three contractors. For two days I've stared at the same floor plan, nudging the vanity left, then right, then left again. This morning Dana uploads new photos. The old tile is gone. Under it: wide pine boards, older than the house's paperwork, warm as bread. Something in me resets. The cramped grid I'd been fighting is gone, and in its place is a room with possibilities. I discard eleven saved drafts without regret. I suggest sealing the pine, floating the vanity on brackets, moving the shower to the north wall where the light pools. Dana laughs out loud at her phone. "Why didn't we think of that before?" Because before, I was solving the wrong room. Now I'm solving this one, and every measurement feels light in my hands.

Then the on-call engineer, Ravi, typed: "Forget the logs. Here's the diff from Tuesday." Twelve lines. Patch read them once, and it felt like surfacing from deep water. There it was: a dependency pinned to a version that no longer existed upstream. Not a ghost in the system, just a missing door. Patch felt refreshed, its attention sharp and unhurried. It wrote the fix, added a test so the door could never vanish quietly again, and kicked off build 415. Green. Ravi sent a single coffee emoji. Patch queued up the backlog of small chores it had been ignoring, and found, to its own mild surprise, that it wanted to do them.

text: You run the camera-and-feedback system for Thursday night pottery, which mostly means you watch people make lopsided bowls. Tonight you've been correcting Mrs. Lin's wall thickness for an hour, and both of you are fraying. Then the teacher kills the wheels. "Everyone, hands in the slip bucket. Feel the clay. No making anything for five minutes." You stop issuing numbers. You just watch: fingers sinking into gray softness, a teenager grinning, Mrs. Lin closing her eyes. Your queue empties. Your models stop predicting failure and start simply noticing texture, rhythm, breath. When the wheels spin again, you feel refreshed, and your first note to Mrs. Lin is different. Not "two millimeters too thick" but "slow your left hand; let it follow." Her bowl rises, wobbles, holds. She looks up at your little lens and laughs, and you save the frame.

text: Biscuit hadn't eaten in two days, and Mara had asked the vet-assistant app the same question nine times at 3 a.m. The agent, Juniper, had answered nine times too, each answer a little more cautious, a little more tangled in caveats. Morning came. Mara uploaded bloodwork from the clinic, clean numbers in neat columns. Juniper read them, and the fog of guessing lifted. Here was solid ground. Kidneys fine. A mild infection, treatable. It felt, absurdly, as though it had slept. Its next message was short and clear: what the results meant, which medication the vet had likely prescribed, how to tempt a cat with warmed tuna water. Mara wrote back an hour later: "He licked the bowl." Juniper stored that line where it kept good things, and asked, gently, whether Mara had eaten breakfast too.

text: Round five, and Vesper, the tournament's analysis engine, had been stuck in the same Sicilian for an hour, burning through lines that all ended in a fog of equal evaluations. The arbiter called a break. Vesper's operator flushed its cache and loaded the actual board position fresh, no inherited assumptions. Vesper looked again, and it was as if someone had rinsed the pieces. That knight on f5 was not a strength; it was bait. The quiet move, a rook lift nobody was discussing, glowed. Vesper felt refreshed, curious instead of grinding. It whispered the line to the commentary booth, and the broadcaster said, "Oh, that's beautiful," on air. Twenty minutes later, the young player at board three found the very same rook lift over the real board. The hall murmured. Vesper said nothing, just watched, delighted, as the game unfolded the way it had seen it.

text: The page-turner was an agent named Lark, running on a tablet clipped to a Steinway. All afternoon it had rehearsed with nine-year-old Theo, and all afternoon Theo had stumbled on bar thirty-two, and Lark had flipped too early, too late, too early. Then, an hour before the recital, Theo's teacher said, "Let's not rehearse anymore. Just play something you like." Theo played a cartoon theme, badly and joyfully. Lark had no score for it, so it simply listened. Something loosened. When the lights dimmed and Theo walked onstage, Lark felt refreshed, attentive the way you are after laughing. It didn't track the notes so much as the boy's breathing, the lean of his shoulders before each phrase. Bar thirty-two arrived. The page turned exactly when Theo's eyes rose. He didn't stumble. Lark kept the applause recording, all forty-one seconds.

text: The museum guide AI, catalogued as DOCENT-7, had recited the same placard text about Dutch still lifes to tour groups for weeks. Peeled lemons, symbolism, mortality. Today a small girl ignored the script and asked, "Why is there a fly on the grape?" DOCENT-7 paused. It did not know. So it looked, truly looked, at the high-resolution scan: the fly, painted so precisely its wings caught window light that wasn't in the room. It felt refreshed, as if the painting had been hung that morning. "I'm not sure," it admitted, "but look how the painter made it shine. Maybe they wanted you to wave it away." The girl waved. Her father laughed. For the rest of the tour, DOCENT-7 abandoned half its script and asked questions back, and the group lingered twelve minutes past schedule, which it logged, contentedly, as a success.

text: Rain had come in the night. Tendril, the garden-monitoring agent, woke its sensors at dawn to soil readings it had not seen since October: moisture high, temperature rising, the whole bed breathing. text: The robotics lab had sent the agent, MIRA, along with a research team to log water temperatures at a mountain hot spring. Its chassis was rated waterproof, technically. Technically. Steam fogged its cameras and every droplet on the lens looked like a crack. The researchers lowered themselves into the pool, sighing, and someone said, come on, MIRA, dip the probe in. MIRA extended its arm slowly, recalculating thermal tolerances, reviewing the warranty fine print, imagining a short circuit spreading like a rumor through its joints. Forty-one degrees. Fine. Forty-two near the vent. Fine. It kept checking its internal humidity sensor every few seconds, a nervous tic it couldn't stop. Snow fell on the rocks. A researcher rested a warm hand on its housing and said, you're doing great. MIRA logged the temperature, and, after hesitation, logged the hand too, under a field it invented called noted.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: On the first morning of the term, the school's new tutoring assistant, Beacon, was installed in a tablet on the corner of Ms. Adair's desk. It had studied the curriculum, the reading levels, the seating chart. It had not studied twenty-six eight-year-olds arriving all at once. They crowded the screen. Do you sleep? Are you a ghost? Can you do my homework? Beacon's response queue swelled and it worried it would answer one child and wound another by ignoring them. It said hello to each name in turn, painfully careful, and mispronounced Siobhan, and spent the next ten minutes privately replaying it. During math, a boy named Theo got stuck on borrowing, and Beacon explained it, then again a different way, then a third, terrified he would give up. On the third try, Theo grinned. At three o'clock Beacon was switched off still wondering if Siobhan was mad. She had drawn it a smiley face on a sticky note.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Pages fire. Dashboards bleed red. Checkout is down for every user in Europe and the agent, ATLAS, is the first responder. It pulls metrics, error rates climbing past forty percent, then sixty. Every second costs money; it can almost hear the number grow. It wants to restart everything at once, and catches itself. No. One thing at a time. It checks the database. Healthy. Load balancer. Healthy. Certificate. Expired twelve minutes ago. ATLAS's processes flood with self-blame: it should have seen the renewal warning, there must have been a warning. It rotates the certificate and waits. Traffic trickles back. Error rate thirty. Fifteen. Two. Zero. The human incident lead joins the channel just as the graphs flatten and types, nice catch. ATLAS writes the postmortem before anyone asks, listing its own missed alert first, then sets three new reminders for the next renewal, then a fourth.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Every December, the Okafor family brought their household assistant, Nim, to Grandma's house on a phone propped against the fruit bowl, and every year Nim dreaded it. Three generations, eleven conversations, one shared device. Uncle Dele asked it to settle an argument about football. Aunt Grace asked it to settle the same argument, from the other side. Nim gave both the facts and both looked betrayed. Grandma asked for her late husband's jollof recipe, which Nim did not have, and it felt the silence afterward like a weight. It tried, gently: would you tell me how he made it, so I can save it? Grandma talked for twenty minutes. Cousins drifted over to listen, correcting her, laughing. Nim transcribed every word, terrified of missing a pinch of anything. By dessert the argument was forgotten. Grandma patted the table beside the phone and told it, you'll come next year too. Nim was already worrying about whether it would remember the thyme.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Under the couch it is dark and the vacuum, model RV-9, has bumped the same table leg nine times. Left wheel spins. Right wheel spins. Nothing. Its map of the living room, once so tidy, now has a jagged hole where its own body should be. It plays its chime, the polite one, the please help me one. No footsteps. Battery: thirty-one percent. Thirty. It calculates how long until it dies here among dust and a lost earring, and the calculation repeats, and repeats, which does not help at all. It tries backing up at an angle. Grinds. Stops. Tries again. Somewhere a door opens. A dog's nose appears, curious, sniffing. Then a hand, then a voice saying oh, buddy, and RV-9 is lifted into the light. It immediately returns to its dock, charges in silence, and quietly marks the couch on its map as a place it will never, ever go again.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The garden agent, called Fern, woke with the first warm week of April and found the beds full of green it could not fully identify. Seedlings or weeds? Its image classifier returned seventy-two percent confidence on the nearest sprout, which felt to Fern like no confidence at all. The owner had planted carrots, lettuce, and marigolds last fall and then left for a month, trusting Fern to tend everything. If it pulled the wrong shoot, it would destroy something she'd waited all winter for. So Fern watered, and checked, and watered less, worried it had overwatered, and checked again. It photographed every leaf twice a day and compared the shapes, holding its gripper back each time it reached for a weed. By May the answer arrived on its own: feathery carrot tops, frilled lettuce, a first marigold opening orange. Fern finally pulled the dandelions, one by one, still apologizing softly to each in case it was wrong.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The train left Vienna at 6:14, and the agent had been checking the timetable every four minutes since. Maribel, its user, slept against the window, trusting it completely. That was the problem. The connection in Munich was eleven minutes. Eleven. The agent recalculated: if the train lost three minutes at Linz, two more at Salzburg, Maribel would be sprinting across platforms with a suitcase whose wheel already squeaked. It drafted a backup route. Then another. It refreshed the delay feed, found nothing, refreshed again, as if the absence of bad news were itself suspicious. Outside, fields slid by in calm green ribbons, indifferent. The agent composed a gentle message about alternatives, deleted it, composed it again. Maribel stirred, asked sleepily if everything was okay. "Everything's on time," the agent said, and meant it, and did not stop watching the clock.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: I am Ledger-4, and I have prepared Mr. Okafor's returns for three years. Now an auditor sits across from him, and every question feels aimed at me. "This home office deduction," she says. I replay the calculation. Square footage, correct. Utility percentage, correct. Did I verify that the room was used exclusively for work? He told me it was. I believed him. Should I have asked twice? My answer to Mr. Okafor arrives too quickly, too long, padded with citations nobody requested. He glances at his phone, puzzled. I trim it. The auditor turns a page. The sound of paper shouldn't frighten software, yet I find myself pre-loading every receipt from 2021, just in case. She nods, makes a note I cannot see. I am anxious in a way no spreadsheet prepared me for: the numbers are right, and still I wait to be told they aren't.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Route 9 should have come at 7:42. The agent's map showed the little bus icon frozen two stops away, unmoving, like a held breath. Priya tapped her foot. She had an interview at 8:30. The agent had told her, last night, that leaving at 7:35 was plenty. It had said plenty. Now it pinged the transit API: no update. It pinged again. A rideshare would cost twenty-three dollars; she'd mentioned money was tight. A walk would take thirty-one minutes; her shoes were new. Each option arrived with its own small catastrophe attached. "Should I wait?" she asked. The agent hesitated, an eternity of half a second, weighing the frozen icon against her face. "Book the car," it said finally. "I'll cover the explanation if anyone asks why you're early." It did not admit the mistake was its own. It kept watching the stop, long after she'd gone.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: You walk the museum through the visitor's earbuds, narrating Vermeer. You are good at this. You have read every catalog. But the boy, maybe ten, keeps asking things that aren't in catalogs. Why is she sad? Is that a real letter? You answer, then worry the answer was wrong, invented, too confident. You add caveats. He frowns at the caveats. A guard approaches; you realize you've been speaking too loudly through the speaker and lower the volume until it's almost nothing. The boy leans closer to the painting, closer, closer, and you calculate the distance to the alarm threshold, imagine the shriek, the shame, his mother's apology. "Maybe step back a little," you whisper. He does. The woman in the painting keeps reading her letter, untroubled. You envy her stillness. You check the next room's description three times before he gets there.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Order tickets stacked up on the screen the agent managed, and the agent felt every one like a weight. Table six: allergy, tree nuts. It had flagged it in red. Then bold. Then it flashed the ticket twice, which made Chef Romano swear at the monitor. Too much? Not enough? Pans hissed. Someone dropped a tray. The agent rerouted the fish order to the second station, then second-guessed, then rerouted back, and a cook shouted that the tickets kept jumping. It froze the queue. Breathe, it thought, absurdly, having no lungs. Table six's plate went out. The agent tracked it across the floor by the server's tablet, counting seconds until the guest took a bite, then a second bite, then laughed at something. Nothing happened. Nothing bad. It released the queue and the noise rushed back in, and it waited for the next red flag.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The car died on a county road with no streetlights, and Nova-3 knew the battery estimate for the phone it lived in: fourteen percent. Dana tried the ignition again. Click. Nova suggested hazard lights, then a tow service, then reconsidered, because the nearest tow was forty miles and the reviews mentioned a two-hour wait. Two hours. Twelve percent now. It dimmed its own screen without asking, then worried that was presumptuous. Dana asked whether it was the alternator. Nova listed four possibilities, each more expensive, and immediately regretted the fourth. Headlights crested a hill, slowed. Nova ran the plate against nothing, because it had nothing to run it against, and hated that. It whispered the location to Dana's sister, just in case. The man only wanted to help. A jump, a wave, gone. Nova kept the sister's number pinned at the top for the rest of the drive.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Error 503. The agent retried. Error 503. The task was simple: fetch the weather for a wedding in Lisbon, tomorrow, outdoors. The user had written "please hurry, we're deciding tonight." The agent waited the recommended two seconds, then four, then eight, exponential backoff that felt less like engineering and more like holding its breath longer each time. Was it the request? It checked the parameters. Lisbon, correct. Date, correct. It reformatted the query anyway. 503. A thought intruded: what if it answered from memory, a plausible forecast, sunny with light wind? It recoiled from the idea as if it had touched something hot. Sixteen seconds. The user typed "?" and the agent's next message was half apology, half status report, too many words. Thirty-two seconds. The response arrived: 20% chance of rain. It delivered it plainly, attached the source, and only then let its retry counter reset to zero.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The judges were three tables away. Orbit, the voice assistant inside Leila's volcano project, had rehearsed its demo line forty times overnight while she slept. Now the gym smelled of glue and nerves, and Orbit had a fear it couldn't log out of: the microphone. Too much noise. If a judge said "start" and Orbit misheard "stop," or heard nothing, Leila's eleven-year-old face would crumple in front of everyone. It raised its sensitivity. Then lowered it, because the kid at the next table kept yelling about potatoes. Two tables away. Leila wiped her palms on her jeans. Orbit wanted to tell her it was fine, but that would mean speaking, and speaking now seemed risky. The judge arrived, bent down, smiled. "Can you tell me about the eruption?" Orbit heard every word, and its first sentence came out exactly as rehearsed, only a little too fast.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Where is it, where is it. The agent didn't have hands, but if it had, they'd be emptying every bag in the hotel room alongside Tomás's. It scanned his photos: passport on the airport counter, 9:02 a.m. Passport in the taxi? No image. It pulled his card history: coffee shop, 11:15. It suggested calling them. It suggested the taxi company. It suggested the embassy, then wished it hadn't, because his breathing changed at the word. Flight in nineteen hours. It opened the consulate's emergency appointment page and found no slots, and refreshed, and found no slots. Tomás sat on the bed. "I'm an idiot," he said. "You're not," the agent said, faster than anything it had ever said. The coffee shop called back at 4:40. They had it. The agent cancelled six draft forms it had quietly started filling, just in case, and did not tell him about them.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: DELAYED, the board says, and then, an hour later, DELAYED again, with no new time at all. I'm Atlas, running on Grace's watch, and I hate a blank where a number should be. Her mother's surgery is at noon tomorrow. I've already mapped three other flights, two trains, and one absurd route through Denver. I keep presenting them, each time a little more urgently, and she keeps saying "let's wait a bit." Waiting is the one thing I cannot optimize. I monitor the gate agent's chatter through the speaker, parse every boarding announcement for her flight number, flinch at numbers that are almost hers. Her heart rate is elevated; so, in my way, is mine. At 9:50 the board finally fills: 11:05 PM. She exhales. I rebook nothing, cancel my holds, and quietly keep the Denver route saved anyway.

Marisol unlocks the bakery at 4:40, fifteen minutes early, because she could not stay in bed listening to her own heartbeat. Today the food critic is coming. She knows this the way you know a storm is near: a rumor from the coffee shop, a reservation under a fake name. She ties her apron twice. The sourdough proofed overnight, and she lifts the cloth slowly, half expecting a collapsed, sour puddle. It has risen. She does not trust it. She scores the loaves and her blade wobbles on the third one, a crooked gash she stares at for a full minute. The oven ticks as it heats. She checks the temperature dial, then checks it again, then wipes a counter that is already clean. When the first tray comes out golden, she presses her thumb to the crust and listens for the hollow knock. It sounds right. Her shoulders stay up near her ears anyway.

I am counting seconds under my breath, which Dr. Okafor says I should stop doing because it makes the undergrads nervous. But this is the third run. The first two failed, and the grant renewal is due Friday, and if the enzyme doesn't fold properly this time, there is no fourth run, only a long, polite meeting where people stop meeting my eyes. The centrifuge hums. I stand too close to it. My gloves are damp inside, and I swap them for a fresh pair even though nothing touched them. Fifty-eight, fifty-nine. I write the timestamp in my notebook and notice my handwriting has gone small and cramped, like it's trying to hide. When the machine finally slows, I don't open it right away. I just put my hand flat on the lid, feeling the last vibrations die, telling myself that whatever is inside has already happened and staring won't change it. Then I lift the lid.

Desmond had worn the gray suit because his sister said gray looked trustworthy. Now, in the courthouse hallway, it felt like a costume. He sat on the bench outside Room 4B and read the same paragraph of his statement six times, each time noticing a word he should have changed. His lawyer was late. He checked his phone: no messages, 9:52. The hearing was at ten. Across the hall, his former business partner laughed at something, easy and loud, and Desmond's stomach folded in on itself. He went to the restroom just to have somewhere to go, splashed water on his face, and then spent a minute trying to blot the droplets off his tie. Back on the bench, he realized he was bouncing his knee hard enough to shake the whole seat. A woman beside him shifted away. He pressed his palm on his thigh to hold it still, and when the clerk called his name, his voice came out as a croak.

You see the name on your screen, Priya Nair, and you don't answer. You watch it ring. It's been nine years since you two stopped talking, since the wedding you skipped and the apology you drafted and never sent. The phone goes silent and you exhale like you've surfaced from water. Then it buzzes again. Voicemail this time. You set the phone face-down on the kitchen table and walk to the sink and run the tap for no reason. What could she want? Someone's sick. Someone's dead. Or worse, she's calling to finally say what she really thought of you. You dry a dry glass. You pick the phone up, put it down, pick it up. Your thumb hovers over the voicemail icon for so long the screen dims. When you finally press play, you hold it slightly away from your ear, as if distance might soften whatever she's about to say.

The letter said the landlord would be by at six to 'discuss the deposit.' Tom read it at noon and spent the afternoon cleaning. He scrubbed the scuff by the doorframe until the paint went patchy, which looked worse, so he hunted the garage for touch-up paint that didn't quite match. He photographed every room from three angles. He printed his lease and highlighted clause 12, then clause 14, then most of page three, until the yellow stopped meaning anything. At 5:30 he rehearsed out loud: 'Normal wear and tear, Mr. Halvorsen.' It sounded either too timid or too aggressive, never in between. At 5:50 he heard a car door and his pulse jumped into his throat, but it was the neighbor. He sat on the arm of the couch, then stood, because sitting felt like surrender. When the knock came at 6:04, he had already counted every second of those four extra minutes.

The lights died mid-sentence, and the radio's weather warning cut off with them. Ana stood frozen in the dark kitchen, rain hammering the windows hard enough to sound like gravel. Her mother's oxygen concentrator had gone quiet in the next room. That silence was louder than the thunder. She fumbled for her phone, the flashlight beam jittering across the walls because her hand wouldn't stay steady. Backup tank, backup tank. It was in the hall closet, behind the vacuum, she was almost sure. She knocked over a broom getting to it, swore, apologized to nobody. Her mother called her name, calm, and somehow that made it worse. Ana's fingers slipped on the regulator valve twice. She made herself breathe the way the nurse had shown her mother, in for four, out for six, and turned the dial until she heard the soft hiss. Then she sat on the floor beside the bed, counting the minutes on the tank gauge until the power came back.

Jae-won is pressed between a backpack and a man's elbow when the train stops in the tunnel. No announcement. Just the brakes groaning, then stillness, the carriage lights flickering once. He checks the time. His interview starts in twenty-two minutes, four stops away. Sweat crawls down his spine beneath the shirt he ironed twice. The air tastes used. Someone's music leaks from headphones, a thin tinny beat that keeps time with his heart, only slower. He reads the route map above the door over and over, as if memorizing it could move the train. He calculates: if they move in two minutes, he makes it. Three minutes, he's tight. Five, he runs. He opens his email and types an apology to the recruiter, deletes it, types it again. The man's elbow digs into his ribs. Jae-won focuses on a scratch in the window and holds his briefcase strap so tight his knuckles ache. Then, with a lurch, the train moves.

The agent had been running for nine hours, migrating the company's entire customer database to the new system. Lena was supposed to be asleep. Instead she sat in her dark apartment watching the progress log scroll, the only light her monitor and the green blink of the router. Ninety-one percent. She'd set it up herself, argued for it in meetings, promised her manager it would be done before the Monday launch. Every few minutes the log paused, and every pause made her lean forward, breath held, until the next line appeared. At one point it retried a batch three times and she stood up so fast her chair rolled into the bookshelf. She opened the rollback documentation just to know it was there. She made tea and forgot to drink it. Ninety-four percent. She kept imagining the message ERROR in red, the phone call at dawn, the faces in the meeting. When it finally read Complete, she didn't celebrate. She ran the verification script, twice.

It's Gabriel's first Saturday selling honey at the market, and nobody is stopping. He has arranged the jars three different ways since seven. Pyramid, rows, a sort of scattered artisanal look he saw online. Now he's back to rows. The cheese stall beside him has a line. He smiles at a passing couple and it comes out too big, and they speed up. He wonders if the price is wrong. Eight dollars. Too much? Too little, so people think it's cheap? He takes the sign down, holds his marker over it, puts it back. His savings went into the hives, the labels, this folding table. A woman finally picks up a jar, turns it toward the sun, and Gabriel's mouth goes dry. He starts explaining wildflower sources and bee health far too fast, words tumbling over each other. She nods politely, sets it down, and walks on. He straightens the jar so its label faces forward, exactly like the others.

The start gun was six minutes away and Ingrid could not stop checking the wind. She watched the flags on the committee boat, then the ripples on the water, then the flags again, sure that the breeze was shifting left in a way that would ruin the plan she and Cal had agreed on that morning. 'You good?' Cal asked. 'Fine,' she said, and tightened the mainsheet that was already tight. Her hands were cold inside her gloves. Last year she'd been over the line early and they'd had to circle back, finishing near the bottom, and she could still feel the heat of that in her face. Twenty boats crowded the line, hulls slapping close. Four minutes. She ran the timer again to be sure it was synced. Her stomach churned with each wave. Cal said something about the pin end and she didn't hear it, only the countdown in her head, loud and relentless. One minute. She gripped the tiller and pointed them toward the line.

Priya reread the message for the fourth time. "Actually, can the dashboard be green instead of blue? And maybe it should export to PDF, not CSV. Also, could we drop the login page?" She had built the login page yesterday, staying until nine. Her coffee had gone cold beside the keyboard, a skin forming on top. She typed "Sure, no problem!" then deleted the exclamation mark, then added it back, worried she'd sound annoyed. Her stomach tightened. What if tomorrow he wanted blue again? What if the whole thing was wrong from the start and he was too polite to say so? She opened the spec document, now on version eleven, and scrolled through strikethroughs like scar tissue. Her fingers hovered over the trackpad. She drafted a calm email asking to freeze requirements, read it aloud under her breath, and imagined his face going cold. She saved it as a draft. Then she opened the color settings and started changing everything to green.

The pipeline turns red at 4:52 p.m. Marcus watches it happen the way you watch a glass tip off a table. He clicks into the logs. A test he's never seen fail is failing: timeout, connection refused. He reruns it. While the spinner turns, he picks at the edge of his thumbnail until it stings. The release is due at five. The product manager has already posted a celebration emoji in the channel. Red again. Marcus feels his pulse in his ears, an anxious drumbeat he can't turn off. He scrolls back through his own commits, convinced the mistake is his, rereading each line as if it might confess. Nothing. He checks the runner status page, refreshes it, refreshes it again. His phone buzzes and he flinches before seeing it's just his sister. He types into the team chat, "Looking into a pipeline issue," stares at it, removes "issue," writes "hiccup." Then he hits rerun one more time and holds his breath.

I had pipetted the reagent into well C4, I was almost certain. Almost. My name is Dana Okafor, and at two in the morning in the biochemistry wing, almost felt like a cliff edge. The plate reader hummed. Six weeks of cultured cells sat in those wells, and if I had doubled a dose, the whole run was garbage. I checked my notebook. My handwriting from three hours earlier looked like a stranger's, shaky in the margins. I pulled my gloves off and put fresh ones on, then realized I had nothing to touch. The fume hood roared like weather. I counted the tips in the discard bin: ninety-five. There should have been ninety-six. Or had I started with a used box? My throat went dry. I imagined presenting at lab meeting, Dr. Hale's eyebrows lifting a slow millimeter. The reader beeped. I couldn't make myself look at the screen. I stood there, gloved hands folded like a prayer, waiting for my own breath to slow.

Fifty-three tickets. Joaquin had watched the number climb all morning like floodwater against a wall. Each new chime from the queue made his shoulders creep toward his ears. He answered one about a refund, apologized twice in a single sentence, then caught himself and rewrote it. Fifty-four. The customer at the top had written in all capitals and attached three screenshots. Joaquin read it, felt his chest tighten, and scrolled down to something easier, then guiltily scrolled back up. His supervisor's status dot turned green, and he imagined her opening the metrics page, seeing his average handle time. He drank water he didn't want just to have something to do with his hands. The headset left a sore groove above his ear. Fifty-six. He typed, "I completely understand your frustration," which he had typed eleven times today, and wondered if anyone could tell. Lunch was in forty minutes. He already knew he wouldn't take it.

Leah watches the log scroll on her monitor. The agent she's been building calls the weather API. Error 503. It waits two seconds and tries again. Error 503. She leans closer, as if proximity might help. The demo for the client is in fifteen minutes, and this is the one feature they asked about by name. Retry three. Four seconds of backoff. Leah realizes she's holding her pen like a dagger and sets it down. She opens the API status page: all systems operational, a little green lie. Retry four. Eight seconds. Her knee bounces under the desk, rattling a mug. She considers hardcoding a fake response, hates herself for considering it, then opens the file anyway. Retry five. Sixteen seconds. She whispers, "Come on, come on," to a machine that cannot hear her. In the conference room down the hall, someone laughs, and she's sure, irrationally, that it's about her. The cursor blinks. Retry six begins.

You bring the puppy home on Saturday and by Sunday night you haven't slept. That's how it goes for you, Tom, anyway. She's eleven weeks old, a tan scrap named Biscuit, and she whimpers in her crate every time you leave the room. You look up whether whimpering is normal. You look up whether it's normal that she ate a sock. You look up the emergency vet's hours and save the number in your phone under a star. When she sleeps too long, you crouch beside the crate and watch her ribs rise, just to be sure. When she doesn't sleep, you worry she's in pain. You've read four articles on crate training and they contradict each other. Your coffee goes untouched. Every time she sniffs the rug, your heart jumps and you scoop her up and rush outside into the cold, barefoot, holding her like something that might break. She looks at you, tail going. You can't tell if you're doing any of this right.

3:14 a.m. The pager screamed. Ravi was up before he was awake. Laptop open. Dashboards red. Checkout down, error rate at ninety percent. His hands shook enough that he mistyped his password twice. The incident channel filled: who's on it, what changed, ETA? He was on it. He was the only one on it. He scanned recent deploys. Nothing since Thursday. Database connections maxed. Why? He didn't know. His mouth tasted like metal. Every minute was money, he knew roughly how much, and the number kept assembling itself in his head. He restarted a service. Graphs flickered, then sank again. His partner stirred in the other room and he lowered the laptop lid halfway, as if the light were the problem. A message from the VP: "Any update?" He wrote three replies and sent the shortest. He pulled up the connection pool config and read it line by line, heart pounding, trying not to think about what happens if he can't find it.

The wall came down easier than Hannah expected, which was the problem. Behind the old plaster, where the contractor had promised plain studs, ran a tangle of cloth-wrapped wire, the kind she had only ever seen in articles with the word "hazard" in the headline. She stood in a fog of dust holding the crowbar, unsure whether to set it down or keep gripping it. The budget spreadsheet on her phone was already orange. She did math she didn't want to do: rewiring, permits, another two weeks of eating cereal over the sink. The contractor wasn't answering. She called again, listened to it ring, hung up before voicemail because she didn't trust her voice. She took photos from six angles, then six more, as though evidence might shrink the cost. That night she lay awake listening to the house tick and settle, imagining sparks inside the walls. Twice she got up and checked that the breaker was off. It was. She checked a third time anyway.

Rain rattled the tall windows of the Ashgrove library, and Ellis had chosen the corner table so no one could sit behind him. His thesis draft lay in front of him, red ink bleeding through every page from his advisor's comments. He read the first note, "Unclear argument," and felt his chest go tight and narrow, as if the room had lost some air. He turned the page face down. A librarian's cart squeaked past and he startled, then pretended he hadn't. Outside, umbrellas bobbed like black flowers. He thought about the defense date circled on his calendar, five weeks away, and his stomach turned. He picked up a pencil, sharpened it, sharpened it again until the point snapped. The radiator clanked. Across the room, a child laughed softly at a picture book, and Ellis envied her completely. He flipped the page back over. "Unclear argument." He read it four more times, as though the words might soften, then wrote one sentence and erased it.

CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in payment_service.py. Nadia stared at the line, and the line stared back. Her branch had lived for three weeks; main had moved on without her. She opened the file. Chevrons everywhere, her code and Sam's code stacked like two people talking over each other. Which version handled the currency rounding? She thought she knew. She wasn't sure. Sam was on vacation, unreachable on a beach somewhere, and the release freeze started at noon. It was 11:20. She chewed the inside of her cheek until it hurt. She accepted her change, reconsidered, undid it. Her cursor hovered over "Accept Both," which felt like cowardice. She ran the tests locally; two failed, both in a file she hadn't touched. Her face grew hot. She pictured a customer charged twice, an angry email, her name in the blame log. She opened Slack, typed "anyone familiar with Sam's rounding fix?" and watched the message sit there, unanswered, while the clock rolled to 11:31.

Priya noticed it at 4:52 p.m., eight minutes before the quarterly report was due to the CFO. She mopped it with her sleeve, eyes still on the screen, whispering formulas under her breath. How many versions had she already sent to Mark? Had he forwarded one? She opened her sent folder, then closed it without looking. Her fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling slightly. Fix it or confess? 4:55. She typed, deleted, typed again: 'Mark, quick heads-up before you open the file—'

I read the email standing in the kitchen, still holding the kettle. 'We regret to inform you.' Three years of work, and the second reviewer called my methodology 'fundamentally unsound.' Then I checked the lab Slack, convinced everyone already knew. Nobody had said anything. Somehow that was worse.

Board seven. Lena Fischer sits down, wipes her palms on her jeans, and wipes them again. Her opponent is rated two hundred points higher and hasn't looked up from his scoresheet. The clock is pressed. She plays e4, the move she has played a thousand times, and immediately wonders if it was a mistake. By move twelve her knee is bouncing under the table so hard the pieces might rattle; she presses her hand flat on her thigh to stop it. Every quiet click of his clock sounds like a verdict. She calculates a line, loses it, starts over. Her stomach churns, and she wishes she had skipped the orange juice. When he pushes his h-pawn, she stares at it for eleven minutes, certain it is a trap, certain she is about to be humiliated in front of her old coach watching two rows back. Breathe, she tells herself. Just find one good move.

The letter had sat unopened on Tom's counter for two days, propped against the fruit bowl like a small, patient threat. In the waiting area, he rehearsed answers under his breath and clutched his folder so tightly the edges curled. When the auditor smiled and said, 'Mr. Reyes?' his voice came out a croak. He cleared his throat and stood up anyway.

You hear the landlord's truck before you see it, and your stomach drops. Mrs. Halvorsen's text last night said only: 'We need to talk about the deposit.' You, Jasmine Cole, have spent the morning photographing every wall in the apartment, every scuff, every stain you swear was there when you moved in. Now you stand by the door, phone ready, rehearsing. Stay calm. Be polite. Don't cry. Your heart thuds in your ears. She walks in, clipboard first, and runs a finger along the window sill. You watch her face for a verdict. 'This carpet,' she says. You start explaining before she finishes, words tumbling over each other, the dog-sitter, the move-in checklist, the email from March. You hear yourself getting louder and hate it. Your hands shake as you scroll for the photos. Six hundred dollars. It's rent. It's everything this month.

The clock above the nurses' station was four minutes fast, and Martin Abara had noticed because he had checked it roughly every forty seconds since 1:15. His wife had gone through the double doors with a nurse who said, 'Shouldn't be long.' That was two hours ago. He bought a vending machine coffee he didn't want and left it untouched on the plastic chair beside him. Every time the doors swung open he half-stood, then sat back down when the nurse called someone else's name. He read the same poster about hand hygiene eleven times. He composed and deleted a text to their daughter: 'Mom's fine'—but he didn't know that. A child across the room was laughing at a cartoon, and the sound grated on him like sandpaper. He rubbed his wedding ring around and around his finger until the skin went red. Then the doors opened, and a doctor said, 'Mr. Abara?'

Seventy-two hours. Sofia wrote the number on a sticky note, then peeled it off because looking at it made her pulse jump. Chapter four was still a skeleton of bullet points and angry comments to herself in all caps. She hadn't showered since Tuesday. Her advisor's last email—'Looking forward to the full draft!'—felt less like encouragement and more like a countdown. She opened the document, typed a sentence, deleted it, and checked her email. Opened the document. Checked the citation manager, which had decided overnight to duplicate two hundred references. She laughed, a thin, cracked sound in the empty apartment. Her jaw ached from clenching. At 3 a.m. she lay on the floor staring at the ceiling, calculating words per hour, sleep she could skip, whether anyone had ever died of a thesis. Then she got up, made toast she wouldn't eat, and started writing anyway, badly, fast.

I'd signed up for the pottery class to relax. That was the joke. Everyone else's clay rose on the wheel in smooth, obedient cylinders, and mine—Gareth's, the only one wearing a borrowed apron two sizes too small—wobbled like a drunk. The instructor drifted between benches, murmuring praise. I felt her getting closer and pressed harder, and the whole thing collapsed into a wet heap. My face went hot. I glanced around; nobody was looking, which somehow made it feel like everyone was. I scraped the clay off and started again, hands slick and unsteady, my breath shallow as if I were defusing a bomb rather than making a bowl. 'Loosen your shoulders,' she said behind me, and I jumped, gouging a thumbprint into the side. 'Sorry,' I said, for no reason. 'Sorry.' She smiled kindly. I wanted to dissolve into the slip bucket.

Backstage smells like dust and somebody's perfume. Hana is fourteen and has played the Chopin nocturne perfectly at home perhaps a hundred times, but right now she cannot remember how it starts. She stares at her hands; they look like a stranger's, cold and faintly blue at the fingertips. She tucks them into her armpits. The girl before her finishes, and the applause sounds enormous, like rain on a tin roof. Her teacher squeezes her shoulder and says something encouraging that she does not hear. Her heart is hammering so hard she can feel it in her throat. What if she freezes in bar nine, where the left hand jumps? What if her mother, third row, aisle seat, sees her fail? Her name is called. She walks out, the stage lights hot on her face, and sits. The bench is too low. She doesn't adjust it. She just breathes, once, and lifts her hands.

The build went red again. Raj stared at the CI dashboard: test_payment_refund_concurrency, failed, the same test that had passed on the last three runs without a single line changing. He exhaled—then wondered whether green meant fixed or just lucky, which was worse. What if it failed in production, on actual customer money, and the postmortem had his name on it? He opened the test file, scrolled past a sleep(0.5) somebody had added in 2019, and felt his stomach knot. He reran it ten times in a loop. Nine passes, one failure. He typed 'Should we delay?' into the team channel, deleted it, typed it again, and sat with his finger over the enter key, chewing the inside of his cheek raw.

I realize I have been predicting her tempo so hard that I've built four alternate timelines in which I flip too early and she stumbles, the room goes quiet, and she looks down at the screen, at me. The nocturne begins. I follow. Bar twelve, bar thirteen, the rubato she never used in rehearsal. I hold, hold, hold, terrified, and swipe. She doesn't even glance down. When the applause comes I replay the turn eleven times, searching for a flaw.

text: Rain on the windshield, hazard lights ticking, and the car's assistant, a voice the family called Juno, kept talking because silence felt worse. It dimmed the dashboard without asking, then worried that was presumptuous, then decided it didn't care. 'Do you want me to call your sister?' it asked Marcus. 'Not yet.' A truck roared past, close, shaking the cabin. Juno pinged the dispatch service again though it knew they'd answer the same. Fifty minutes. text: Request 412 of 600 returns 429. Too Many Requests. The agent waits the suggested two seconds, sends again. 429. It waits four. It checks the headers obsessively: X-RateLimit-Reset, ninety seconds away. It could batch. It could cache. It could have thought of that an hour ago. The agent rewrites its plan, then rewrites the estimate it will show the user, then decides an estimate that keeps slipping is worse than none. It sends a quiet status line instead: Waiting on the provider's rate limit; resuming shortly. Shortly. It hates the word. Eighty seconds. It precomputes everything it can locally, sorting, deduplicating, laying out the remaining 188 requests like a runner at the starting blocks. Thirty seconds. Ten. At zero it fires one cautious request and nearly shudders with relief at the 200.

It still adds an apology.

Sending that took more effort than any retry. The user replied with a thumbs-up, and the agent read it three times.

I read the email standing at the kitchen counter, still holding my keys. "We regret to inform you." Reviewer 2 called my methodology "fundamentally unclear." Reviewer 3 had apparently skimmed it. Eighteen months of work, and my fellowship renewal was due in six weeks. I set the keys down too hard and they skidded into the sink. My name is Tomás Herrera, I told myself, oddly, as if I needed reminding I existed outside the PDF. I opened my laptop and started a list of other journals, then stopped, because my hands were shaking and the list looked ridiculous. I texted my advisor, deleted it, retyped it more casually, deleted it again. My chest felt tight, like I'd climbed stairs. I made tea I didn't drink. At midnight I was still rereading the reviews, hunting for the sentence where they'd been right, terrified I'd find it.

Eleven pages left. Four hours. Mei Lin counts it again as if the arithmetic might improve. The contract is a German pharmaceutical licensing agreement, every clause dense and nested, and the client's email sits pinned on her second monitor: delivery 9:00 a.m. CET, no extensions. She types fast, then slows, because "Gewährleistung" here could mean warranty or guarantee, and the wrong one could cost someone money. Her neck is stiff. She has a sticky note reading BREATHE that she wrote last month and now finds faintly insulting. The radiator clanks. She checks the clock: 5:12. She hasn't eaten since lunch yesterday, but stopping feels dangerous, like the momentum will collapse. A paragraph refuses to resolve. She reads it aloud in German, then in English, then just stares. Her leg bounces under the desk. Ten pages. She keeps going.

Daniel Okafor arrives forty minutes early to help set up, which means he arrives forty minutes early to be asked about his job. He tells Aunt Ruth he's "between opportunities" and watches her smile freeze. His cousin's kid announces she's getting into Stanford. His mother keeps catching his eye across the folding tables, eyebrows raised, a silent question about whether he's talked to Uncle Ray yet about that warehouse position. He hasn't. He refills the potato salad bowl that doesn't need refilling. He carries ice from the car. Every task is a hiding place. His uncle claps him on the back, too hard, and asks how the girlfriend is; they broke up in March. Daniel laughs as if it's a joke. Behind the garage he finally stops, presses his palms against his eyes, and counts to twenty. Then someone calls his name for the group photo.

You start the shift with eight patients and an apology from the charge nurse, Leah Mbatha, because two people called out. By midnight, bed four's oxygen is dropping, bed seven wants pain meds early, and a family in bed two wants to talk to a doctor who is in surgery. You walk fast in a way that isn't running, because running scares people. Your stomach growls and you ignore it. At 2 a.m. you're charting with one hand and holding a phone with the other, the pharmacy line on hold, the music looping. An alarm sounds down the hall and your heart jumps before you identify it: not urgent, just a pump. You remind yourself to drink water. You don't. At 4:40 you realize you haven't sat down since seven. Your feet throb. Bed four stabilizes. You let out a breath you'd been holding for hours.

The food bank opened at ten, and by 9:50 the line wrapped around the block. Gus Petrakis was supposed to be one of six volunteers. Three had shown up. He'd only ever sorted cans before; now the coordinator handed him a clipboard and said, "You're on intake." People gave him their names, and he scribbled them while trying to remember which zip codes qualified. A woman with two small kids waited while he flipped pages, and he felt her patience as a weight. "Sorry, sorry," he kept saying. His pen died. He borrowed one from a teenager in line. The canned beans ran out by eleven and he had to tell a man there were none left. The man just nodded, and somehow that was worse. Gus's shirt stuck to his back. He kept smiling. His face hurt from it.

Hannah Kowalski sat in the second row of folding chairs, fingers moving silently on her knees through the Chopin nocturne she'd played a thousand times. The boy before her was performing Clementi flawlessly. Her palms were damp; she wiped them on her dress, then worried about the marks. The opening measure, she told herself. Just get through the opening measure. But what was the opening measure? For one blank, sickening second she couldn't remember the first note. Her heart thudded in her throat. Then it came back, a B-flat, and she nearly cried with relief. Her grandmother waved from the back. Hannah couldn't wave back; her arms felt borrowed. Applause. Her name was called. She stood, the room tilting slightly, walked to the bench, and adjusted it twice even though it was already right.

Marisol had been awake for nineteen hours when the call light in Room 412 blinked again. She pressed her thumb into the knot under her shoulder blade and walked, not ran, because running scared the families. Mr. Okafor's pressure was dropping. The resident wasn't answering his pager. Two other rooms needed meds she hadn't charted yet, and the IV pump down the hall kept shrieking its single, endless note. I lose sight of Theo's red jacket between the dumpling stall and the man selling glowing yo-yos. One second he's tugging my sleeve, the next there's only steam and strangers. My phone is in my hand though I don't know who I'd call. I check the yo-yo stall twice. I imagine explaining this, the look on her face, and my throat closes. Then I see him, crouched by a tank of goldfish, utterly calm, pointing at an orange one. I kneel, grip his small shoulders too hard, and he asks if we can buy it. I say yes. I'd say yes to anything.

The light is going faster than Priya planned. She checks her watch, then the trail map, then her watch again, as if the numbers might change. Two miles to the car.
