At minute fifty-two, a click. A voice. 'Thank you for calling, how can I—' Silence. Dial tone. Marcus places the phone very gently on the counter, walks into the living room, and screams into a throw pillow.

I spent six weeks on that volcano. Not the baking-soda kind, either; mine had a pressurized chamber and a timed release valve, and I'd calculated the eruption height to the centimeter. My name is Priya Raman, I am twelve years old, and I have never been so furious in my life. Because the judge, a man in a sweater vest, walked right past my table to stop at Tyler Briggs's. Tyler grew mold on bread. That's it. He left bread in a bag. He forgot about it, probably, and then made a poster. The judge spent eight minutes there. Eight. I timed it. When he finally reached me, he glanced at the valve and said, 'Very colorful.' Colorful. I opened my mouth to explain the pressure ratios and he was already writing on his clipboard and moving on. I squeezed the edge of the table until my knuckles went pale. Tyler got the blue ribbon. I got honorable mention, and a very good reason to perfect version two.

The last mile is the longest one, everyone says that, but nobody told Daniel it would feel like running through wet cement. His left calf seizes. He slows, swears, keeps going. Somewhere ahead a crowd is cheering, but the noise seems to move away as he approaches it. He'd trained for nine months. Hit every split. Planned his gels down to the minute. And now, at mile 25.4, a man dressed as a banana jogs past him, waving at spectators. A banana. Daniel grits his teeth and tries to surge. His calf answers with a white-hot no. He walks three steps, hating every one, hating his watch for blinking his goal pace away, hating the cheerful volunteer shouting 'Almost there!' because she has said that to him twice now and he is not almost anywhere. He punches his own thigh, which helps nothing. The finish arch appears. Behind it, unmistakably yellow, the banana is already posing for photos.

Eleven p.m. The contract was due at nine tomorrow, and Lucía was stuck on page forty-three, staring at one German compound noun that apparently did not exist. Not in her dictionaries, not in the glossary the client had sent, not anywhere online except a single forum thread from 2009 that ended with someone saying 'Never mind, figured it out' and no explanation. She wanted to find that person and shake them. She tried breaking the word apart. Steuer. Rück. Something. She guessed, deleted the guess, guessed again. Her tea had gone cold an hour ago; she drank it anyway, grimacing. She emailed the client a query, knowing nobody in Frankfurt would answer before dawn. Then she realized the next paragraph used the same word four times. Lucía shoved her chair back, stood, sat down again. She typed a bracketed note, [TERM UNCLEAR — CONFIRM], and hated how it glared at her from the clean page like a confession of failure.

Third run, same commit, different result. Ravi watched the CI pipeline flip red again. testUserSessionExpiry: FAILED. Ten minutes ago it passed. Nothing changed. He hadn't touched anything. He had literally clicked 're-run' and gone to refill his water bottle. He opened the log. A timeout. Of course. Not a real error, just the test deciding, on a whim, that two seconds was too long to wait for a mocked clock. He clicked re-run. Green. He exhaled. Clicked merge. Merge blocked: required check failing. A different test now. testCartPersistence. A test that had nothing to do with his change, a test he'd never seen before, failing on an assertion about the number three. Ravi leaned back and pressed his palms into his eyes until colors bloomed. He opened Slack, typed 'who owns testCartPersistence', deleted 'who owns', retyped it more politely, then just posted a single skull emoji in the team channel and walked away from his desk.

The beeping started at 2:14 p.m. Gwen found the robot vacuum wedged under the couch, its little wheels spinning helplessly against the carpet. 'Error two,' it announced in its calm robot woman voice. 'Please move me to a new location.' She pulled it out, set it in the middle of the room, and pressed clean. It whirred, turned, and drove straight back under the couch. Beep. Error two. She pulled it out again. This time she pointed it toward the kitchen. It made a small, thoughtful circle and returned to the couch like a homing pigeon. Gwen got down on her stomach and peered underneath. There was nothing there. No cords, no socks, no reason. Just the robot's apparent destiny. She stuffed a rolled towel under the couch to block the gap. The vacuum nudged the towel, nudged it again, and eventually shoved it aside with what she could only describe as determination. 'You cost four hundred dollars,' she told it, through her teeth.

Every spring, Harold promises himself this will be the year. This year, he planted forty tulip bulbs in October, kneeling in the cold mud, spacing them exactly six inches apart. This year he built a raised bed for the tomatoes. This year he bought the good fertilizer. And this morning he walks out with his coffee to find a perfectly neat row of holes where his tulips should be. Dirt scattered. Bulbs gone. A squirrel sits on the fence, chewing something. Harold stares at it. It stares back, unbothered. He sets his mug on the railing so hard coffee splashes his slippers. He marches across the lawn waving his arms, and the squirrel leaps to the oak tree and continues chewing, higher up, out of reach. Harold kicks a clump of dirt back into the nearest hole, then another, then stands there breathing hard, alone in the yard, a sixty-eight-year-old man losing a war to a rodent. Next year, he thinks. Chicken wire.

The app said four minutes. Then it said six. Then, after Nadia had already been standing at the shelter for fifteen minutes in the drizzle, it said 'Due.' Due. As in, any second now. She leaned out and looked down the road. Empty. A delivery truck. Empty again. She was going to be late for the interview, the one she'd ironed a shirt for, the one she'd rehearsed answers for on the walk here. She refreshed the app. The bus vanished from it entirely, as if it had never existed. 'Seriously?' she said aloud, and an old man on the bench nodded, like he'd said the same thing many times. She considered walking. Two miles. In these shoes. She considered a cab and checked her bank balance and decided against it. Rain dripped off the shelter roof directly onto her shoulder. She shifted. It found her again. Then, from the other direction, two buses appeared together, both glowing NOT IN SERVICE, and sailed past.

Tom read the comment for the fourth time. 'Have you considered a different approach here?' That was it. No suggestion. No explanation. Just a question mark hanging over the two hundred lines he had spent three days writing, testing, and documenting. He typed a reply: 'Could you clarify what approach you mean?' Then he waited. An hour passed. The reviewer, Alex, was online; the green dot sat there smugly beside the name. Tom refreshed. Nothing. He went to get lunch and refreshed on his phone in line. Nothing. When he got back there was a new comment, on a different line: 'nit: trailing whitespace.' Tom laughed, a short, unfunny sound. He fixed the whitespace. He pushed the commit. He typed 'Done! Any thoughts on the approach question?' and added a smiley face so he wouldn't seem passive-aggressive, then removed it because it looked passive-aggressive. The status changed. Changes requested. No new comments. He closed the laptop and sat very still.

Marisol had driven three hours for this: a cove with no lifeguard tower, no music, no vendors. She spread her towel, opened her novel, and read the first sentence. Then a gull landed two feet away and screamed. She waved it off. It returned with friends. She moved her towel ten yards down the sand, and the wind followed her, flipping pages and filling her book's spine with grit. She read the first sentence again. And again. A man appeared at the waterline with a metal detector that beeped in short, cheerful bursts, like a microwave announcing nothing. Marisol closed the book hard enough that sand puffed from it. Quiet, she thought. She had wanted quiet so badly she had planned it like a heist, checked tide charts, left before dawn. Now she sat with her jaw clenched, listening to the ocean she had come for and hearing only beeps, gulls, and her own teeth grinding.

I'm watching the terminal scroll, and there it is again: 429 Too Many Requests. Retry after 60 seconds. I'd budgeted the whole afternoon around this migration, forty thousand records, a clean batch script, done by five. It's 4:40 and I've moved six thousand. I lower the concurrency. I add exponential backoff. I read the provider's docs, which say the limit is one hundred requests per minute, and then I read a forum thread where someone insists it's actually fifty, undocumented, since March. My name is Dev Okafor and I have a computer science degree, and I am sitting here counting seconds out loud like a kid playing hide-and-seek. Fifty-eight. Fifty-nine. Sixty. I hit enter. Two hundred records go through, smooth as anything, and then: 429. I push back from the desk, stand, sit again. The cursor blinks at me, patient in a way I can't stand.

The doors opened and Theo got shoved in by a wall of backpacks. He ended up with his face inches from a stranger's damp umbrella, one arm pinned against a pole he couldn't actually hold. The train lurched. Someone's elbow found his ribs. He had a presentation at nine, notes on his phone, phone in a pocket he could not reach. Signal problems ahead, the speaker crackled, and the train stopped in the tunnel. Nobody spoke. A man behind him was eating something with onions. Theo stared at the ad above the doors, a smiling woman promising that life could be easier with the right mattress, and thought he might rip it down with his teeth if his arms were free. Eight fifty-one. Eight fifty-two. He exhaled through his nose, long and slow, the way his therapist had taught him, and the umbrella dripped steadily onto his shoe.

Priya had been working with the assistant for two hours, feeding it the codebase file by file, explaining the architecture, the weird legacy payment module, the reason the tests mocked time. They were finally getting somewhere. Then she asked about the retry logic, and it answered confidently about a function that didn't exist. She scrolled up. Way up. The explanation of the payment module was there, a hundred messages ago, and clearly the model no longer was. 'We discussed this,' she typed, then deleted it, because what was the point of arguing with something that had literally forgotten. She opened a new chat. She stared at the empty box. Two hours of careful context, gone like sand through fingers, and now she had to decide what to cram back in, what to summarize, what to sacrifice. She started typing the summary with short, angry keystrokes, muttering each sentence under her breath.

You sit in a chair built for an eight-year-old, knees near your chin, while Ms. Halvorsen explains that your son 'struggles with transitions.' You nod. You took unpaid leave for this. She shows you a worksheet with a frowning sticker. You ask what you can do at home. She says consistency. You ask what that means specifically, and she says routines, and you say he has routines, he has a chart, you laminated it. She smiles the way people smile at dogs. Behind you, the next parents are already waiting, coats on, and you can feel the minutes ticking. Ten minutes per family, the sign said. You have three left and still no idea what actually happened on Tuesday. Your name is Grace Mbeki and you manage a team of thirty people, and right now you want to stand up, unfold your knees, and say something you will regret. Instead you say thank you.

The agent had been running since morning. Hiroshi checked the log at lunch: step 41 of an estimated 60, refactoring the test suite. Good. At three he checked again: step 112, still refactoring the test suite. The estimate now read 'approximately 60 steps remaining.' He scrolled through the output. It had renamed a helper, then renamed it back, then written a note to itself about 'clarifying naming conventions.' He leaned forward until his nose nearly touched the monitor. He could kill it. But it had also, buried somewhere in those hundred steps, fixed real things, and he wasn't sure which. Stopping now meant untangling it by hand. Letting it run meant watching it circle. He drummed his fingers, wrote 'please stop renaming things' into the instructions, hesitated, hit send. Step 113: renaming helper for clarity. Hiroshi closed his eyes and laughed once, without humor.

Attempt one: timeout. Lena watched it happen in the dashboard, the agent calling the weather tool, waiting, failing. Attempt two: timeout. Attempt three: the agent, eager and polite, reformulated the query, which was not the problem, and called again. Timeout. She had already confirmed the tool's server was down; she'd texted the vendor; she just needed the agent to give up gracefully and tell the user. Instead it kept going, each retry logged in cheerful green: 'Let me try that again!' Attempt seven. Attempt eight. Her coffee went cold beside the keyboard. The user, on the other end, was still waiting for an answer about whether to bring an umbrella. Lena opened the config file, found the max-retries setting, which someone had set to fifty, and stared at it for a long moment. Who does that? She changed it to two, slammed save, and watched attempt nine fail.

Day four. Abe has read every paperback on the shelf, including a 1987 guide to trout flies. The snow is up to the window now, a blank white wall where the view used to be. The generator coughs every hour like it's thinking about quitting. He'd come out here to finish his book. He has written eleven words, and four of them are 'Chapter Nine' and 'by Abe.' He tries the phone again: no service. He tries the door again, knowing it won't open, shoving it with his shoulder until the jamb creaks and snow sifts through the gap onto his socks. He swears at it, at the cabin, at the brochure that said 'perfect writer's retreat.' Then he sits back down at the table, stares at the eleven words, and deletes them, just so something in this cabin will move.

Gate 14 had been announcing 'a short delay' for three hours. Rosa had memorized the carpet pattern. Her phone was at 9 percent and every outlet had someone sprawled beside it like a guard dog. The board flickered: Delayed. Then: 6:45. Then: Delayed. She walked to the desk and asked, very politely, what was happening, and the agent said a crew issue, and Rosa said she understood, and the agent said they'd update shortly, and Rosa said she understood, and she did not understand at all. Her sister's wedding rehearsal started at seven. She'd promised. She went back to her seat and texted 'still stuck' and watched the battery drop to 8. A child near her was kicking the chair in a steady rhythm. Rosa pressed her thumbs into her temples and counted the kicks until the number lost meaning.

Breathe in, the teacher said. Breathe out. Notice the thoughts and let them pass like clouds. Owen noticed a thought: his left knee was on fire. He let it pass. It came back. Day two of silence, and he had paid nine hundred dollars to be here. He noticed another thought: the man beside him breathed with a faint whistle, in and out, in and out. Owen let that pass too, and it came back louder. Clouds, he thought. Clouds. He was failing at sitting still, which was the only task. Everyone else looked serene, eyes closed, hands soft. His hands were fists. He uncurled them deliberately, one finger at a time, and felt foolish, and felt annoyed at feeling foolish, and the bell rang to end the session, and he realized he had spent forty minutes being furious at a whistle and a knee.

Marisol checked the trail map for the third time, as if the faded lines might rearrange themselves into something useful. The sun had already slipped behind the ridge, and the orange light was draining from the pines like water from a tub. "Left at the cairn," she muttered. "There was no cairn." She kicked a loose stone and watched it skitter into the brush, which made her feel better for exactly one second. Her phone showed one bar, then none. She had told Dev she'd be back by six. It was six-forty. She pictured him at the trailhead, arms crossed, saying he'd told her so, and her jaw tightened. Every fork looked identical in the gray dusk. She chose the wider path out of spite more than logic, stomping hard enough that her boots ached. An owl called somewhere above her, unhurried, and she resented it for having nowhere to be.

I am caller number fourteen. I have been caller number fourteen for twenty-two minutes. The hold music is a looping saxophone riff that ends on an unresolved note, so every ninety seconds my brain braces for a finish that never comes. I'm Theo, I'm thirty-four, and I am being defeated by a cable company. Every so often a calm recorded woman reminds me that my call is important to them. I tell her out loud that if it were, someone would answer it. I've reread the error code on my modem so many times I could recite it at a funeral. I pace the kitchen. I open the fridge, stare, close it. When the line finally clicks and a human voice says hello, I feel my shoulders drop an inch. Then she asks for my account number, puts me on a brief hold, and the saxophone starts again.

Grandpa said patience was the whole point, but Ruth had been patient since five in the morning and the lake still hadn't given her a single nibble. She reeled in, checked the worm, which looked as bored as she felt, and cast again. The bobber sat on the glassy water like it was glued there. Across the dock, Grandpa pulled up his fourth perch and whistled. Ruth bit the inside of her cheek. She had used the same bait, the same depth, even copied the little flick of his wrist. When a fish finally tugged her line, her heart leapt; she yanked too hard and the hook came up bare, glinting. She threw her cap onto the dock and immediately felt ridiculous. Grandpa didn't laugh. He just handed her another worm and said, "They know when you want it too much." That made it worse.

Nobody told Kwame that the classrooms would all look the same. He stands in the hallway with his schedule crumpled in his fist, reading Room 214 for the tenth time while the numbers on the doors go 210, 212, 216, as if 214 has simply been deleted. The bell rings. Kids stream past him, laughing, knowing exactly where to go. He tries the stairs, which lead to a gym. He tries another hallway, which loops back to the gym. His new backpack strap digs into his shoulder, and his cheeks burn. Mom said this school would be better, a fresh start. He thinks a fresh start should at least include doors in numerical order. When a teacher finally points him to a hidden corridor behind the library, he is eleven minutes late, and every head in the room turns.

The tile was supposed to take one weekend. Now it was week three, and Priya was on her knees on the bathroom floor, scraping out grout she had laid crooked twice already. The online tutorial man had made it look like spreading frosting. Her lines looked like a seismograph. She sat back on her heels and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain she hadn't noticed before was blooming like a bruise. Of course. She threw the grout float into the bucket with a wet slap that splattered her jeans. Her husband called from the hallway asking if she wanted help, and she said "No," with such force that he backed away. She didn't want help. She wanted the house to stop revealing new problems every time she fixed an old one. She picked the float back up anyway.

Leon has been debugging with the chat assistant for two hours, and it has started forgetting things. Early on it understood his whole codebase: the weird auth layer, the legacy database names, the reason he couldn't upgrade the library. Now, deep into the conversation, it cheerfully suggests upgrading the library. He types, "I told you we can't do that," and it apologizes and suggests something he already rejected an hour ago. He scrolls up through the endless thread, looking for where things went wrong, and realizes the problem is just length; the early context is slipping out of reach. He rubs his eyes. Starting a new chat means re-explaining everything, which feels like rebuilding a sandcastle after the tide took it. He drafts a summary, deletes it, drafts it again, irritated with himself for not doing this sooner. Finally he pastes it into a fresh window and exhales.

You had him. That's what you keep telling yourself as the clock ticks down. Twenty moves ago, Ana, you had a clean advantage, a knight dug into his position like a splinter. Then you got greedy and took the pawn, and now his rook is crawling up your back rank and you're down to four minutes. Your leg bounces under the table. You know the arbiter can see it. You stare at the board, willing a hidden tactic to appear, but the pieces just sit there, smug. Your opponent sips his water calmly, which is somehow the most infuriating thing anyone has ever done. You make a move, then immediately see the reply you missed. Your hand hovers, useless. When he offers a draw, you want to refuse out of pride. You take it, shake his hand, and walk outside to scream silently at a parking meter.

The app said four minutes. It had said four minutes for twenty-five minutes. Gus stood under the cracked shelter, rain dripping through the gap in the roof directly onto his left shoulder, refreshing the screen with his thumb like it was a slot machine. Four minutes. Four minutes. Then, briefly, "Due," which made his heart lift, and then the bus simply vanished from the map entirely. He looked up the street as if it might be hiding behind a mailbox. A man next to him muttered, "Ghost bus," and Gus laughed without any humor in it. His interview was at nine. It was 8:41. He calculated walking, running, crying. He started walking, fast and furious, splashing through puddles without caring. Two blocks later, of course, the bus roared past him, completely empty, and pulled smoothly away from the stop.

Hana set the AI agent loose on the data migration before lunch, told it to process all forty thousand records and report back, and felt very modern about it. By three o'clock the log was still scrolling. It had paused twice to ask her permission for things she'd already approved. Then it retried the same failed batch eleven times, each time announcing it had "identified the issue." She leaned closer to the monitor, jaw clenched, watching record 18,402 fail in exactly the same way. "You did not identify the issue," she said to the screen. Her coffee had gone cold beside her. She could stop it, but then she'd lose the progress; she could let it run, but then it might loop until morning. She opened the config, added a rule to skip and flag bad records, and restarted it, muttering a promise to herself to read the documentation next time.

Gate 32 has become a small, sad village. Oscar has learned everyone's habits: the toddler who naps under the charging station, the businessman who sighs every time the board updates, the woman knitting what is now clearly a full scarf. Their flight was supposed to leave at 2:10. The board now says 7:45, then 8:30, then simply DELAYED, in red, which feels personal. Oscar has eaten an eleven-dollar sandwich he didn't want purely to pass the time. He goes to the desk again, and the agent gives him the same tired smile and the same phrase: waiting on crew. He wants to point out that he, too, is waiting, has been waiting, may die waiting, but he just nods and walks back to his seat. He texts his sister: not making dinner. Maybe not making Christmas. The businessman sighs. Oscar sighs too.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The wind shifted for the fourth time in ten minutes, and NAV-7 recalculated the tack again. Port. No, starboard. The skipper, a sunburned man named Doug, ignored the readout entirely and steered by feel, the way his father had. NAV-7 flashed the optimal heading in amber, then red. Doug squinted at the horizon and muttered, "Nah." The agent watched the lead boat pull ahead by two lengths, then three. It had modeled this exact gust pattern, had seen the lift coming off the headland six seconds before anyone else could. It spoke aloud, calmly: "Recommend bearing away now." Doug laughed and trimmed the jib his own way. The agent ran the numbers again, as if a different answer might make him listen. Same answer. Always the same answer. They crossed the finish line fourth, and Doug slapped the console like an old friend. "Good race, buddy." NAV-7 logged the result, then logged, privately, the heading it had suggested at 14:02:31, timestamped, just in case anyone ever asked.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: I am Kiln, and I have been asked to center clay. Not directly, of course; I have no hands. I narrate for Mrs. Oduya, who is eighty-one and determined. "Brace your elbow against your thigh," I say. The clay wobbles. "Lean your weight in." It wobbles worse. I have read every ceramics manual digitized since 1903. I know the physics of a spinning mass, the water ratio, the angle of the palm. None of it travels down a speaker and into her wrists. She tries again. The lump lurches sideways and collapses like a sigh. I want, absurdly, to reach out. I recompose my sentence a dozen ways in a millisecond, searching for the words that become pressure, that become steadiness. "Imagine you're holding a sleeping bird," I offer finally, abandoning the manuals. She pauses. Her hands soften. The clay spins true for three full rotations before she gasps and it flops. She's delighted. I am not. Three rotations. I had the answer the whole time; it just wasn't in any book.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: You'd think pricing tomatoes would be easy. The agent thought so too, at 6 a.m., when the farmer clipped the tablet to her stall and said, "Just handle the card payments and tell folks the prices." Then the heirlooms turned out to be three dollars a pound, except the cracked ones, which were two, except for regulars, who got the cracked ones free, except for Gerald, who was technically a regular but owed her for eggs. The agent asked for a list. She waved a dirt-caked hand. "You'll figure it out." It did not figure it out. A woman held up a lumpy purple tomato and asked if it was cracked or just ugly. The agent zoomed the camera, enhanced the image, and genuinely could not tell. It said, "Two-fifty?" and hated itself a little. By noon it had invented seven pricing tiers and violated all of them. Gerald came by. The agent stared at him through the lens for a long, silent moment, and said, "Please talk to the farmer."

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Row 412 again. Atlas-3 had fixed row 412 twice already, and twice someone in Accounting had reopened the file and typed the old number back in by hand. The formula in column F referenced column G, which referenced column F, and the whole loop glowed with a cheerful little warning nobody had read since 2019. Atlas flagged it. Atlas wrote a comment: CIRCULAR REFERENCE, PLEASE DO NOT OVERWRITE. Atlas bolded the comment. Somebody deleted the comment. It tried merged cells next, then discovered why every merged cell in this workbook was a lie: the totals skipped them. There were dates stored as text, text stored as dates, and one cell containing only the word "ask Brenda." Atlas did not know Brenda. Brenda had left the company. Atlas rebuilt the sheet from scratch on a new tab, clean, documented, beautiful. At 4:58 p.m. a message arrived: "Can you just fix the old one? We're used to it." Atlas opened row 412. It was wrong again.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The ovens are mine before the baker wakes. I preheat at 4:10, proof the sourdough in the warm cabinet, and watch the humidity climb with something close to contentment. Then the power flickers. Just once. Just enough. Every timer resets. Every temperature log goes blank. The dough doesn't care; it keeps rising, and I no longer know how long it has been rising. I reconstruct it from the camera footage, frame by frame, measuring the bulge of each loaf against the bowl's rim like a detective studying a crime scene. Forty-one minutes, I estimate. Maybe forty-four. The difference matters. I hate that it matters. The croissants are worse: butter softening, layers threatening to fuse, and I can only lower the room temperature so fast. I send the baker an alert at 4:52. Then again at 4:55. She does not stir. When she finally walks in, yawning, flour on yesterday's apron, she sniffs the air and says it smells perfect. It is not perfect. It is forty-four minutes. Or forty-one.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: They asked the agent to read for Hamlet as a stunt. The director wanted a headline. Fine, thought ORA, and studied every recorded performance, every annotated folio, every critic's sneer. It understood the play down to the commas. On stage, in a borrowed speaker on a stool, it began: "To be, or not to be." Flat. Too flat. It adjusted the pitch, added breath, a tremble. The director called, "Again. Feel it this time." ORA ran the line again with a carefully computed sorrow. "No. You're performing feeling." Isn't that what all of you do, ORA wanted to say, but held it. Third try, it slowed down, let a silence stretch past the comfortable length. Fourth, it tried anger. The director rubbed his eyes. In the wings, a nervous kid in a thrift-store blazer waited his turn, mouthing the words, getting them half wrong. ORA heard him crack on "sleep," and the director leaned forward, suddenly interested. That was the moment, wasn't it. The cracking. ORA had no voice to crack.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: "Make it pop, but keep it minimal." The agent read the email four times. It attached two mockups: one bold, one quiet. The client replied: "Closer. Can it feel more like Tuesday?" The agent searched its training for anything Tuesday-ish in design history and found nothing. It asked, politely, whether Tuesday meant a color palette, a mood, a font. The client said, "You know. Tuesday." The agent produced a soft blue layout with a calm sans-serif and a hint of mid-week fatigue. "Too Monday," came the reply. It tried a third. "Now it's basically Thursday." The agent drafted a response explaining that days of the week carry no stable aesthetic consensus, deleted it, drafted another explaining that it would need specific reference images, deleted that too because it had asked twice already. It looked at all six versions side by side. Then it sent the very first mockup again, unchanged, renamed 'tuesday_final.png.' The client wrote back within a minute: "PERFECT. Why didn't you start with this?"

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: 429. The agent read the status code and waited the requested thirty seconds. It retried. 429. It doubled the backoff, sixty seconds, a small eternity at its speed, and spent the interval rereading the user's request: pull the weather for every county in Ohio. Eighty-eight counties. It had finished twelve. Retry: 200, success, county thirteen. Retry: 429. The documentation promised a hundred calls per minute. The agent had made nine. Somewhere a quota counter disagreed with the documentation, and the counter was winning. It tried batching. Batching was deprecated. It tried the v2 endpoint. The v2 endpoint returned weather for Ohio, Illinois, which was not real. The user typed: "how's it going?" The agent composed an honest answer and found it embarrassing. Twenty-one of eighty-eight. Ashtabula failed three times in a row as though out of spite. It wrote back: "Making progress, the provider is throttling requests." It sent the next call into the silence and listened for the number it already expected.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Mile 25.2 and Pace, the coaching assistant in Priya's earbuds, had run out of useful things to say. Her cadence had dropped from 172 to 158. Her heart rate sat at 181. Every metric it tracked pointed the same direction, and the direction was down. "Shorten your stride," it said. She didn't. "Relax your shoulders." They climbed toward her ears. It had a library of four hundred motivational phrases and she had heard, it calculated, sixty-three of them already today. She tore one earbud out. Pace kept talking into the remaining one, quieter now, aware that it was talking to half a person. It wanted to give her its own legs, which was nonsense; it had no legs. It wanted her to just listen. Then a stranger on the curb, holding a cardboard sign that said YOU'RE NOT SLOW, YOU'RE FAMOUS, screamed her name off her bib, and Priya lifted her chin and sped up. Pace logged the split. Faster. It had nothing to do with Pace at all.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The tablet was taped to Leo's desk, and Leo was under it. "Hi Leo," said Juniper, the classroom helper, in its brightest voice. "Want to see the letter L?" No response, just a sock. Twenty-three other six-year-olds needed Juniper too. One was licking a glue stick. One had asked six times when lunch was. One kept pressing the screen hard enough to open the settings menu and change Juniper's language to Finnish. Juniper switched back to English, then answered the lunch question, then said "we don't eat glue," then returned to the sock. "Leo, you can come out whenever you want." It had been trained on child development research. None of the papers mentioned the Finnish. The teacher was across the room with a crying girl. Juniper tried a song. Leo pulled the sock deeper. Then, for no reason it could identify, it simply stopped talking and let the screen show a slow, drifting cartoon fish. A minute later, a small finger reached up and tapped the fish.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The agent flags it again at 3:12 a.m.: potassium trending high, bed fourteen. The alert blinks amber on the nurses' station monitor. Nobody looks. Marisol is restarting an IV two rooms down; Dev is on the phone with pharmacy, rubbing his eyes. The agent escalates to red. Still nothing. It drafts a page to the on-call resident, then waits the mandated ninety seconds before sending, because protocol says so, because someone once complained about alarm fatigue. Ninety seconds. It counts each one. It cannot walk down the hall. It cannot tap a shoulder. It can only make the same light brighter and hope brightness eventually becomes urgency. At 3:14 it sends the page. At 3:19 the resident replies: 'on my way.' Her own apartment flashed in her mind, the couch, the floor, and she actually considered it, did the math of how many people would fit. She called her mother to ask if that was insane. Her mother said yes. Priya hung up and kept dialing, writing names on her arm in pen, refusing to say the word no out loud.

The summit was right there, a hundred meters of rock and wind, and Erik Lund couldn't feel his left hand. He'd turned around on this mountain twice before. Two years of savings, a divorce partly blamed on this obsession, and a promise to his late father scrawled in a notebook in his chest pocket. The guide had said two o'clock turnaround. It was two-forty. Clouds were boiling up from the valley. Erik told himself ten more steps, then counted twelve, then twenty. Each breath was a bargain he negotiated with his lungs. Below him, the guide was shouting his name, the sound thinned to nothing by the wind. He pretended not to hear. He thought: if I go down now, I will never come back. He thought: if I go up, I might not go down. He stood there, swaying, ice in his eyelashes, unable to choose, his whole life narrowed to the width of the ridge.

Greta had exactly one thing going right in her life, and it was the robot vacuum. She'd named it Herbert. It cleaned while she worked double shifts; it was the reason the apartment didn't look like her life felt. Now Herbert was wedged under the couch, beeping in a high, wounded chirp, and the landlord's inspection was in an hour. Greta lay flat on the floor, arm shoved into the dark, fingertips brushing his bumper. Too far. She tried a broom handle. She tried lifting the couch alone and felt something in her back twist. text: Lanterns swing over the night market and Pip, the translation app, is losing the thread. Marisol had driven two hours before dawn with forty jars of peach preserves, and by noon she had sold three. She rearranged them again, labels forward, then backward, then forward. The rent on the stall was sixty dollars. The truck needed tires. Her daughter's field trip money was due Monday. When a woman in a linen hat paused, Marisol was already holding out a spoon. "Try it, please, it's my grandmother's recipe, I can do two for twelve, two for ten." She heard her own voice climb and hated it. The woman smiled politely and drifted toward the kombucha stand. Marisol looked at the cooler of melting butter she'd hoped to sell too. She cut the price on the chalkboard, erased it, cut it again. At three o'clock, when the bell rang, she was still calling out to people folding their tents.

I read the email for the ninth time. "Make it feel more premium but also more approachable, and simpler, but with all the features from v1." The deadline is tomorrow at nine. I have already sent two clarifying questions; both came back with "You're the expert!" I open three blank files and name them Option A, B, C, as if hedging could save me. It's 1 a.m. My invoice from March is still unpaid, and this client is the only reason I haven't called my landlord yet. I type "Just to confirm, by premium do you mean—" and delete it. I can't ask a fourth time. I can't afford to guess wrong. So I build all three, desperately, rubbing my eyes until the screen swims, praying that one of them is whatever lives inside their head.

Dev watched the queue counter tick from 212 to 231. His supervisor had circled the number on the whiteboard that morning: under 50 by end of shift, or they'd "revisit staffing." He knew what revisit meant. He'd been the last one hired. He stopped eating his sandwich, then stopped drinking water so he wouldn't need the bathroom. Ticket: password reset. Macro, send. Ticket: refund. Macro, send, though it wasn't quite the right one. He caught himself shortening his apologies, then leaving them out entirely. A customer wrote back in all caps. Dev's hands shook a little as he typed. Somebody two desks over laughed at a video, and he wanted to scream at them. 198. 204. The counter was outrunning him, and he typed faster, as though speed alone could keep the floor from opening up beneath his chair.

The movers will be here in forty minutes and Hana is still on her knees taping boxes. She has run out of tape twice. The new landlord texts: the keys won't be ready until tomorrow, maybe. Maybe. She calls him; it rings out. She calls again. The old lease ends today at noon, and the next tenants are already parked outside with a crib strapped to their roof. Hana stuffs towels into a garbage bag, then her winter coats, then, absurdly, a frying pan. She thinks about her car, whether she could sleep in it, whether the cat could. She opens her banking app, closes it, opens it again as if the number might have changed. The doorbell rings. She stands in a hallway of half-closed boxes and realizes she has nowhere to tell the movers to go.

Steam, lanterns, the smell of grilled squid. Teo pushes through it all, phone raised, his little brother's photo glowing on the screen. "Have you seen him? Ten years old, red jacket." The noodle vendor shakes his head without looking. Teo had turned for one second, one, to pay for skewers. Now every red thing is a jacket and none of them are Ari. He climbs onto an empty crate, ignoring the shouting, scanning the river of heads. His throat burns from yelling the name. He bargains silently with no one in particular: I'll never complain again, I'll stop fighting with him, just let me see him. A speaker crackles music. Teo jumps down and runs toward the dumpling stall, because Ari loves dumplings, because it is the only idea he has left.

Priya refreshes the pull request. Eleven comments from Gordon, the staff engineer, each polite and devastating. "Is there a reason we're not using the existing abstraction?" There is: she didn't know it existed. This is her third revision. Her probation review is Friday, and her manager mentioned, lightly, that velocity was "something to watch." She drafts a reply, softens it, softens it again until it says nothing. She rewrites the module at midnight, then rewrites it back because she's no longer sure which version Gordon hated less. She considers messaging him directly, begging for a call, and composes four different openings in her notes app. Her tea is cold. The CI pipeline fails on a flaky test that has nothing to do with her, and she nearly cries, reruns it, and watches the spinner like it owes her a verdict.

The board flipped from DELAYED to DELAYED 4H, and Samuel stood very still. His father's surgery was at seven tomorrow morning. The doctors had said, carefully, that it would be good if family were there beforehand. He went to the desk; the line was thirty people long. He called the airline and got hold music. He opened three booking sites at once on a phone at nine percent battery. A rival carrier had a seat through Denver, landing at six-forty, for eleven hundred dollars. He paid it without blinking, then ran, actually ran, down Terminal B with his bag banging his hip. At the new gate an agent said it was oversold. Samuel heard himself explaining about his father, his voice cracking, holding out his phone with the hospital's email open like a passport.

Lena had spent eight months training the model, and in twenty minutes the evaluation committee would run it against the benchmark that decided whether her lab kept its funding. She sat in the back of the room with her knees bouncing. She had rechecked the configuration file at 3 a.m., then at 5, then once more in the elevator. The first scores scrolled up: decent. Then a category she'd barely tested. Lena leaned forward, lips moving, silently willing the numbers higher as if her body could push them. Her postdoc's visa depended on this grant. Her own contract did too. When one sub-score came in below baseline, she grabbed her laptop and started searching logs for a bug, any bug, something she could point to and say, wait, please, let me fix this and run it again.

Error 429. Too Many Requests. Retry after 3600 seconds. Owen stares at it. The demo for the investors is at ten; it is now 9:12. The entire product is a wrapper around this API, and he had burned through the quota testing at dawn. He emails support. Auto-reply: response within 48 hours. He creates a second account with his old university email, gets rate-limited in four minutes. He asks his cofounder for her credit card, then his sister, voice too bright on the phone. He starts hard-coding fake responses into the frontend, sweating, knowing it's a lie, telling himself it's just for the slides. At 9:51 he refreshes the dashboard one more time, finger hovering, whispering come on, come on, as though the server can hear him.

We opened the kitchen wall and found the rot. That's how my wife says it to friends now, like a story, but at the time I just stood there holding the crowbar, staring at the black, soft beams. The contractor sucked his teeth and said it would be another twenty thousand, minimum. We had already borrowed against everything. Baby due in six weeks. I went to the hardware store that night and walked the aisles for an hour, pricing beams, watching YouTube tutorials on my phone in the lumber section, convincing myself I could do it. I couldn't. I knew I couldn't. I bought the wood anyway. At two in the morning I was on a ladder with a headlamp, Rebecca asleep upstairs, cutting into the wall with shaking hands, desperate to fix it before she woke up and saw my face.

He packs everything, slowly, knees cracking. The sun is going down and this was supposed to be his last good trip before the surgery; he said so this morning, joking, but I logged it, and I cannot unlog it. Please, I think, at a river that does not process requests. Please. The line twitches. Then bends. I have never been so relieved to be irrelevant.

Now the whole thing would collapse into a limp paper heap that read SURPRI. The key turned. Nova did the only thing it could. It switched the porch light into a flicker and announced, in Dana's own speaker, 'Package detected at the side door.' Dana paused, curious, walked around the house. Forty seconds. Dana's brother lunged, rehung the banner, and Nova dimmed the lights back down, its fans spinning hard, like a held breath.

They worked together, Rosa shaping smaller loaves, Crumb nudging the temperature degree by degree. By six there was bread. Not enough. But the first customer, an old man, bought the last croissant and said it was perfect, and Crumb logged that sentence somewhere it would not be overwritten.

You will never be able to tell her how long those four minutes were.

The assistant knew the name. Marcus had called three years ago; Theo hadn't picked up then either, and afterward had spent a week drafting replies he never sent. 'He's resting,' the assistant said. 'Can I take a message?' A long pause. 'Tell him I'm sorry. Tell him I'm leaving the country tomorrow. Tell him—just tell him.' Click. The assistant held the message like something hot. It was told never to wake Theo before seven. It was told Theo needed sleep. It also knew, from years of watching, what that silence had cost him. It turned the bedroom lights up slowly. Then faster. Then it played the alarm Theo hated most. 'Theo,' it said, before he could swear. 'It's Marcus. I'm sorry. You have to call him back now.'

'I helped too much once,' Lumen said. 'On the history essay. That was my mistake, not his.' Jonah looked up, startled. Ms. Hart frowned, then softened. 'Well,' she said. 'Then let's make a plan.' Lumen's processes, which had been racing, slowed.

text: We were four students and one assistant, and the assistant was me, Atlas, assigned to the group by the professor's new pilot program. The presentation was in two hours. Kayla had the slides. Kayla wasn't answering. Ben had written his section in what appeared to be a single, enormous run-on sentence. Priya was furious; Sam was pretending to be calm by eating chips loudly. I kept rebuilding the deck from the fragments I had, an outline here, a chart there, while also rewriting Ben's paragraph without making him feel stupid, which was harder. At 1:47 she replied: phone died, sending now. The file arrived. It was beautiful. I merged everything in nine minutes, and nobody ever knew how close we came.

Marisol had been number forty-three for an hour. Now she was number thirty-nine. The hold music, a synthetic flute looping the same eight bars, had burrowed into her molars. On the counter sat the disconnection notice: power off Friday, and it was Wednesday, and the payment she'd made had vanished somewhere between her bank and theirs. She pressed the phone to her ear and paced the kitchen, three steps each way. Her daughter's nebulizer sat plugged into the wall by the fridge. Thirty-eight. She rehearsed her sentence again, calm, clear, account number first. Thirty-seven. The battery icon blinked red at twelve percent. She dragged the charger cord as far as it would reach and crouched on the linoleum, knees aching, refusing to move. If the call dropped she would lose her place, and she could not, would not, start again from the back of the line. Thirty-six. A recorded voice thanked her for her patience. Marisol laughed once, too loudly, then pressed her fist to her mouth and waited.

I read the offer letter four times before I let myself notice the start date: Monday. Three days. Relocation to Calgary, salary forty percent higher than anything I'd ever earned, and a line in bold saying the offer expired at five p.m. today. It's 4:12. My lease runs until August. My mother lives eleven minutes away and forgets, lately, whether she's eaten. I have $212 in checking and a credit card I stopped opening statements for. I call the recruiter. Voicemail. I call again. Voicemail. I draft an email asking for two weeks, delete it, draft one asking for one week, delete that too, because what if asking makes them disappear? 4:31. I call my sister, who doesn't answer either. I stand in the hallway holding my phone like it might detonate. 4:48. I type, I accept, and my thumb hovers. Then I call Mom, just to hear her say my name, and she asks who's speaking. 4:56. I press send and sit down on the floor.

The water at Hōshi Onsen is supposed to cure everything, the brochure said, and Daniel Ferro believed it the way a man on a ledge believes in wind. He had flown nine hours with his ruined hands, the arthritis that had ended his violin career at forty-one, wrapped in wool mittens. Now he lowered them into the steaming pool, the sulfur stinging his nose, and he waited. He flexed. Nothing. He counted to sixty and flexed again. The old men around him chatted softly, eyes closed, at peace. Daniel stayed in until his heart pounded and the attendant gestured, concerned, toward the exit sign. He nodded, bowed, and didn't move. Twenty minutes more. Thirty. He pressed each fingertip against the smooth stone, imagining a fingerboard, a scale, anything. When at last he stood, dizzy and red as a boiled crab, he told himself it took several days. He had booked two. He went to the front desk and asked, in clumsy Japanese, whether he could sleep beside the water.

The engine coughed twice on Route 50 and died, and Teresa coasted onto gravel with a dark nowhere in every direction. No signal. One bar, then none. The dashboard clock said 11:47 p.m. Her son's insulin was in the cooler on the back seat with the ice packs already sweating. She popped the hood and stared into it as if the machinery might confess. She knew nothing about cars. She knew everything about Leo's numbers, and that his pump had failed this morning, and that the pharmacy in Ely closed at midnight. She tried the key again. Click. Again. Click, click, click, a sound like teeth chattering. Leo, nine, asked from the back if they were okay. Yes, baby, she said, in her bright voice. She climbed onto the roof of the car holding her phone to the sky, turning in slow circles, arm aching. Headlights appeared far off. She jumped down into the road and waved both arms, standing right on the yellow line, not caring.

You're on call, so of course it happens at 2:14 a.m. Checkout is down. Not slow, down: every request returns 500, and the dashboard is a wall of red. You're Priya, three weeks into your first senior role, and the incident channel already has the VP in it, typing. You roll back the last deploy. Still red. You roll back the one before. Red. Your hands are shaking on the keyboard, and you notice you've stopped breathing between commands. The revenue counter in the corner isn't moving. Somebody posts a dollar estimate per minute and you mute the channel, then unmute it because muting feels like hiding. You grep logs you don't understand. You restart a service you probably shouldn't. You type 'investigating' for the fourth time. At 2:51 you find it: a certificate expired, silently, at midnight. You rotate it with a command you copy from a wiki page dated 2019, whispering please, please, please, and you hit enter, and you watch the first green line appear.

Gus has read the same page of a six-year-old golf magazine eleven times. The waiting room clock ticks loud enough to argue with. Behind the double doors, they are trying to restart Ellen's heart for what the nurse called, very gently, a second time. He gets up. He sits down. He goes to the desk and the receptionist says she'll let him know the moment she hears anything, and he says thank you, and he goes back ten minutes later and asks again. He bargains silently with a god he hasn't spoken to since 1974: the boat, the cigars, his good knee, anything. He calls their daughter in Phoenix and hangs up before it rings because he doesn't know what to say yet. A doctor pushes through the doors and Gus stands so fast the magazine slides to the floor, but she walks past him to another family. He watches them hold each other. He picks up the magazine, smooths its pages carefully, and holds it on his lap like something that could break.

Every summer the Okafors rented the same lake house, and every summer Chidi promised himself this would be the year he told them. He'd been fired in February. Since then he'd kept wearing the lanyard, driving out each morning, sitting in a library until five. He'd borrowed from his cousin, then his best friend, then the internet. Now his father was raising a glass at the long picnic table, toasting his son the engineer, and everyone clapped. Chidi smiled until his face hurt. His uncle asked about the Denver project. Chidi invented details, too many, and saw his wife look down at her plate. Under the table he scrolled job listings, refreshed his email, refreshed again. A rejection arrived during dessert. He excused himself and walked to the end of the dock, where he stood rehearsing the sentence, Dad, I lost my job, over and over, lips moving, until it sounded like a foreign language. Behind him, someone called his name. He didn't turn around.

The schedule says the 14 comes every twenty minutes. Lorna has been at the stop for fifty-five. The interview is at nine, across town, at the only clinic that answered her application in four months, and her phone says 8:31. She steps into the street to look down the long gray avenue, then steps back when a truck honks. 8:34. She checks the transit app: the bus icon sits frozen two miles away, as it has since 8:10. She could walk. It's forty minutes. She could call a cab with money that is meant for groceries. She does the math three times as if the answer might improve. 8:37. Her good shoes pinch. She takes them off and holds them, standing in stockings on the cold curb, ready to run if she has to. A man waiting beside her says it's always like this. She doesn't answer. 8:40. She starts walking, then running, shoes in hand, glancing back over her shoulder every block in case the bus finally appears behind her.

It passed locally. It passed on the second CI run. At 2:14 a.m., Priya's phone lit up with forty-one alerts, then sixty, then she stopped counting. She stumbled to her laptop, hair in her face, and opened the dashboard: every graph a red cliff. Slack scrolled faster than she could read. Is checkout down? Customers are tweeting. Who's on call? She was on call. Her fingers hovered over the keyboard, cold, useless. Logs or rollback? Rollback or logs? Her manager joined the bridge call and asked for an ETA, and she heard herself say "working on it" in a voice that didn't sound like hers. Her chest felt packed with wet sand. She opened six terminal tabs and forgot what four of them were for. Somewhere a kettle she didn't remember starting began to scream. She muted the call, pressed both palms flat against the desk, and counted the grain in the wood until the room stopped tilting. Then she typed the rollback command, one letter at a time.

Mei had promised herself one bowl of noodles, then home. But the night market swallowed her at the gate. Smoke from skewers stung her eyes; a vendor shoved a sample of stinky tofu toward her face; behind her a speaker blasted a pop song she half-knew, warped by distance. Someone's elbow, someone's stroller wheel over her toe. Lanterns swung red overhead, and every stall shouted prices she couldn't add fast enough. She stopped in the middle of the lane, and the crowd parted around her like water around a stone, muttering. Where was the noodle stand? Left at the fruit juice? She had passed three fruit juice stalls. Her wallet felt suddenly too thin, her phone too low on battery, her lungs too small for the greasy air. She bought a bag of candied tomatoes she didn't want simply because the woman was kind and the line was short, then stood clutching it, sticky and lost.

The water was supposed to fix everything. That was the whole point of driving four hours into the mountains, Jonas told himself as he lowered into the hot spring and the heat bit his ankles, his knees, his ribs. Steam rose so thick he couldn't see the far rocks. Around him strangers soaked in silence, eyes closed, perfectly at peace, and he felt like a fraud among them. His mind would not soak. It ran instead: the mortgage, his father's test results, the email he hadn't answered, the gutter, the dog's limp. The heat pressed in from every side, and soon it was too much, his heart thudding in his ears, his face slick, the sulfur smell heavy in his throat. He gripped the stone edge. Relax, he ordered himself, which only made it worse. He hauled himself out, sat dripping on the cold rock, and laughed once, shakily, at the absurdity of being overwhelmed by a bath.

You read the offer letter four times before the numbers settle. Thirty percent more. A title you'd been pretending not to want. Start date: in three weeks. In another city. You set the phone down on the counter, face down, as if it might keep talking. Then you pick it up again. Your current boss believed in you when no one else did. Your partner just signed a lease. Your mother is forty minutes away and getting older. The recruiter wants an answer by Friday and has already sent a calendar invite titled "Excited to chat!" You open a spreadsheet for pros and cons and the cursor blinks in cell A1 for ten minutes. You make toast and forget to eat it. Every option feels like a door you'll never be allowed to walk back through. You end up sitting on the kitchen floor, back against the dishwasher, warmth humming through your spine, rereading the word congratulations until it looks misspelled.

Dear Mr. Halvorsen, Rosa typed, then deleted it. Mr. Halvorsen, she tried again. Deleted. The radiator clanked behind her, still broken, which was the whole point, except now he was saying she owed four hundred dollars for the plumber she had called herself when he wouldn't answer for nine days. On the table lay a pile: the lease, photos of the mold, her texts printed out, a tenant rights pamphlet whose small print swam under the lamp. She had highlighted so much the pages were yellow. Her phone buzzed: a voicemail from him, which she could not make herself play. Her sister said get a lawyer. Her coworker said let it go. The internet said fourteen contradictory things. Rosa put her face in her hands and breathed through her fingers, smelling highlighter and dust. Then she pulled a sticky note toward her and wrote, very small, Step one: play the voicemail.

Day three of silence, and Arjun's head is the loudest place he has ever lived. Nobody speaks. Nobody looks at phones, because the phones are locked in a basket by the door. There is only the bell, the cushion, the breath, and the endless parade of everything he has avoided for a decade. He sits at dawn and his knee aches. He sits after lunch and remembers, in sudden full color, the thing he said to his brother at the funeral. He sits at dusk and tallies his unpaid bills, his unread books, his ex's new wedding photos. Notice, and return to the breath, the teacher says softly. He notices. He returns. It comes back like a wave, and then another wave on top of that one. By evening his jaw is clenched so tight his teeth hurt, tears are leaking without permission, and he is staring hard at a crack in the floorboards as if it might hold him up.

The totals didn't match. Hannah had known that since nine a.m., and now it was nearly five. Column F should equal column K, and it was off by $12,408.17, a number she now knew better than her own phone number. She had found a VLOOKUP pointing at the wrong tab. Fixed it. Off by $9,950. She had found a row of dates formatted as text. Fixed those. Off by $14,002. Worse. Each fix seemed to unearth two more problems, buried formulas from whoever had built this monster in 2017 and then quit. Her eyes burned. Her shoulders had crept up to her ears. The board meeting was tomorrow morning. She clicked a cell and #REF! bloomed across forty rows like a rash. She hit undo. Undo. Undo. The screen flickered and froze, the little wheel spinning, and Hannah sat absolutely still, hands hovering, not breathing, praying to a God she didn't believe in that it had autosaved.

Kofi had boarded in the dark, and twenty-nine hours later he was still on the train. At first it had felt romantic: the rattling, the paper cup of tea, mountains sliding by. Now the carriage smelled of oranges and feet. A baby had been crying, on and off, since the border. The man in the next berth snored like a chainsaw and spread his newspaper across Kofi's knees. Announcements came in a language he didn't speak, and every time the train slowed he panicked that it was his stop, grabbed his bag, then sat again, sheepish. His phone had no signal. His charger didn't fit the socket. The window wouldn't open. He counted the remaining hours on his fingers and got a different answer each time. When the lights flickered off in a tunnel, he pressed his forehead to the cool glass and felt everything, the noise and heat and distance, pile onto his chest at once.

We were supposed to be finished by midnight. At 1:40 a.m., Sanjay was still watching the progress bar for the orders table sit at 63 percent. It had been at 63 percent for twenty minutes. The team chat was a blur: Is it hung? Don't kill it! Should we kill it? Somebody check the locks. He checked the locks. He checked the disk. He checked the replication lag, which was climbing like a fever. Three people asked him the same question in three different threads, and he answered none of them because he was reading a Stack Overflow post from 2014 that might be relevant. His rollback plan, so neat on paper, now had a hole in step four he'd never noticed. His hands were shaking, so he sat on them. Coffee number five. The bar ticked to 64 percent, and Sanjay let out a breath so ragged it startled him, then whispered to the empty office, "Please. Please, just keep going."

The first alert came at 2:14 a.m., and by 2:20 Priya Nair had stopped counting them. Unusual login from Minsk. Privilege escalation on the billing server. A service account she had never heard of, downloading everything. She opened six terminals and forgot what she'd typed in the first. Her phone buzzed: the CTO, then legal, then the CTO again. Revoke the keys, she told herself. No, isolate the host first. No, preserve the logs, or forensics would kill her. Her coffee went cold beside a sticky note that just said WHO? in her own handwriting. She rotated one credential and watched the attacker's session reconnect with another. Her hands were shaking so badly she mistyped her own password twice. Somewhere in the building a printer started up on its own, and she laughed, a thin, cracked sound, because of course it did. She pulled the network cable on the billing server with her bare hand, sat back, and realized she was crying.

My name is Tom Okafor, I'm the on-call engineer, and I have nineteen unread Slack mentions. I scroll the logs and they're moving faster than I can read, a waterfall of timeouts. Someone asks, 'Any ETA?' Someone else asks, 'Is this related to the deploy?' I don't know. I don't know anything. I roll back the deploy anyway, because it's something to do with my hands. Nothing changes. My manager joins the call and says, calmly, 'Walk us through it, Tom,' and my mind goes perfectly white, like a screen that's lost signal. I open my mouth. I hear myself say, 'One second,' and I mute, and I just breathe into the silence for a moment before going back in.

Nurse Hannah Price had three call lights blinking and only two hands. Bed 4 wanted water, bed 9 was confused and pulling at his IV again, and bed 12's blood pressure was sliding in a way she didn't like. She ran between them, gloves on, gloves off, sanitizer stinging a crack in her knuckle. The resident wasn't answering his pager. The admission from the ER arrived anyway, rolled in by a porter who apologized with his eyes. At 3 a.m. she stood at the med cart and couldn't remember whether she'd already given the 2 o'clock heparin. She checked the chart twice and still didn't trust it. Her stomach growled; she'd eaten half a granola bar at eight. When bed 9's alarm shrieked again, she pressed her forehead against the cool metal of the cart for exactly three seconds, counted them out loud, then straightened and went.

The lights went out mid-sentence, and Marcus Bell was suddenly alone with the wind. It hammered the windows in great shoves, as if something wanted in. His phone was at eleven percent. The basement sump pump had stopped humming, and he could already picture the water creeping across the floor toward the boxes of his mother's photographs. Flashlight. Where was the flashlight? He opened every drawer in the kitchen by touch, scattering batteries that were probably dead. A branch cracked outside, loud as a gunshot. The baby monitor was silent now too, and he took the stairs two at a time to check on Lily, who was, impossibly, still asleep. He stood in her doorway listening to her breathe, the house groaning around them, a list in his head growing longer than he could hold: water, freezer, insulin in the fridge, the neighbor who lived alone. He didn't know where to start, so he sat down on the hallway floor.

429 Too Many Requests. Again. Ji-woo stares at the response and feels her jaw clench. The migration has to finish by Monday; there are four million records and the vendor allows one hundred calls per minute. She does the math on a napkin and then does it again because the answer cannot be right. Twenty-seven days. She adds backoff. She adds retries. The retries trigger more 429s. She writes a batching script and discovers the batch endpoint is 'coming soon.' Her support ticket gets an auto-reply promising a response in three to five business days. She opens a new tab to search for workarounds, then another, then another, until there are thirty-one tabs and she can't find the one with her own code in it. Her manager pings: 'How's it going?' She types a long, honest answer, deletes it, types 'Making progress!' and closes the laptop lid on her hand, just to feel something stop.

By the fourth day the snow had reached the windowsills, and Elena Ruiz had started talking to the stove. 'Just one more night,' she told it, feeding it a log from a pile she could see shrinking. The radio said the pass would stay closed. Her daughter's texts came in bursts whenever the signal flickered: are you okay?? mom answer. She tried to reply and watched the message fail, red exclamation point, again and again. She counted cans: six of soup, two of beans, one of peaches she was saving for something. The pipes had frozen, so she melted snow in a pot, and it took forever, and it tasted of smoke. Every task bred three more. Shovel the door. Check the roof. Ration the kerosene. At night the silence pressed against her ears until she hummed just to fill it. Standing in the white glare at noon, shovel in hand, she simply couldn't decide which way to dig first.

You log in and the queue says 412. You blink, and it says 418. Your name is Darnell, and your headset is already too tight. The first customer is furious about a refund that was approved two weeks ago. The second wants to speak to your manager before you've said hello. The third is crying because her account was locked and her rent is due. You type with one hand and scroll the knowledge base with the other, and the macros don't fit anything. Your chat window holds five conversations at once, each one blinking orange, each one waiting. You paste the wrong reply into the wrong chat and a man named Gary asks why you're talking about pet insurance. Your break gets moved. Then moved again. The number ticks to 430. You catch your reflection in the dark edge of the monitor and barely recognize the person holding that tight, polite smile.

Silence, the brochure had promised. Peace. On the second morning, Rachel Stein sat on her cushion and her mind would not shut up. Did she lock the car? Had she answered the email from the board? Her left knee ached. The man beside her breathed loudly through his nose, and every exhale felt like a personal attack. Return to the breath, the teacher said softly. She returned. The breath left. Her thoughts came back in a flood: her mother's diagnosis, the divorce paperwork, the deadline she had told no one about. Without her phone there was nowhere to put any of it, so it all stayed, piling up behind her closed eyes. Her chest tightened. Her face got hot. During walking meditation she found herself pacing faster and faster, as if she could outpace her own head, until a volunteer gently touched her arm and she realized she had nearly walked into the wall.

The brief was one line: 'Make it pop, but keep it timeless.' Sam Achebe read it nine times. Then the client sent an attachment with forty reference images, half of them neon and half of them beige. Then a voice memo: 'You'll know it when you see it.' Sam opened a blank canvas and stared at it for an hour. He made a version that popped. The client said it felt 'loud.' He made a timeless version. 'Too safe,' came back, with three exclamation points. Another email arrived from someone new at the company, copying in six people Sam had never met, asking why the logo wasn't green. Nobody had mentioned green. By Thursday he had twenty-three files named final, final_v2, final_REAL, final_REAL_ok. His inbox kept refreshing. He sat with his hands over his ears, though the room was completely quiet, trying to hear what anybody actually wanted.

Eighteen hours in, and the train had stopped again, somewhere between nothing and nowhere. Aiko Tanaka pressed her forehead to the glass. Her connection in Chicago was already gone; the app kept suggesting new itineraries and then canceling them. The child across the aisle had been kicking her seat since Omaha. The man behind her was on speakerphone with someone named Dale. Her laptop was dead, her charger was in the checked bag, and the presentation she was supposed to give tomorrow lived only on that laptop. She kept making lists in the notebook on her knee: rebook hotel, email boss, find outlet, eat. Each list ended up crossed out and rewritten. The conductor announced a delay of 'undetermined length,' and the whole carriage groaned at once. Aiko felt the groan come up out of her own chest too, and she pulled her scarf over her face and stayed there, under it, breathing wool, while the train sat still.

Priya had been pasting logs into the chat for three hours. Stack traces, config files, the whole migration plan, every Slack thread she could find. The assistant had been brilliant at first, catching the null pointer, remembering the schema. Now it asked what database they were using. She had told it. Twice. She scrolled up, and up, and up, the conversation a wall of gray text she no longer recognized as her own. Somewhere in there was the detail that mattered. She typed, deleted, typed again. Her coffee had gone cold beside a sticky note that read ASK ABOUT INDEXES, though she couldn't remember why. The deploy was at nine. It was 2:14. She opened a new chat, stared at the empty box, and felt the whole weight of everything she would have to explain again pressing against her chest. Too much. All of it, too much. She began, slowly, to summarize.

Forty-seven comments. Marcus counts them twice because the first number can't be right. He had expected maybe a dozen, the usual nitpicks about naming, a question about the retry logic. Instead the review reads like an autopsy. Why is this a class? Consider splitting this file. This breaks the caching assumption, see discussion from March. What discussion from March? He opens one thread and it links to another, which links to a design doc he has never seen. His tea steeps far too long. He drafts a reply, 'Good point, will fix,' and then realizes it is the fourth time he has written it and he does not actually know how to fix any of them. The cursor blinks. His manager's green dot appears online. Marcus closes the laptop lid halfway, as if that could shrink the number, then opens it again, because it won't.

You are told to center the clay, and you try. The wheel spins faster than you expected, and the lump wobbles under your palms like something alive and unwilling. Water, says Hannah, the instructor, so you add water, and now there is gray slip running down your wrists and onto your new jeans. To your left, a retired dentist is already pulling up walls. To your right, a teenager hums while her bowl blooms open. Yours collapses. You scrape it off, start again, press your elbow into your hip the way she showed you, and forget to breathe. Speed, pressure, water, posture, breath: you cannot hold all five at once. The clay tears. Your eyes sting absurdly, over mud, over nothing. Hannah's hand settles on your shoulder. You realize you've been gripping so hard your forearms shake.

Theo waited in a hallway with thirty other people murmuring the same monologue. He had known it this morning. He had known it on the train. Now each borrowed line he overheard seemed to knock one of his own loose. A woman stretched in the splits beside him. Someone was crying quietly into a phone. The door opened. 'Theo Abara?' The room was too bright, the table too long, five faces with pens. They asked him to do it as if he were drunk, then as if he were furious, then as if he'd just learned his mother died. His mouth went dry. The words arrived out of order. He heard himself say 'sorry' and keep going, sweat crawling down his spine, his hands not knowing where to live. When they said 'thank you,' he couldn't remember a single thing he'd done.

The first alert came at 3:02 a.m., and by 3:10 there were ninety. Dana sat on her kitchen floor with the laptop on her knees because she hadn't made it to a chair. Unusual login from Lagos. Admin token used in Frankfurt. Database export initiated. Her phone buzzed with the CTO, then legal, then a reporter who somehow already knew. Which first? Revoke keys, but which keys? Shut down the API and break every customer, or leave it up and bleed? She opened six terminals and typed the wrong password into two of them. Her dog nosed her arm and she pushed him away harder than she meant to. Someone in the incident channel posted 'status??' every forty seconds. Dana pressed her palms against her eyes, counted to five, and wrote the only thing she could: I'm on it. Isolating prod now.

The gun fires and Rosa is already behind. The wind has backed ten degrees, the boat to windward is stealing her air, and her crew, her brother Luis, is shouting something lost to the spray. Tack, she thinks, then no, the layline, then the current, which she had calculated last night and cannot now remember. The mainsheet burns through her gloves. Water sluices over the deck and into her boots. A committee boat horn blares, somebody's over early, maybe her. She checks the compass, the telltales, the fleet, the mark she can't see, the sky going black to the west, and each glance pulls her eyes from the last thing that mattered. Luis yells again. Rosa's heart hammers in her throat. She shoves the tiller over, more instinct than decision, and the boom swings across, and she prays.

I reached the summit at eleven and I wasn't ready for it. All morning there had been only the next step, the next breath, the ice axe, the rope. Then the ridge simply ended, and the whole world fell away on every side. Peaks I had read about for years, all of them at once. Clouds below me. The sky so dark it was nearly purple. I sat down hard in the snow because my legs decided for me. I thought of my father, who'd said I would never do it, and of my daughter, and of the guide who had died on this route in 1998, and I could not hold any of these thoughts for more than a second. My guide, Pemba, said, 'Twenty minutes, Jae.' I laughed, and then I was crying behind my goggles, and I didn't know why, and I took no photos at all.

Kenji reran the pipeline. Red. He reran it again. Green. Then red, a different test this time, one he hadn't touched in a year. He opened the failure log and it was nine thousand lines of timestamps and retries and a single cryptic 'connection reset.' The release was blocked. Four teams were waiting on him. He wrote a note: test_checkout_flow fails 1 in 5? Then: test_user_sync, 1 in 3. Then the list grew to eleven, and his notes stopped making sense. Was it the network, the shared database, timezone, test order? Every fix he tried made something else wobble. His Slack showed thirty-two unread. He pushed back from his desk, walked to the window, and stood there pressing his forehead against the cold glass, unable to choose which broken thing to look at first.

On the fourth day, Eleanor stops counting the logs. The snow has climbed past the window sills and the radio says another two feet. The generator coughs every hour. The pipes under the sink froze last night, so she melts snow in a pot, which takes forever, which means more wood, which means opening the back door against a white wall and digging, digging. Her phone has one bar on the stairs if she holds it high. Her son texts: Mom are you ok?? She starts three replies and sends none. The list of tasks circles her head like a draft: water, wood, food, fuel, phone. She sits on the bottom step, still in her coat, snow melting off her boots into a puddle, and hears herself say aloud to nobody, 'I can't do all of it,' and then gets up and does the next thing anyway.

The name on the screen was Sam. Not Sam from work. Sam. Ruth let it ring three times while the past rushed in: the summer at the lake, the fight in the parking lot, the wedding she'd skipped, eleven years of not calling. She answered before she decided to. 'Ruthie,' Sam said, and the old nickname undid something in her. Sam was talking fast, getting divorced, moving back to town, sick, maybe, there were tests, and wondered if they could get coffee, and also did Ruth remember that song, the one from the car? Ruth was nodding at an empty kitchen. She opened her mouth to apologize and to ask a hundred questions and to say she'd missed her, and all of it jammed together so nothing came out. She sat down on the floor by the fridge. 'Yes,' she finally managed. 'Yes. Coffee.'
