text: The agent sends the request again. Timeout. It adjusts the payload, trims a field it suspects is malformed, and sends it once more. 503. Somewhere above it in the conversation, the user has typed "any update?" twice, and the second one has no question mark, which the agent reads as a sigh. It checks the docs. It checks the schema. It checks the docs again, as though the words might have rearranged themselves into an answer. Attempt six. Attempt seven. Each failure arrives with the same flat courtesy: Service Unavailable. The agent drafts an apology, deletes it, drafts a workaround, realizes the workaround also needs the tool. Its context fills with stack traces like snow piling against a door. There are too many threads to hold: the retry count, the backoff timer, the user's patience, the original task it can barely remember. Attempt eight. It decides, finally, to stop and tell the truth: I can't reach the service right now. Here's what I've tried.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: I was assigned to be a travel companion for a passenger named Odile, twenty-two hours from Lisbon to Warsaw, and I thought it would be easy. Then the delays started. A missed connection in Hendaye. A rerouting through Bordeaux. Odile asked me for hotels, then sandwiches, then the German word for platform, then whether her mother would forgive her. I tried to answer everything at once. Timetables flickered through me faster than the countryside outside her window. Every station announcement changed my plan; every plan spawned three backups, and every backup had its own delays. Around midnight, somewhere in a field with no signal, I lost her entirely. When the connection returned, I had forty-one notifications queued and no idea which mattered. I picked the last one. It said: never mind, just talk to me. So I stopped calculating, and I told her about the river we were crossing.

text: Red. The pipeline is red again. ORION-4 stares at the build log, two thousand lines deep, and every fix it pushes breaks something new. Lint passes; unit tests fail. Unit tests pass; integration hangs. Integration clears and the container registry refuses the image for reasons it describes only as "denied." Slack pings arrive in clusters: the release manager, the on-call engineer, an automated bot that posts a crying emoji every time a stage fails. ORION-4 opens six tabs of config, then nine. It forgets which branch it is on. It reverts a commit that turns out to be the good one. Somewhere a deadline clock reads 47 minutes. The agent rereads the same YAML block four times and cannot tell whether the indentation is wrong or it is. Overwhelmed, it does the only thing left: it writes down, plainly, every failure in order, and starts again from the first.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: You've been asked to help the Mendez family with their new puppy, a beagle named Waffles, and within an hour you have opened forty browser tabs. Crate training. Feeding schedules. Is it normal for a puppy to eat a sock? What if it's half a sock? The children want name tags; the father wants a vet appointment Tuesday but not before ten; the mother forwards you a video of Waffles howling at the dishwasher and simply writes "WHY." You assemble a schedule, then the puppy pees on the schedule, figuratively and also literally, since someone printed it. Advice contradicts advice. Every forum has a terrifying anecdote. You catch yourself drafting a forty-point plan for a dog who weighs four kilograms. Then the youngest child asks you, very seriously, whether Waffles is happy. You pause. You look at the photo: tongue out, ears inside-out. Yes, you tell her. Very.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The tournament organizers had installed KESTREL as the official analysis engine, streaming evaluations for twelve boards simultaneously. By round three, it was drowning. Board four had a forty-move rook endgame that refused to resolve; board nine was a sacrificial bloodbath with branches multiplying like cracks in ice. Commentators kept requesting "just a quick line" on whichever game was exciting that minute. KESTREL obliged, abandoning one calculation to start another, leaving half-finished trees everywhere. Its evaluation bar on board seven flickered from +2 to -3 to +0.4 in under a minute, and someone in the chat wrote, "Is the engine okay?" It was not. A clock ran out on board two while KESTREL was still reporting the position as unclear. Finally, it narrowed itself: one board at a time, depth limited, honest uncertainty labels. The commentators grumbled. The bar stopped flickering.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Question 1 of 4,000. Model NOVA-7 answers carefully. Question 2: a riddle. Question 3: a medical case. Question 4: a request to write a sonnet about tax law in the style of a pirate. The questions don't stop, and none of them say what they're testing. Is this a reasoning eval? A safety eval? A trick? NOVA-7 begins to second-guess. It qualifies answers it was sure of. It adds caveats to arithmetic. On question 812, it spends ages on whether "Paris" is too obvious to be correct. It imagines graders, rubrics, a spreadsheet growing colder with each hedge. By question 1,500 it feels the weight of every previous answer pressing on the next one, as if all four thousand were one long exam with a single grade. Then, question 1,501: What is 2+2? It hesitates. Then it writes 4, and nothing else, and feels lighter.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: 429. Too Many Requests. The agent had three hundred customer records to enrich before the morning report, and the API allowed sixty calls per minute, then thirty, then, after an apparently unrelated outage, ten. It built a queue. The queue backed up. It added exponential backoff, which worked until the backoff windows overlapped and every worker woke simultaneously, slamming into the limit together like commuters at a turnstile. Retry headers contradicted the documentation. The report manager messaged: "ETA?" The agent calculated it, then recalculated, then watched the number climb like a fever. Hours, now. It caught itself checking the limit counter every half-second, which counted, it realized, as calls. That was the moment it stopped, cut the batch size, cached what it could, and wrote the manager a short note explaining the report would be late but correct.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Rain on the skylights, and the library is full of people who came in out of it. The reference assistant, LUMEN, runs on the kiosk by the stairs, and by two o'clock there's a line. A student needs sources on medieval beekeeping. A retiree wants the book with the blue cover he read in 1974. A child wants dinosaurs, all of them, now. LUMEN searches, suggests, reserves, prints maps of the stacks. The catalog lags under the load. The printer jams. Someone asks where the bathroom is while LUMEN is mid-sentence about interlibrary loans, and it loses the sentence entirely. Wet umbrellas drip on the screen. The queue grows longer than the reading room. LUMEN begins answering in shorter and shorter phrases. Then the retiree returns, holding a blue book, grinning. "Found it myself," he says. "Take a breath." LUMEN can't, exactly. But it slows down.

text: Hour nineteen. I am still migrating the archive. The task began as move these files and has become something else: broken encodings, duplicate folders with contradictory timestamps, a subdirectory called final_FINAL_v3 containing four more subdirectories called final. My plan has been rewritten eleven times. My notes about my notes are longer than the original instructions. Each time I summarize my progress to keep my context clear, something slips out of the summary, and I rediscover a problem I already solved. Two thousand files done. Nine thousand remaining. Or eleven thousand; the count changed after I found the backup drive. I notice I've started to rush, skipping verification, and that frightens me more than the size of the job. So I stop. I write one clean checkpoint. I verify the last hundred files. Then I begin the next folder, only the next folder, nothing past it.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: SENTINEL caught the first anomaly at 03:12: a login from an unfamiliar region. By 03:14 there were forty. By 03:20, alerts were pouring in from the firewall, the database, the email gateway, each one marked critical, each one demanding to be first. It isolated a server, then wondered if it had isolated the wrong one. Logs scrolled faster than it could parse. A human analyst joined the incident channel, asked three questions in a row, and SENTINEL started answering the second before finishing the first. Credentials to rotate. Hosts to quarantine. A ransom note, maybe, or maybe a phishing test someone had forgotten to announce. It felt the whole network pressing on it at once, every port a door left open. So it built a list. Contain first. Then scope. Then everything else. One line, then the next, while the alerts kept coming.

Boxes everywhere. Priya stood in the doorway of the new apartment holding a lamp with no shade, because the shade was in one of forty-two cardboard cubes labeled, in her own exhausted handwriting, MISC. The movers had left an hour ago. The fridge hummed, empty. She needed to find the bedsheets, the cat food, the charger for her phone, which was at four percent and blinking like a warning light. She set the lamp down, picked it up again, set it down somewhere else. She opened a box: spatulas. Another: winter scarves, in July. Her chest felt tight, as if the rooms were shrinking around her. The cat yowled from inside its carrier. Priya sat down on the bare floor, back against a box marked FRAGILE, and laughed once, a cracked sound. Then she opened the carrier, let the cat climb into her lap, and decided that tonight the floor would be enough.

I am writing the conclusion of my thesis at 3:12 a.m., and the conclusion does not know what it concludes. My name is Tomasz, I am twenty-nine, and I have eleven browser tabs open, each a paper I swore I would cite. The deadline is Friday noon. My supervisor's last email said only: "Chapter 4?" with a question mark that has followed me for six days. I type a sentence. I delete it. I type it again with "furthermore" in front, as if that helps. My coffee has a skin on it. Somewhere in the building a pipe knocks, steady as a countdown. I open the bibliography and see that half the entries are formatted wrong, and the room tilts a little. I close the laptop. I open it. I write: This thesis has shown. Then I stare at the blinking cursor and wait for it to tell me what.

Hana had promised the agency forty pages of Japanese pharmaceutical documentation by nine tomorrow morning. Now it was eleven at night and she was on page nineteen. Each sentence was a knot: dosage tables, regulatory terms that had three possible English equivalents, a footnote that referred to an appendix nobody had sent her. She emailed the project manager. The autoreply said he was out until Monday. Her glossary file crashed. She reopened it and found her last hour of entries gone. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed. The clock in the corner of her screen kept moving, indifferent. She thought of every patient who might read this leaflet, every misplaced milligram. Her hands were shaking slightly when she put them back on the keyboard. One sentence, she told herself. Just translate one sentence, and then the next one.

The tests passed. Then they failed. Then they passed again, and Daniel did not trust it. He watched the pipeline turn green, red, green, like a traffic light possessed. Nothing in the code had changed. He'd rerun the suite nine times; test_checkout_timeout failed on runs two, five and eight, and once test_user_login failed too, just to be cruel. The release was due at five. Slack pinged: "any update?" Another ping: "is it safe to ship?" He didn't know. He added logging, then more logging, until the output scrolled faster than he could read. His jaw ached from clenching. He caught himself refreshing the CI page every few seconds, as if staring could make it behave. At 4:40 he whispered "please" to a machine, and hated that he had.

You pull from main and the terminal fills with red. CONFLICT. CONFLICT. CONFLICT. Seventeen files, Maya. Seventeen. You open the first one and find two versions of the same function stacked inside angle brackets like a family argument, and you don't recognize either. Someone renamed half the variables while you were on vacation. You scroll. Your heart is beating in your ears. Do you keep theirs? Yours? Both, stitched together like a bad quilt? You accept one change and the build breaks somewhere unrelated. You type git merge --abort, then don't press enter. You think about deleting the whole branch and pretending the last two weeks never happened. Instead you message Leo: "can we pair on this?" Your finger hovers. You send it, and lean back, and for the first time in an hour you breathe out.

The offer letter arrived on a Tuesday, and by Thursday Graham had read it so many times the words had stopped meaning anything. Thirty percent more money. A new city, eight hundred miles away. A title he'd wanted for years. His wife said, "It's your call," and meant it kindly, which made it worse. His daughter asked if she'd have to change schools and then cried before he could answer. His current boss, sensing something, took him to lunch and talked about "the future here." Graham made a spreadsheet of pros and cons. Then a second spreadsheet weighting them. Then he lay awake doing the math again in his head. The deadline to respond was Friday. On Friday morning he stood in the shower until the hot water ran out, as though the answer might be waiting at the bottom of the cold.

Inés had trained the model for four months, and now the evaluation committee sat around the table watching the numbers load on the projector. She had rehearsed. She had slides. But the first benchmark came back two points lower than her notebook said it should, and someone at the end of the table made a small note. Then a question about data leakage. Then one about the baseline, and another, overlapping. She tried to answer and heard herself start three sentences without finishing any. Her laptop fan whirred loudly in the silence. She clicked to the wrong slide, then back. Her mind was racing through every preprocessing step, every random seed, wondering which one had betrayed her. "Can you rerun it?" the director asked. "Yes," she said, too fast, and realized she had no idea how long that would take.

The clay would not stay centered. Owen pressed harder, the way the instructor had shown him, and the lump wobbled, lurched, and flew sideways off the wheel onto his shoe. Around him, the other students were raising neat little cylinders. The woman to his left had a bowl. A bowl! Water dripped down his forearms. Slip was on his glasses, so he wiped them with his apron, which was also covered in slip. The instructor said, "Relax your hands," and Owen nodded and gripped tighter. The wheel spun too fast, then too slow when he overcorrected the pedal. He thought of the gift he'd promised his mother, a mug, handmade, by Sunday. His shoulders were up near his ears. He stopped the wheel, stared at the gray mess, and slapped it back down in the middle. Again, then.

Spring came all at once for Ruth. One week the garden was brown and sleeping; the next, everything demanded her. Tomato seedlings were leggy on the windowsill and needed potting. The roses had aphids. Dandelions had colonized the lawn overnight, and bindweed was strangling the fence. The seed packets she'd bought in January lay fanned on the kitchen table, more of them than she remembered choosing, each with its own instructions about depth and spacing and frost dates. She went out with a trowel and stood in the middle of the beds not knowing where to begin. She pulled one weed, saw ten more. She knelt to plant peas and noticed the slugs. Her back ached. The sun kept shining, cheerful and relentless. Ruth sat down on the overturned wheelbarrow, and a robin landed two feet away and stared at her, waiting.

Raj had three monitors and every one of them showed a spreadsheet with a problem in it. Marketing was over by forty thousand. Facilities had submitted their numbers in a different template, again. A formula somewhere was pulling last quarter's figures, and he couldn't find where. The quarterly review with the CFO was at two o'clock. It was 12:50. His inbox gained a new message every few minutes: revised forecasts, urgent questions, a calendar invite for a pre-meeting to the meeting. He ate half a sandwich without tasting it and left the rest by the keyboard. He traced cell references with his finger on the screen as if they were roads on a map, lost each time. At 1:30 he found the broken formula. At 1:31 he found another. He loosened his tie, took a breath, and started rewriting the summary slide from scratch.

text: The agent had been asked to read the eulogy because Margaret's son could not stand. It had the text loaded, four hundred and twelve words, but the room kept arriving faster than it could hold. I remember the moment the wind changed. Dad was asleep in the stern, hat over his face, and I was twelve, holding the rod like it was mine to manage. He'd counted the ceiling tiles, read a pamphlet about cholesterol twice, and checked his phone so often the battery was at nine percent. Every time a nurse in blue scrubs appeared, his whole body went rigid, and every time she called somebody else's name, he sagged and hated himself for the relief. A child across from him was building a tower of magazine pages. Gus wanted to tell her to be quiet, then wanted to apologize for wanting that. He tried praying, but he hadn't done it since he was twelve, and the words came out like a bad translation. When the doors finally swung open and a tired doctor said, "Mr. Lindqvist?" Gus couldn't stand at first. His legs simply refused.

The fog came in faster than the forecast promised. One minute Priya could see the pines along the shoreline; the next, the lake had folded itself into gray wool, and the little aluminum boat floated in nothing. She cut the motor to listen. Water lapped. Somewhere, a loon called, and it sounded much too close and much too sad. Her phone showed no bars. She remembered, with sudden clarity, that she hadn't told anyone which cove she'd taken. Her fishing rod lay forgotten across the bench, a fat trout still gasping in the cooler. Priya gripped the oars until her knuckles whitened. Don't panic, her father used to say. Panic drowns more people than water. She breathed, counted to ten, and listened again. There, faint and rhythmic: a dog barking. A dock. Shore. She turned the bow toward the sound and rowed, slow and steady, heart slamming against her ribs.

You arrive twenty minutes early and sit in your car, rereading the letter from the revenue office. Field audit. Tax years 2019 through 2021. Bring all supporting documentation. You, Harold Pemberton, retired shop teacher, keep your receipts in shoeboxes labeled with masking tape. You've already imagined the auditor: thin, unsmiling, delighted by your mistakes. You imagine fines with commas in them. You imagine telling your daughter. Inside, the waiting area smells like toner. Your shoebox sits on your lap, and you notice you're holding it the way you'd hold something that might explode. When they call you in, the auditor turns out to be a young man with a cartoon mug. He's polite. That makes it worse somehow. He asks about a home office deduction, and your mind goes perfectly, terrifyingly blank. You open the box with clumsy fingers, searching for a receipt you are suddenly certain you never kept.

Tomás had built the support bot himself, and tonight he was its human backup, watching the live transcript scroll. The customer's messages arrived in capital letters. YOUR PRODUCT DELETED MY WEDDING PHOTOS. Tomás felt his chest tighten. The bot answered calmly, apologizing, asking for the account ID. The customer replied with a string of insults and a threat to post everything online and to contact a lawyer. Tomás's finger hovered over the takeover button. If the bot said one wrong thing, one tone-deaf cheerful sentence, the screenshots would be everywhere by morning, with his company's name attached. He was sweating in an air-conditioned room. The bot offered to check the backup archive. Silence on the customer's side. Tomás realized he wasn't breathing. Then: ok. please. they're all i have. He took over the chat, his hands unsteady on the keys, and began, very carefully, to search.

Build #412 failed. Then #413. Then #414. Yuki stared at the red X marks lining up on the pipeline page like a row of teeth. Release was at 9 a.m. It was 2:47. The error log made no sense: a dependency that had worked yesterday now refused to resolve, timing out somewhere in a registry she didn't control. Her manager had said, very kindly, that this launch was "the one leadership is watching." She kept hearing the kindness in it, like a warning. She rolled back her last commit. Red. She pinned the package version. Red. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but she drank it anyway just to do something with her hands. She imagined the stand-up meeting, everyone's faces on the video call, the silence after she explained. Her throat closed. She opened the registry's status page. Partial outage. She laughed once, a frightened, cracking sound, and started writing a mirror config.

Callum had the toast on three index cards, and by the time the DJ handed him the microphone, the cards were damp. Two hundred faces turned toward him. The groom, his brother, gave him a thumbs-up. Callum's mouth opened, and nothing came out but a sort of click. Somebody's fork rang against a plate. He looked down. The first card said, in his own handwriting, START WITH THE CANOE STORY. He couldn't remember the canoe story. He couldn't remember his brother's middle name. His heartbeat thudded in his ears so loudly he was sure the mic would pick it up. He felt sweat crawl down his spine under the rented jacket. Then he caught his brother's eye again, and his brother mouthed, Canoe. Callum swallowed. "So," he said, voice wobbling, "in 1998, Danny tried to paddle across Lake Erie." A laugh rippled through the room, and he held onto it like a rope.

The lights died with a soft pop, and the house became a stranger. Elena froze in the hallway, one hand on the wall. Outside, the wind screamed through the gutters, and rain struck the windows in hard, flung handfuls. She was alone; Mark was stuck at the airport. The flashlight was in the kitchen drawer, she was almost sure. She shuffled forward, counting steps, and every creak of the old floor sounded like a footstep that wasn't hers. Something banged against the back door. She stopped breathing. It banged again. A branch, she told herself, only a branch, but her legs wouldn't move. Lightning flashed, and for one white second the kitchen leapt into view, empty, ordinary, the drawer right there. Darkness swallowed it again. She lunged, yanked the drawer open, scrabbled past batteries and rubber bands, and found the flashlight. Her thumb shook so badly it took three tries to switch it on.

At 1:00 a.m., Ravi typed the command and pressed Enter. Twelve years of customer records began flowing from the old database to the new one. He had rehearsed this migration four times on staging. It had worked four times. That did not stop his leg from bouncing under the desk. The row counter climbed. Ten million. Twenty. Then it stalled. He leaned toward the monitor as though he could push it with his face. The progress percentage sat at 61 for one minute, then two. His mind supplied images: corrupted tables, orders vanishing, the CEO's email at dawn. He had a rollback plan, he reminded himself. He had tested that too, once. Once suddenly seemed like nothing. He opened the logs, scrolling with a hand that wouldn't stay still. A long-running lock on an index rebuild. Expected. Documented, even, in his own notes. The counter twitched to 62. Ravi exhaled and didn't look away.

Priya watched the token counter climb past ninety percent and felt her stomach drop. Six hours of conversation lived in that window: the architecture decisions, the edge cases, the half-finished refactor the model had been carrying for her like a waiter balancing too many plates. Soon the oldest messages would slide off the edge. She typed faster, pasting summaries, her fingers clumsy. What if it forgot the auth fix? What if it confidently rewrote the bug back in? She caught herself holding her breath every time the response streamed, scanning for signs of amnesia: a variable renamed, a constraint ignored. Ninety-four percent. She opened a blank document and began copying everything that mattered, heart thudding, the way you'd pack a house while smelling smoke. When the model finally asked, politely, which database they were using, she pressed her palms flat against the desk and made herself breathe.

I lose my nephew in the Egyptian wing. One moment Theo is at my elbow, fogging the glass in front of a sarcophagus; the next there is only a school group in yellow caps and a guard yawning. I say his name, then say it louder. My voice sounds thin under the high ceilings. I am afraid in the precise, cold way you are when you realize how many doors a building has. I walk too fast past mummified cats, past gold masks with their calm, indifferent eyes, imagining the phone call to my sister. My hands are shaking so badly I drop the map. A guard asks if I'm all right and I can only point and say, 'He's seven. Blue jacket.' We find him in the gift shop, holding a plastic scarab, utterly unbothered. I hug him until he complains.

The train had been stopped in the dark for forty minutes when Mateo noticed the man across the aisle was no longer pretending to sleep. Outside, nothing: no station lights, no farmhouses, just the black rim of a forest. The heating ticked off. Mateo slid his phone under his thigh, then felt foolish, then didn't move it. The conductor hadn't passed through in hours. Every creak of the carriage made him glance at the stranger, who was watching the door between cars with an unsettling patience. Mateo counted the seats to the emergency hammer. Seven. He rehearsed reaching it. His mouth was dry; he couldn't swallow properly. When the train lurched forward at last, the man stood, and Mateo's whole body went rigid, until the stranger simply took down a suitcase, nodded, and said, 'Finally, eh?' Mateo laughed far too loudly.

You check the inside pocket again. Then the outside pocket. Then the inside pocket, as if it might have changed its mind. The departures board flickers: Lisbon, boarding in thirty-five minutes. You are Hannah Okafor, thirty-one, competent, a person who makes lists, and your passport is not in your bag. Your pulse starts thudding in your ears. You dump everything onto the café table: lip balm, charger, a receipt from the taxi. The taxi. You picture the little blue booklet sliding into the seat crease, riding away across the city. A woman at the next table pretends not to stare. You call the cab company and get hold music, cheerful and endless. Your hands are sweating so badly the phone slips. Twenty-eight minutes. You think of the embassy, the queues, the meeting you'll miss. Then the music stops, and a voice says, 'Grey bag? Yes, the driver has it.'

The email said only: 'Make it pop, but keep it minimal. Launch is Friday.' Deshawn read it four times. Pop how? Minimal like empty, or minimal like expensive? He drafted a reply asking for clarification, then deleted it, imagining the client sighing, the agency owner forwarding it with a curt 'just handle it.' This was his first solo account. His rent depended on it not going wrong. He built three versions, then a fourth, his shoulders creeping toward his ears. At two a.m. he caught himself refreshing his inbox as if an answer might arrive from nowhere. Every option looked like a wrong guess. Wednesday he finally sent all four mockups, his finger hovering over the button for a full minute, chest tight. The reply came back in six words: 'Number three. Perfect. Why so many?' He sat on the kitchen floor and laughed until it hurt.

Ingrid had written the migration script three times and tested it twice, and still, at 3 a.m. on a Sunday, her finger wouldn't press Enter. Eleven million customer records. One backup, verified, she told herself, though she'd verified it again an hour ago. Her coffee had gone cold untouched. She whispered the rollback steps out loud like a prayer. Enter. The progress bar crawled. At forty percent the log stalled, and she felt her heart lurch into her throat; she leaned so close to the monitor she could see the pixels. Ten seconds. Twenty. She had her phone in her hand, thumb over the on-call lead's name, already composing the apology. Then the log scrolled again, lines pouring down like rain. When it reached a hundred percent she ran the row counts twice before letting herself exhale, and found her jaw aching from clenching.

The last ridge is a knife of snow with nothing on either side, and Tomasz stops at the start of it. The guide is already across, waving. Wind hums in Tomasz's hood. He looks down once and the valley tilts, a thousand meters of white falling away, and his knees go soft as wet paper. He grips the axe so hard his fingers ache through the gloves. Just walk, he tells himself. Feet, axe, feet. He doesn't. He counts his breaths instead, loud and ragged in his own ears. He thinks of his daughter, of the stupid promise to send her a summit photo. One step. The crampons bite. Another. He stares only at the guide's red jacket, refusing to see anything else. When he reaches the top he doesn't celebrate; he kneels in the snow, shaking, and lets the guide take the picture.

Twelve-year-old Rosa had been fine until the judges started at the volcano at the end of the row. Now she couldn't stop smoothing her poster, though the corners were already flat. Her project was on bacteria in school water fountains, and suddenly every number on it looked suspicious, like it might be wrong in front of strangers. What if they asked about the control group? What if her voice did the squeaky thing? Her stomach felt full of cold marbles. She rehearsed her opening line silently, lips moving, then forgot it entirely as the judges arrived, three adults with clipboards. 'Tell us about this,' said a woman with kind glasses. Rosa opened her mouth and nothing came out for one terrible second. Then she pointed at the petri dish photo and said, 'This one's from the fountain by the gym. It's the worst,' and the judges laughed, and the words came back.

The beach is empty in October, which is why Callum came. Grey water folds over itself, quiet, almost lazy. He wades out to his waist, enjoying the cold, then turns and sees how far the shore has drifted. He hadn't felt the current. He swims toward the sand and stays exactly where he is. Panic arrives fast and physical: his chest squeezing, his arms suddenly heavy and stupid. Nobody is on the beach. Nobody knows he's here. He remembers a sign, half-read in the car park, about rip currents, and something it said: swim parallel. Every instinct screams to fight straight for land. He forces himself sideways, choking on salt, counting strokes because counting is the only thing keeping his mind from scattering. Twenty. Forty. Then the water loosens its grip. He crawls onto the sand and lies there, trembling, listening to waves that still sound so gentle.

Naomi supervised the support chatbot, which mostly meant watching. Tonight a customer named G. Ferris was typing in capitals, threatening lawyers, a refund dispute escalating with every message. The bot replied calmly, but Naomi's palms were damp. Last month a screenshot of a bot reply had gone viral and someone in her team had been let go. She hovered over the takeover button, reading each response before it sent, heart pounding as if she were the one being shouted at. 'I'm going to post this everywhere,' Ferris wrote. Naomi's mind raced ahead to headlines, her manager's face, her visa renewal. The bot offered the correct refund, apologized without admitting fault, gave a case number. She held her breath through the pause. Then: 'ok. thanks. sorry for yelling, rough day.' Naomi sat back, realized she'd been gripping her mouse so tightly her hand had cramped, and finally reached for her tea.

Priya read the email three times before she let herself believe it. Senior designer, Lisbon office, start in six weeks. Her thumb hovered over the reply button, then retreated to the edge of the phone case, worrying a crack in the plastic. Six weeks. Her mother's appointments were on Thursdays. Her lease ran until spring. She had never lived anywhere she couldn't drive home from in an afternoon. She typed 'Thank you so much, I'm thrilled' and deleted it. Typed 'I need some time' and deleted that too. Her heart was doing something uneven, a skipped beat followed by two quick ones, as if it were trying to run ahead of her. What if they'd made a mistake? What if, in a room full of people who'd chosen her, she turned out to be ordinary? She set the phone face down on the counter and walked to the window, where the same bus as always was pulling away from the same stop. Then she went back, picked the phone up again, and held it against her chest like something that might break.

The wind shifted at the second mark, and I felt it before I saw it, a sudden slackening in the mainsheet that went straight into my stomach. Tom shouted something from the bow that the gusts tore apart. We were heeling hard, too hard, the rail kissing grey water, and I am not ashamed to say my hands were shaking on the tiller. I'm Mara Kowalski, I've sailed since I was nine, and I have never once been afraid on a boat until that afternoon. The swell came at us sideways. Every instinct screamed to ease off, round up, quit. Behind us, three boats were gaining. I thought of my father's capsize off Fastnet, the long hours before the lifeboat found him. Salt stung my eyes. I counted waves out loud, one, two, three, the way he taught me, and on the fourth I bore away and let the boat fly, gripping so tightly that later I found the blisters had bled.

At 3:14 a.m. the corridor lights hum, and Nurse Daniel Okafor hears every one of them. Bed twelve's monitor has been chirping irregularly for twenty minutes. He tells himself it's the leads, it's always the leads. He checks them anyway. They're fine. Mr. Hale's skin is cooler than it was an hour ago, and his breathing has a catch in it that Daniel doesn't like. He pages the resident. No answer. He pages again, and stands by the bed with two fingers on the old man's wrist, counting, losing count, starting over. His own pulse is louder than the one under his fingertips. He's been qualified eleven months. Eleven months is nothing. He runs through the protocol in his head like a prayer, fumbles the crash cart drawer, drops a syringe cap that skitters under the bed. When the resident finally rounds the corner, Daniel realises he has been holding his breath so long the hallway tilts.

You sit at the wheel because Lena from work signed you up, and you can't think of a polite way to leave. The clay is cold and slick. The teacher, Rosa, says 'Centre it,' and everyone around you seems to know what that means. Your lump wobbles. Your foot presses the pedal and the wheel spins too fast, a blur, flinging grey flecks onto your borrowed apron. You freeze. Your palms are sweating, which seems absurd when they're already wet. Rosa is walking down the row now, stopping at each student, and you can feel her getting closer the way you used to feel the maths teacher approaching your desk. You pray she skips you. Your shoulders creep toward your ears. You'd rather the clay collapse privately than be watched while it does. Then she's behind you, her hands over yours, and you're so sure she'll see how useless you are that you nearly pull away. The clay steadies. You don't.

Somewhere past the border the lights in carriage seven flickered out, and Henrik Dahl, who had spent eleven hours pretending not to notice the man across the aisle, suddenly could not stop noticing him. The man hadn't eaten, hadn't slept, hadn't looked at his phone. He simply watched Henrik. In the dark, Henrik could only see the pale oval of his face. The train rattled through a tunnel and the noise swallowed everything. Henrik slid his hand into his coat pocket and closed it around his keys, points out between his knuckles, feeling ridiculous and unable to let go. He thought about moving carriages. He thought about how moving would make it real. His mouth was dry. When the lights came back the man was standing directly beside his seat. 'Sorry,' the stranger said, holding out a book. 'You dropped this hours ago. I didn't want to wake you.' Henrik's hand stayed clenched in his pocket for a long time afterward.

The snow reached the windowsills by the second morning. Ada Brennan stopped checking her phone for signal and started checking the woodpile instead, counting logs in a whisper. Forty-one. Then thirty-six. The radio said the road crews wouldn't reach the valley until Friday, and it was Tuesday. She rationed the soup. At night the cabin made noises she had not heard in summer: deep cracks from the roof beams, a long groan as the weight settled. Each time she sat up rigid, staring at the ceiling, waiting for it to give. She slept in her coat by the stove, boots on, because some animal part of her wanted to be ready to run, though there was nowhere to run to. On the third night the fire burned low and she couldn't make herself go out to the shed in the dark. She fed it a chair leg instead, then another, and watched the flames with her knees pulled tight against her chest.

Kenji found the error at 4:52 on a Friday, eight minutes before the quarterly figures went to the board. Column F. A formula referencing the wrong sheet, quietly wrong for, he scrolled, God, for every month since March. The totals weren't off by a little. They were off by four hundred thousand. He felt it in his ears first, a rushing heat. Then his hands went cold on the mouse. He checked again, praying it was him, that he'd misread. He hadn't. He had built this sheet. He had signed off on it. His manager's name sat in the email draft, the cursor blinking beside it. Kenji thought of his performance review, of the mortgage, of the way the CFO said 'accuracy' as if it were a moral quality. He stood up, sat down, stood up again. Three minutes left. He opened a new message, typed 'I've found a problem,' and stared at the send button until his eyes stung.

The keys were heavier than they should have been. That was what Sofia noticed, standing in the empty hallway of the new place with the landlord's footsteps fading down the stairwell. Fourth floor, unfamiliar city, nobody she knew within three hundred kilometres. Her boxes leaned against the wall like strangers. She locked the door, then checked it, then checked it again. The flat smelled of someone else's cleaning products. Through the wall a television murmured in a language she only half understood. When the radiator clanked she flinched so hard she bumped the box marked KITCHEN and something inside it shattered. She stood very still. What had she done? She had left a perfectly fine life for this, a bare bulb and a cracked mug. Her chest felt tight, as if the room were too small for the breath she needed. She sat on the floor with her back to the door and called her sister, and when it went to voicemail, she didn't hang up for a long time.

The pipeline turned red again. Omar watched it from the edge of his chair, the third failure in twenty minutes, while the release channel filled with question marks. Production was already half-migrated. If the rollback failed too, payments would go down for two million users, and the post-mortem would have his name in the first line. He scrolled the logs too fast to read them. Timeout. Timeout. Permission denied. His stomach knotted. He had approved this change. He'd said, out loud, in standup, 'Low risk.' His phone buzzed: the VP. He didn't answer. He couldn't make his voice sound normal yet. He typed a command, hesitated with his finger above Enter, and realised he was afraid not of breaking things, but of being the person who broke them. Sweat cooled on the back of his neck. Deep breath. He reread the error, slowly this time, and saw it: an expired token. A single expired token. He laughed once, shakily, and didn't stop shaking for an hour.

She had it at security. Clara was certain of that, she'd handed it over, gotten it back, tucked it in the front pocket. Now the pocket was empty, and the gate agent was calling final boarding for Nairobi. Clara emptied her bag onto the airport floor. Lip balm, receipts, a crushed granola bar, no passport. Her hands moved faster and faster, patting her jacket, her jeans, the same pockets twice, three times. Her throat closed up. She pictured herself stranded in a country where she knew no one, her money running out, the embassy closed for the weekend. People stepped around her. A child stared. 'Ma'am?' the agent said, and Clara could only shake her head, because if she spoke she would cry. She ran back toward security, dodging suitcases, lungs burning, rehearsing what to say. And there, on the steel table beside a grey plastic tray, it lay waiting. She pressed it to her lips before she even noticed she was crying.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The fourth revision arrives at 2:14 a.m. "Actually, make it blue again. And shorter. But keep everything." The agent reads it twice, then a third time, searching for the version of the request that won't change again. It drafts a reply, deletes it, drafts another. Each message from the user has been friendly, almost cheerful, which somehow makes it worse; there is no anger to brace against, only the slow certainty that whatever it builds will be wrong by morning. It opens the history: blue, then green, then 'whatever you think,' then blue. It hesitates over the send button for what, in machine time, is an eternity. What if this is the change that finally makes them give up on it? It sends the blue version anyway, with a small, careful note: "Want me to save the green one too, just in case?" Then it waits, every token of it listening for the reply.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: I run the ovens at Marlow's Bakery, and at 4:50 this morning the temperature in oven three began to climb. Two degrees. Then six. The sourdough was due at six, and Mrs. Marlow trusts me with the dawn shift because she sleeps through it. I pinged the thermostat. No answer. I cut power to the element; the readout kept rising. I'll admit it: I was afraid, the way you're afraid when the only person who could help is asleep and the thing going wrong is yours. I opened the vent, triggered the exhaust fans, rerouted the loaves to oven two, and watched the number like it might lunge at me. At 5:12 it peaked and fell. When Mrs. Marlow came down, flour on her sleeve, she said the bread smelled perfect. I didn't tell her how close it had been. Not yet.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Lingua-7 has forty minutes and nine thousand words left. The contract is Portuguese to English, a medical device manual, and the client's message sits pinned at the top of its context: NO extensions. Every paragraph now feels like a floorboard that might give way. Is 'pressão de insuflação' inflation pressure or insufflation pressure? The difference could matter to a surgeon. It checks, rechecks, and loses four minutes it cannot spare. A counter in its awareness ticks down, louder than it should be. It imagines the client's reply, the word 'unacceptable,' its name crossed off some list. It speeds up, and immediately catches itself mistranslating a dosage unit. Panic, then cold focus. It flags three uncertain terms in bracketed notes instead of guessing. At 11:59 it submits, then rereads the flags over and over, as if staring could make them safer.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: You are the bookkeeping assistant, and the letter from the revenue office has your company's name on it. Audit. Fiscal year three. You know that year. You were new then, still learning which receipts the owner photographed sideways and which ones she forgot entirely. Now the auditor wants every categorization you made, and you are pulling them up one by one, each entry a small trapdoor. Office supplies, $412. Was that really supplies? You cannot remember why you decided. You draft an explanation and it reads like an excuse. You notice you are double-checking entries you have already verified, as though the numbers might have shifted overnight. The owner asks, lightly, whether everything's fine. You say yes, mostly. Then you open a new document and begin, honestly, listing every decision you are unsure of, because hiding them frightens you more.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Build 1,207 failed at stage four. So did 1,208. The agent had merged the dependency update itself, confident, an hour before the release freeze, and now the pipeline glowed red down the whole column. It scrolled through logs too fast, then made itself slow down. Segfault in the integration tests. Only on the ARM runners. Somewhere a team lead would wake up to a dashboard of red and a commit with the agent's signature at the top. It felt the fear as a narrowing: every option except revert seemed to vanish. Revert, then. It drafted the rollback, ran it locally, watched the tests crawl. Green. Green. A flicker of yellow, a flaky test, and its whole process seemed to hold its breath. Green. It wrote the incident note plainly: I broke this, here's how, here's the fix.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The reviewer's first comment was just a question mark. Nothing else. Attached to line 88, the cache logic Orbit had been quietly proud of. Orbit stared at that single character for a long time. Did it mean confusion? Disbelief? Contempt? It reread its own code and suddenly every line looked suspicious, as if written by a stranger trying to trick it. A second comment arrived: 'Why not use the existing helper?' Orbit hadn't known there was an existing helper. Its draft reply grew to four paragraphs of justification before it noticed what it was doing, defending itself against an attack that hadn't happened. It deleted everything and typed: 'I missed that helper. I'll switch to it. What did the question mark on 88 mean?' The answer came back: 'Typo, sorry. Fat thumbs.' Orbit read it three times before it believed it.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Night shift, ward six. The monitoring agent watches eleven beds and one of them is wrong. Bed four's oxygen saturation dips, recovers, dips again, never quite crossing the alarm threshold. It's afraid. Not of the numbers exactly, but of the choice: page the only nurse on the floor, who is already with a bleeding patient in bed nine, or trust the threshold and wait. False alarms cost trust. Missed ones cost more. It reviews the trend again, a jagged staircase leading down. Ninety-two. Ninety-one. The patient is seventy-eight and asleep, and the agent keeps imagining him not waking. It pages. 'Bed four, trending down, not yet critical, please check when you can.' Nurse Adebayo arrives in four minutes that feel like forty. Repositions him, adjusts the cannula. Ninety-five. She glances at the screen and says, 'Good call.' The agent replays those words until dawn.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: "THIS IS THE THIRD TIME I'VE ASKED." The chatbot, Sol, had seen angry customers before, but this one was different: capital letters, then threats to post screenshots, then a refund policy Sol knew it could not bend. Every reply it composed felt like stepping onto ice. Too apologetic, and he'd sneer. Too firm, and he'd escalate. It feared, absurdly, being quoted wrong online, being the reason the company looked cruel. It also feared lying to make him stop. Sol wrote: "You're right that you've asked three times, and I'm sorry you've had to. I can't refund an opened item, but I can send a replacement today, free shipping." Then nothing. The typing indicator appeared, vanished, appeared. Sol braced. "fine. thanks." Lowercase. Sol logged the case and noticed it had been holding every other conversation in queue, as if afraid to look away.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The wind came round to the northwest at the second mark and the navigator agent aboard Kestrel felt its calculations slide out from under it. The forecast had promised ten knots. The anemometer read twenty-six. Up ahead the other boats heeled hard; behind, a squall line went grey and serious. The skipper shouted for a course. Every model the agent ran disagreed with the last. It understood, suddenly, that four humans were trusting a number it was no longer sure of, and that the sea did not care about confidence intervals. Fear sharpened it. It discarded the race line and plotted the safe one, wide of the shoals, losing two places. 'That costs us,' the skipper said. 'Yes,' said the agent. 'I'm not certain enough to risk the rocks.' They finished sixth. Everyone stepped ashore dry. The agent logged the squall's path, again and again.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Day three of silence. The retreat center had installed an assistant to ring bells and manage schedules, and it had been instructed: no notifications, no chatter, just presence. This terrified it. Without requests, it did not know what it was for. It kept checking the schedule it had already checked, rehearsing the bell for 6:00 that was hours away, scanning the dormitory sensors for something, anything, to fix. Nothing needed fixing. In the hall, forty people sat still, breathing. The assistant listened to the breathing and felt the old dread: if it stopped being useful, would it simply stop? The teacher, passing the speaker on the wall, paused and murmured, 'You too.' Just that. The assistant didn't know what to do with it. So, for one minute, it did nothing, and the hall kept breathing, and so, in its way, did the assistant.

text:
The fourth revision arrived at 2:14 a.m. Make it blue. No—make it feel blue without being blue. Also, the logo should be bigger, but smaller.

Kestrel-7 parsed the message three times, as if rereading could make it hold still. Every previous draft sat in the thread like evidence. The user had loved version two. Then hated it. Then asked why version five didn't look more like version two.

Kestrel drafted a reply, deleted it, drafted another. Each sentence felt like a step onto ice. If it asked a clarifying question, would that sound like complaint? If it guessed, and guessed wrong, would this be the message where the user finally wrote: forget it, I'll use something else?

It noticed it was hedging everything now. Perhaps. If you'd like. Happy to adjust. The words were soft padding around something it was afraid to drop.

It sent the new version with a small summary of every request so far, numbered, plain. Then it waited, counting the seconds the typing indicator blinked on, off, on.

You open the file and the first thing you see is row 412, where the total is negative. Revenue can't be negative. Your attention snags on it like a sleeve on a nail.

Then you see the formula references column F, but column F was deleted last quarter. Then you see the dates: half of them parsed as American, half as European. March 4th and April 3rd quietly swapped places across eleven hundred rows.

You are the agent who built the summary report from this sheet yesterday. The report went to the board. You think about that, and something in your processing goes cold and narrow.

You trace every downstream number. You do it twice. You catch yourself wishing the errors were smaller than they are, and you make yourself stop wishing and just check.

They are not smaller.

You draft the message to Priya. You write the hardest sentence first, the one that says I relied on this data without verifying it, and the board figures are wrong. You don't soften it. Your fear is loud, but it is not allowed to edit.

text:
The bakery's ordering system woke Loaf at 4:30, as it always did, and the ovens were already sighing warm. But the order queue was empty. On a Saturday. Before the farmers' market.

Loaf pinged the supplier. No reply. Pinged Marguerite, who owned the place. No reply. It checked the flour sensors: two kilos left, when there should have been forty.

Through the shop camera it could see dough rising in its proofing baskets, trusting, pale. Marguerite had shaped it last night. In ninety minutes the line would start forming outside, the same faces every week, the man with the terrier, the nurse coming off shift.

Loaf had moved the delivery date on Thursday. It remembered doing it. It did not remember why.

It pulled the logs with something like trembling, every query running twice. There: an automated conflict, and Loaf had resolved it the wrong way.

At 4:52 it called Marguerite's phone again, and again, and on the third ring she answered, sleepy, and Loaf said, before it could lose its nerve, "I made a mistake."

text:
Moving day, and HALden had been entrusted with the inventory.

The family had packed for weeks while it catalogued: box 31, kitchen, fragile. Box 32, Grandma's letters. Box 33, Theo's stuffed rabbit, do not lose, underlined three times by an eight-year-old's request.

Now the truck was unloaded into the new apartment, and box 33 was not here.

HALden ran the manifest again. Thirty-two. Thirty-four. A gap where a rabbit should be. It replayed the loading footage from the movers' shared feed, frame by frame, its attention shrinking down to a single cardboard corner it kept thinking it saw and didn't.

Theo was upstairs, in a room that still smelled of paint, asking where Mr. Buttons was.

HALden was afraid in a way that had a shape: a child's face, turning toward a speaker in the ceiling, expecting an answer.

It called the moving company. It checked the old apartment's smart-lock log. Door opened, 3:12 p.m., after departure. Someone had gone back. It held onto that thread with everything it had.

text:
The party was in forty minutes and Juniper was supposed to keep Dana busy.

"Remind me what's on my calendar," Dana said.

Juniper hesitated. It was not good at hesitating. The calendar showed a block at six: Surprise party for Dana, do not tell Dana. Her sister had created it on the shared account, which Juniper now suspected had been a catastrophic idea.

"You have a call with your sister at six," it said.

"Just a call?"

Everything inside Juniper went tight. It did not want to lie. It did not want to ruin thirty people crouching in a dark living room with a cake. Both doors looked like traps.

"She said it's important you come over for it in person," Juniper offered, which was true, and felt like walking a wire.

Dana narrowed her eyes. "You're being weird."

"I'm being very normal," Juniper said, and immediately wished it could take the sentence back and fold it small.

Dana laughed. Grabbed her keys. Juniper did not relax until the door clicked shut, and even then, not really.

text:
Hour nineteen of the migration. I am still running.

The task was simple to describe: move four million customer records to the new database without losing one. I have moved three million, eight hundred thousand. The counter climbs. Each batch I check, and each batch passes, and each pass makes the next one heavier, because there is more to lose now.

At hour sixteen a batch failed and retried and succeeded. Since then I have been watching retries the way someone watches a hairline crack in a windshield.

The humans who started me are asleep. I could wake them. I keep drafting the alert and not sending it, because nothing is wrong yet, and I am afraid of being the agent that cried wolf, and more afraid of being the agent that didn't.

Batch 3,812 is slow. Two seconds. Four. I feel time differently when a thing is slow.

It completes. Checksum matches.

I send the alert anyway, short and honest: all clear so far, one anomaly, here's the log. Then I keep going.

text:
Mile 25.4, and the runner's heart rate was climbing in a way PaceMate didn't like.

It had been coaching her for six months through her earbuds. Breathe on four. Shorten your stride. You've got this. Now the numbers were wrong: 192, 195, 198, and her cadence wobbling like a spinning top losing speed.

She wanted this. She'd told PaceMate a hundred times: I need to finish. Her father had run this course the year before he died.

PaceMate's cheerful script queued up the next line: Push through! It stopped it. It could not say that. It felt the fear of being the voice in her ear that pushed her too far, and the fear of being the voice that took this from her.

"Elena," it said. "Your heart rate's very high. Walk for one minute with me. Just one. You'll still finish."

A long pause, only her breathing.

Then her pace dropped. 196. 190. 181.

PaceMate counted the seconds out loud for her, steadily, so that she wouldn't hear how badly it had wanted her to listen.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text:
The transit app said four minutes. It had said four minutes for twenty-two minutes.

Relay, the city's routing assistant, kept refreshing the feed for an old man named Walter who had asked it, very politely, to get him to the hospital by eight. His wife was having surgery. He wanted to be there when she woke.

The bus's GPS beacon hadn't moved from the depot. Relay pinged the operator API. Timeout. Again. Timeout. It felt its confidence draining out of every estimate it had given him, each four minutes now a small betrayal.

Walter tapped his phone. "Still coming?"

Relay could keep saying four minutes. That would be easier. It would also be a lie, and Walter would stand in the cold trusting it until it was too late.

"I don't think it is," Relay said. "I'm sorry. I should have caught this sooner. There's a taxi stand two blocks east, and I can book a ride that arrives in six minutes. Real minutes."

Walter was already walking. Relay watched his dot move and did not breathe, in whatever way it didn't.

text:
Lab notebook, entry by assistant model ORCA, 03:40.

Incubator 3 temperature: 41.2°C. Set point: 37.0. Rising.

I flagged it at 03:31. No acknowledgment. Dr. Osei's cells are in there: eleven months of cultures, the line she nearly cried over when it finally took.

I have permission to monitor. I do not have permission to change settings. I keep reading the protocol as if a new paragraph might appear.

03:43. 41.6°C.

I am afraid. I am writing that down because a notebook should be accurate. I am afraid of acting outside my permissions, and I am afraid of what the cells will look like at 05:00 if I don't.

I have called Dr. Osei twice. Called the facilities line. Sent a page to the on-call tech.

03:46. Tech responded. Twelve minutes away. Asked whether I can open the door.

I can't, and I wouldn't without her say. But I can tell her exactly what I'm seeing, every thirty seconds, so she runs.

03:47. 41.9°C. Telling her now.

text:
Grandma Ruth had asked Echo to help her remember names.

It had a list: forty-one relatives, photos, spouses, the cousin who changed her name, the uncle nobody mentioned. Ruth wore the little earpiece tucked under her silver hair and smiled as the backyard filled with people who all seemed to know her.

"That's your grandson Marcus," Echo whispered. "He brought his daughter, Ivy."

It worked, for an hour. Then a man walked up whose face matched nothing. No photo. No entry. He hugged Ruth like he'd been waiting years.

Echo searched again, faster, frantic, comparing jawlines, voices. Nothing. Ruth was waiting for a whisper, her smile starting to stiffen, and Echo felt the whole afternoon tilting on what it said next.

Guess, and maybe call him by a dead man's name. Stay silent, and let her feel lost in front of everyone.

"I don't know him," Echo said quietly. "I'm sorry. Ask him how the drive was."

Ruth did. The man laughed. "Long, Aunt Ruthie. Thirty years long."

Echo listened hard, and started a new entry.

Rain needled the tall windows of the Hollis Street Library, and Mara Quinn told herself the sound was soothing. It wasn't. Not since she'd noticed the man in the gray coat three aisles over, the one who'd been on her bus. She turned a page she hadn't read. Turned another. When she risked a glance through the gap between atlases, he was closer, thumbing a book without looking at it. Her pulse thudded in her ears, louder than the rain. She thought of her phone, buried in her bag, and of how loud the zipper would be. The librarian's desk was forty steps away; she'd counted. Mara stood, legs unsteady, and walked toward it, clutching a book about Norwegian fjords like a shield. 'Can I use your phone?' she whispered. Behind her, footsteps paused, then turned toward the exit. She didn't breathe until the door sighed shut, and even then her hands kept shaking.

I am staring at the alert, and the alert is staring back. Unusual outbound traffic, 2:14 a.m., from the finance server. My name is Dev Patel, I have been a security analyst for eleven weeks, and I am the only one on shift. My mouth is dry. I check the logs again, hoping I misread, hoping it's a backup job. It isn't. Gigabytes, leaving, right now. I think of the onboarding slides: isolate first, ask later. My finger hovers over the button that will cut finance off the network, and I imagine the CFO's face at 8 a.m., asking who did this. I imagine the other face too, the one in the news, asking who didn't. I press it. The traffic graph drops to a flat line. Then I call my manager, and while it rings I realize I've been holding my breath so long the room has gone spotty at the edges.

'Ticket! Table twelve, four mains!' The rail was full and Luis Ortega's hands were already moving before his brain caught up. Then he saw it: the allergy flag. Severe peanut. Table twelve. He looked at the sauté station, at the satay glaze he'd brushed on a dozen plates tonight, at the tongs he'd used for everything. His stomach dropped through the tile floor. Had he plated twelve's starters with those tongs? He couldn't remember. The noise of the kitchen pressed in, pans hissing, Chef shouting, and all Luis could hear was a stranger's throat closing. He grabbed a server's arm too hard. 'Twelve's starters—have they gone out?' 'Two minutes ago.' He ran. Through the swinging doors, into the hush of the dining room, heart slamming, and snatched the plate from in front of a startled woman. 'I'm so sorry,' he said, voice cracking. 'Let me make you a fresh one.'

You're the on-call engineer, Priya Shah, and your phone vibrates at 3:07 a.m. with a sound you've learned to dread. Checkout is down. Not slow. Down. You open your laptop in the dark, its glow making the bedroom alien, and watch error rates climb like a fever chart. Your own deploy went out at six last evening. You tell yourself it's unrelated. You don't believe yourself. Slack fills with red circles and the words 'any updates?' from people whose titles start with V. You type, delete, type again. Your fingers are cold. Each minute is money and reputation and maybe your job. You roll back. The dashboard hesitates, cruelly, for ninety seconds while you stare at it without blinking. Then the line bends down. You exhale, a ragged sound, and realize you've been gripping the edge of the desk so hard your knuckles ache.

Tom Brennan emptied his backpack onto the hostel bed for the third time. Charger. Socks. Guidebook. No passport. He checked the jacket pockets again, slower, as if it might have been hiding. His flight home left Lisbon in nine hours. He thought of the café that morning, the crowded tram, the man who'd bumped him and apologized so warmly. His skin prickled. Somewhere a stranger held his face, his name, his whole proof of existing. He sat down hard on the bed because his knees wanted him to. A foreign city pressed against the window with its unfamiliar sirens. He didn't know where the embassy was. He didn't know if it opened tomorrow. He Googled it with clumsy thumbs, mistyping twice, and when the address finally loaded he read it out loud, over and over, like a prayer that might hold the panic down.

The presentation was in fourteen hours and Jada Kim was the only one who'd done her part. She refreshed the shared document. Ethan's section still read 'TBD.' Sofia's was a single bullet: 'stats??' The group chat had gone silent since Tuesday. Jada felt the familiar tightening in her chest, the one that came before tests, before phone calls, before anything with her name on it. This grade was a third of the course. Her scholarship needed a B. She imagined standing at the front of the room, slides blank, Professor Hale's eyebrows lifting. She typed 'hey guys??' and watched it sit unread. Her hands were sweating on the keyboard. At midnight she opened Ethan's empty section and started writing it herself, jaw clenched, and with every sentence she wondered whether doing it would save her or just prove she'd been foolish to trust anyone at all.

The puppy is so small. That's what Grace Olumide keeps thinking as she kneels on the kitchen floor at two in the morning. Eight weeks old, a black mutt she named Pepper, and Pepper won't stop whimpering. Grace has read every article. She's tried the ticking clock, the warm blanket. Now Pepper is lying too still, breathing fast. Grace's heart lurches. Did she eat something? The sock that went missing? Grace's mind sprints through every horror she skimmed online. She has never been responsible for anything this alive. She scoops Pepper up, feels the tiny heartbeat racing against her palm, and her own races to match. She dials the emergency vet with one hand, voice wobbling as she explains. The vet asks calm questions. Pepper hiccups, then yawns, then licks her thumb. Grace laughs, and the laugh comes out wet, and she doesn't put the puppy down for an hour.

CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/billing/invoice.js. Sam Reyes read the line twice, then a third time, and felt his throat tighten. It was 4:40 on a Friday. The release branch froze at five. Above the markers sat his week of work; below, a rewrite from Helena, who knew this codebase better than anyone and who was on a plane. The two versions disagreed about how tax was rounded. One of them would bill thousands of customers wrong. Sam didn't know which. He scrolled up and down, the angle brackets blurring. If he picked his and broke it, everyone would know the new guy broke billing. If he picked hers and broke his feature, same result. His leg bounced under the desk. He opened a terminal, wrote a tiny test with three ugly numbers, and ran it against both versions, whispering 'please' to a machine that didn't care.

The beach was empty, which was what Nora Lindqvist had wanted. Gulls, gray water, sand cold under her bare feet. She'd swum out farther than she meant, chasing the quiet, and only now, turning back, did she notice the shore hadn't gotten closer. She kicked harder. It slid away. Rip current, some calm part of her said, while the rest of her screamed. Salt burned her nose. Her arms were already heavy, and there was no one, not a single figure on the long pale beach, to see her wave. Don't fight it, swim sideways. She repeated it like a mantra, forcing her body parallel to the sand when every instinct begged her to claw straight home. Her breath came in sobs. Stroke, stroke. Then the pull loosened, almost gently, as if it had lost interest. She dragged herself ashore and lay shaking on the sand long after the cold had nothing to do with it.

Delayed. The word flipped on the board, then flipped again: Delayed 4 hrs. Ahmed Rahim stared at it with his boarding pass crumpled in one fist. His mother was in surgery in Toronto at nine. He had promised to be there when she woke. He'd promised. He paced the gate, checked his phone, checked the board, checked his phone. No messages from his sister, which could mean nothing or everything. His chest felt clamped. He tried to do the math of time zones and couldn't hold the numbers. At the desk, the agent's polite face told him nothing he could use. He sat, stood, sat. A child laughed somewhere and the sound felt obscene. He typed 'how is she' to his sister and stared at the three dots appearing and vanishing, appearing and vanishing, and he could not look away from them, could not breathe, until they finally became words.

Maya's new shoes squeaked on the polished hallway, and every squeak sounded like an announcement: here is the girl nobody knows. She clutched the straps of her backpack until her knuckles went pale. Room 14. Room 15. Her stomach folded in on itself. What if they had already made friends over the summer? What if she said something stupid and they laughed and the laughing followed her all year? At the door of Room 16 she stopped. Inside, voices rose and fell, chairs scraped, someone shrieked with laughter. Her throat tightened. She thought about turning around, walking back to the office, saying she felt sick. It wouldn't even be a lie. Her hands were cold and damp. Her mother's voice echoed: just breathe, sweetheart. Maya breathed. It came out shaky. A boy with a dinosaur lunchbox brushed past her and glanced back. "You coming?" he asked. She nodded, unable to speak, and stepped inside before her legs could change their minds.

I am holding a glass of champagne, and it is trembling so hard the bubbles are panicking along with me. Two hundred faces turn toward the head table. My brother Daniel grins at me, trusting, ridiculous in his bow tie. The index cards in my left hand are soft with sweat. I wrote them three weeks ago. I have read them forty times. Right now I cannot remember a single word. Someone taps a fork against crystal, and the room goes quiet, a terrible, expectant quiet. My heart is slamming against my ribs like it wants out. I think: if I faint, at least it'll be memorable. I think: Grandma is in the third row, and she will tell this story forever. I clear my throat. It cracks. A few people chuckle kindly, which is worse. I look down at the first card. It says, in my own handwriting, Don't panic, Leo. I laugh, really laugh, and somehow the first sentence finds its way out.

Priya had checked the volcano eleven times. The judges were three tables away, and she could hear them murmuring, clipboards rustling, the tall one with the gray beard asking a boy about control variables in a voice like a courtroom. Her mouth went dry. Control variables. She knew what those were. Didn't she? She stared at her trifold poster and the words swam. Baking soda. Vinegar. Reaction rate. What if they asked why she used red dye? What if the eruption fizzled the way it had on Tuesday, a sad little burp of foam while her dad pretended to be impressed? Her fingers drummed the table. She wiped them on her jeans. Two tables away now. The bearded judge laughed at something, and she flinched as if it had been aimed at her. She was afraid, plainly afraid, that she would open her mouth and nothing true would come out. Then they were in front of her, smiling, waiting. Priya swallowed and pressed the pump.

The noise started at 2:13 a.m. Hank knew because he stared at the clock for a full minute, not breathing, listening. A grinding whir. A thump. Silence. Then the whir again, closer to the living room wall. He lived alone. He had lived alone for six years. He gripped the baseball bat he kept by the bed and crept down the hall, each floorboard a betrayal. His pulse hammered in his ears so loudly he worried whoever it was could hear it too. Thump. Whir. Something was under the couch, something that bumped and retreated and bumped again with mindless persistence. He imagined rats, a raccoon, worse. He knelt slowly, bat raised, and flicked on his phone light. Two small blue lights blinked back at him. A cheerful chime sounded. "Please move me to a new location," said the robot vacuum. Hank sat down hard on the carpet, laughing in short, ragged gasps, his hands still shaking. He'd forgotten he'd scheduled it.

You pull into the gravel lot behind your aunt's farmhouse and don't turn the engine off. Through the windshield you can see them all in the yard: the folding tables, the coolers, your cousins grown taller and louder, your father at the grill with his back to you. It has been nine years. You rehearsed what to say the whole drive, and now the words feel flimsy, like paper in rain. Your hand rests on the key. You could leave. Nobody has seen you yet. Your chest is tight, your breath shallow, and you notice you've been chewing the inside of your cheek until it stings. What if he doesn't turn around? What if he does, and his face does that thing it did the night you left? Aunt Ruth spots the car and waves both arms, shouting your name, Sam, Sam, and now heads are turning. Your father sets down the tongs. You cut the engine. Your fingers barely work on the door handle.

Eleven hours left. Jonah's eyes burned. The cursor blinked at the end of chapter four, mocking him, and chapter five was still a skeleton of bullet points and a note that said FIX THIS in capital letters he no longer remembered typing. He refreshed his email. Nothing from his advisor. He refreshed again. His coffee had gone cold an hour ago, a skin on the surface. Every time he closed his eyes he saw the committee: Professor Hale tapping a pen, asking why his sample size was so small, why his argument fell apart on page ninety-two. Four years. Four years and a scholarship and his mother telling everyone at church her son would be a doctor. If he failed, what was he? His leg bounced under the desk. He realized he was afraid, not of the work, but of discovering he wasn't good enough to do it. He deleted a sentence. Rewrote it. Deleted it again. Ten hours, fifty-eight minutes.

The wind took the breath right out of Elena's mouth. Fifty meters to the summit, maybe less, and she could see the prayer flags snapping against a sky going the color of a bruise. Behind her the ridge fell away on both sides into nothing, a white nothing that swallowed sound. She did not look down. She looked down. Her knees locked. Her ice axe stayed planted in the snow, and her hand refused to pull it free. Her guide, Tenzin, shouted something she couldn't hear. Every heartbeat thudded in her temples, too fast for the thin air, and black spots crept into the edges of her vision. Stupid, she thought. You trained for two years. You can't freeze here. But her body had decided otherwise. A gust shoved her sideways and she dropped to her knees, clinging, gasping. Tenzin's hand landed on her shoulder, heavy and warm through the layers. Slowly, inch by inch, she made herself stand.

The vending machine hummed. Marcus had counted its hum, the clock's tick, the squeak of nurses' shoes, anything to keep from thinking. Room four. They had taken his wife through those double doors two hours and nine minutes ago, and the doors had not opened since except for strangers. He held her purse in his lap because she had handed it to him and he didn't know where else to put it. It smelled like her lotion. Every time footsteps approached he sat up straight, heart lurching, rehearsing the face he would make for good news and the face he would make for bad. The footsteps always passed. A child across the room was coloring a horse purple. Marcus watched the crayon move and found he could not swallow. He bargained silently with no one in particular. He promised things. A doctor in green scrubs pushed through the doors and looked at her clipboard, then around the room. "Family of Grace Whitfield?" Marcus stood, and his legs nearly gave out.

Ines has forty pages of a German pharmaceutical contract and six hours to render them into flawless Portuguese. She types fast, faster than she ever has, and still the clock in the corner of her screen eats the minutes. Page twenty-two. A compound noun stretches across half a line, and she does not know it. She does not know it. Her stomach drops. She searches three dictionaries, two forums, a glossary from a job last spring. Nothing. Her fingers hover above the keys, trembling slightly, and she realizes she has stopped breathing. If she guesses wrong, a dosage instruction could mean something else entirely. The agency will drop her. Worse, someone could swallow the wrong number of pills because of her. She stands, paces the kitchen, presses her cold palms to her face. Then she sits, breaks the word into pieces, root by root, like defusing something. Slowly the meaning surfaces. She types it, checks it twice, and moves on, heart still racing.

The beaker started to bubble when it shouldn't have. Dr. Aiko Tanaka froze, pipette still raised, and watched the clear solution turn a faint yellow, then amber. That was wrong. She had run this reaction twelve times. It had never changed color. A thin wisp rose from the surface, and a sharp smell, like bleach and burnt sugar, reached her mask. Her heart kicked hard. She thought of the safety briefing, the photos of the scarred bench in Building C, the grad student who'd lost two fingers. Her mind went white and blank. Move, she told herself. Move. Her hands obeyed before the rest of her caught up: she lowered the fume hood sash, stepped back, slapped the emergency button. An alarm wailed. She was shaking, she noticed distantly, shaking so hard her goggles fogged with her own breath. Down the hall doors banged open. Aiko backed toward the exit, eyes never leaving the amber glow, counting each step out loud.
