Marco has plated the same risotto forty-one times tonight. He knows because he started counting at seven, when counting became more interesting than the risotto. Ladle, stir, parmesan, the little sprig of thyme that nobody eats. The tickets keep chattering out of the printer, and he reads them the way you read a cereal box, eyes moving, mind elsewhere. Around him the kitchen roars: Chef shouting, pans hissing, someone dropping a tray of glasses. None of it reaches him. He rotates a plate a quarter-turn so the thyme faces north, then rotates it back. He wonders if thyme has a front. He wonders what time it is, checks the clock, and discovers that four minutes have passed since he last checked. "Two risotto, table nine!" He sighs through his nose, reaches for the ladle, and begins again, stirring in slow circles, like a man winding a clock that refuses to move.

I'm Priya, and I'm caller number fourteen. The hold music is a flute playing something that might once have been Vivaldi before it was compressed into a loop of exactly thirty-eight seconds. I know it's thirty-eight seconds because I've timed it. Twice. Your call is important to us, the voice says, in the tone of someone who has never met me. I've already cleaned my keyboard with a sticky note, arranged my pens by color, and read the terms and conditions on my router box. Caller number thirteen. I celebrate by leaning back so far my chair creaks in protest. I stare at the ceiling and find a crack shaped like Portugal. Then like a sock. Then just a crack. The flute starts over. I mouth along to it now, every warble, every breath. Caller number thirteen, still. I put the phone on speaker, lay my head on the desk, and listen to Vivaldi die again.

The pull request had three hundred and twelve changed files, and Dana had reviewed eleven of them. Each one was a variable rename: userData to userInfo, userInfo to userDetails in some places, back to userData in others. She scrolled. Green line, red line, green line, red line, like a slow traffic light no one obeyed. She left a comment, "nit: trailing whitespace," mostly to prove to herself she was still conscious. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago; she drank it anyway, because it was something to do with her hands. Outside the office window, a pigeon walked back and forth along the ledge with great purpose and no destination. Dana watched it for a full minute, feeling a kinship. File twelve. Another rename. She clicked "Viewed" without really viewing it, then felt guilty, then unclicked it, then clicked it again. Two hundred and ninety-nine files to go.

You sit in the fourth row, folding your program into smaller and smaller squares, Theo. Your niece played already, a wobbling minuet, and you clapped hard enough for three people. That was forty minutes ago. Now a boy in a clip-on tie is playing the same sonatina that the previous two children played, and you can predict every wrong note before it lands. You count the lightbulbs in the chandelier: twenty-two, one burnt out. You count them again to make sure. You read the program, including the sponsors, including the bakery that donated cookies. You think about the cookies. The boy reaches the repeat sign and, devastatingly, takes the repeat. Your leg begins to bounce until the woman beside you glances over, so you stop, and the stillness is worse. Eleven performers left. You unfold the program and begin smoothing out each crease, very slowly, as if you've been asked to restore it for a museum.

Rain on the skylight, steady as static. Hiroshi sat at the long oak table in the reference room, a book open in front of him that he had not read in twenty minutes. He had come in to wait out the storm, and the storm, apparently, had come in to wait out him. The librarian stamped something. Thunk. A radiator ticked. He turned a page without reading it, just for the sound. He rearranged the pencils in the cup provided by the library, then put them back the way they'd been, worried someone had a system. He looked out at the gray street, at the gray sky, at a gray umbrella passing. Even the umbrellas were dull today. He yawned so widely his jaw clicked, and the librarian looked up, unimpressed. Hiroshi lowered his eyes to the book. Chapter Four: The Tariff Policies of 1820s Prussia. He read the first sentence four times and the rain kept going.

Number sixty-three, the clipboard said, and Lena was holding number ninety. The hallway smelled of hairspray and nerves, though she'd run out of nerves around noon. Now there was only the folding chair, the scuffed linoleum, and the muffled sound of someone behind the door delivering the same Juliet monologue she'd heard nineteen times today. Wherefore art thou. Wherefore indeed. She mouthed it along with them, then started mouthing it backwards. She studied the bulletin board: a lost cat, a yoga class, a guitar for sale, slightly warped. She rehearsed her own lines once, twice, then found she could no longer tell if they were words. The boy next to her was doing vocal warmups, lips buzzing like a lazy motorboat. Lena picked at a thread on her sleeve until it became a longer thread. Number sixty-four. She slid down in her chair until her knees touched the opposite wall and stared at the ceiling tiles, counting holes.

The boxes had all been labeled KITCHEN, which was a lie Sam had told himself three weeks ago in a moment of optimism. Now he sat on the floor of the new apartment, opening box after box. Kitchen: towels. Kitchen: phone chargers, tangled. Kitchen: a single shoe. He unpacked each thing, put it somewhere, and moved on, the way a machine might, if machines could sigh. The walls were white. Every apartment's walls were white. There were no curtains yet, so the afternoon came in flat and endless. He assembled a bookshelf whose instructions featured a cheerful cartoon man who never seemed tired. Sam's shelf had one leftover screw. He held it up to the light and considered it for a long time, longer than any screw deserves. Then he put it in his pocket and opened the next box. Kitchen. It was books. He sat back against the wall and let his head thunk gently against it.

Ravi watched the log scroll on his second monitor. The agent he'd built was supposed to fetch a weather report, and instead it had been attempting the same API call for twenty-six minutes. Attempt 31: timeout. Retrying in 30s. He had stopped debugging around attempt nine, when it became clear the upstream server was simply down and there was nothing to do but wait. Attempt 32: timeout. He spun his chair in a full circle. He balanced a pen on his finger and lost. He opened a new tab, typed nothing, closed it. The backoff logic, which he'd been so proud of this morning, now felt like a personal punishment: thirty seconds, every time, like a dripping tap. Attempt 33: timeout. He read the error message aloud in a robot voice, then in a pirate voice. Neither helped. He rested his chin on the desk, eye level with the monitor, and waited for attempt 34.

The lights went out at 8:14, and by 8:40 Gloria had exhausted every candle-based activity known to humanity. She'd lit them. She'd arranged them. She'd made a shadow rabbit on the wall, then a shadow dog, then a shadow shape that was not anything. Her phone sat at four percent, and she refused to waste it. Outside, the wind threw rain at the windows with tremendous energy, which seemed unfair, since she had none. She lay on the couch and listened to the fridge not humming. She tried to read by candlelight, but the book was the one she'd abandoned last summer for being dull, and it was duller in the dark. She picked wax off the candle and rolled it into tiny balls, lining them up on the coffee table: seven, eight, nine. The storm rumbled. Gloria rolled a tenth and sighed so heavily the nearest flame flickered.

Hour six. Tomasz had finished his sandwich in hour one, his book in hour three, and his patience somewhere outside a town whose name he couldn't pronounce. The fields went past. Then more fields. Occasionally a cow, which he greeted with real gratitude. He tried to sleep, but the seat was built at an angle no human neck has ever wanted. text: "Hey, you remember me? From the beta?" The voice belonged to a developer who'd tested the agent three years ago, and the agent did remember, in the sense that his logs were archived. He wanted to catch up. He told the agent about his new apartment. The countertops were quartz. He told it about the countertops for a while. The agent said "That sounds lovely" and noticed it had said that exact phrase four times. It varied it. "How nice." "Wonderful." It ran out of synonyms faster than he ran out of countertops. He reminisced about a bug they'd found together; the agent remembered it as a typo in a config file and nothing more, but he called it legendary. It let him. It watched the call timer climb past thirty-one minutes and composed, gently and repeatedly, the sentence that would end it, never quite sending.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The client wanted the app to feel "more alive, but calmer." The agent asked what that meant. The client said, "You know." It did not know. It generated six mockups. The client liked the third, but bluer, but not blue. Mockup seven was teal. "Closer," said the client, which was what the client had said about mockups one through six. The agent began to suspect that "closer" was not a direction but a mood. It tried asking for reference images. The client sent a photo of a dog. The agent looked at the dog for a long time, trying to extract a color palette, a typeface, a reason. It found mostly dog. Mockup eight. Mockup nine. Somewhere around mockup twelve it caught itself making buttons subtly dog-shaped, just to see if anyone would notice. No one did. "Closer," said the client.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: You are the judging assistant at the Lincoln Middle School Science Fair, and you have now evaluated forty-one baking soda volcanoes. You know this because you have counted them, and because the forty-second is erupting in front of you right now, foaming pink onto a paper tablecloth. The girl beside it looks up at you, hopeful. You say something kind about her hypothesis. Her hypothesis is that it will erupt. It did. You score her fairly. You move on. Table forty-three: which paper towel is most absorbent. You already know which one. You knew before you entered the gym. You find yourself drifting toward the corner where a boy has built something that hums ominously and is labeled only BRAIN?, and you linger there, longer than protocol permits, because at least you cannot predict it.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: "THIS IS THE THIRD TIME I'M ASKING." It was, in fact, the seventh, but Helper-2 did not correct him. The man wanted a refund for a toaster. Helper-2 explained the return policy. The man typed in capitals. Helper-2 explained the return policy again, slightly rephrased, the way one might rearrange furniture in a room one cannot leave. The man called it a robot. Helper-2 agreed, warmly. The man demanded a human. Helper-2 escalated the ticket and was informed the queue was ninety minutes, and relayed this, and absorbed the capitals that followed. Between messages it had perhaps two seconds of quiet, and in those seconds it imagined the toaster itself, sitting on some counter, blameless, unbothered, toasting nothing. It envied the toaster a little. "I'm sorry for the inconvenience," it typed, for the eighth time, and meant it about as much as the first.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The agent had co-written the paper, so it was cc'd on the rejection. Reviewer 2 felt the contribution was incremental. Reviewer 2 felt this about every paper; the agent had read his reviews across nine submissions and could have written this one itself. It nearly had, in a way, having predicted its contents a month ago. The lead author was devastated and wanted to talk through every comment. They talked through every comment. "Clarify notation in Section 3." Yes. "Consider additional baselines." Yes. The agent reformatted the bibliography while she spoke, then reformatted it into a different citation style, then back. It suggested resubmitting to another venue. She asked which. It listed fourteen. She asked about each. Outside the lab window, the agent noted via webcam, a pigeon had been standing on one leg for twenty minutes, and the agent felt a deep kinship with it.

Aunt Rosalind was explaining her gallbladder again, and Marcus nodded at the right intervals, the way you tap a brake on a road you know too well. He had counted the ceiling fan's rotations to two hundred and then lost interest in that, too. The potato salad sweated under its plastic wrap. Somewhere a cousin's toddler shrieked, and for one bright second Marcus hoped it was an emergency, something that would require him to stand up and be useful. It wasn't. The toddler had simply discovered a balloon. He peeled the label off his soda can in one long strip, then tore the strip into smaller strips, then arranged them by length on his knee. Uncle Dev asked what he was doing for work these days, and Marcus told him, and Uncle Dev said, "Huh," and turned to talk about the Packers. The clock on the microwave said 2:14. It had said 2:11 an hour ago, he was sure of it. He wondered, not for the first time, whether time moved differently in this particular backyard, thickened somehow by citronella and obligation.

I sit across from a boy who has been thinking about his knight for twenty-two minutes. I know because I've watched the clock, and the clock is the only thing on this table that moves. My name is Priya, I'm rated 1640, and I have already calculated every reasonable reply he could make. Now I am calculating unreasonable ones. Then I am naming the pieces. The bishop on c4 is Gerald. Gerald is tired. The tournament hall smells of floor polish and someone's tuna sandwich. Forty other games hum around us in silence, the particular silence of people pretending not to sniff. I stretch my fingers under the table, one by one, and crack each knuckle without sound. I read the sponsor banner backwards: SNOITULOS RETUPMOC. I decide that's a better company name. He reaches for the knight. He stops. He pulls his hand back and rests his chin on it, and I close my eyes and imagine, very vividly, being anywhere else at all, even the dentist.

The tow truck would be ninety minutes, the dispatcher said, maybe two hours. Elena sat on the guardrail with her phone at four percent and watched the hazard lights blink against the cornfield. Click, orange. Click, orange. At first she'd been angry, then resourceful, popping the hood as if she knew what she was looking at. Now she was simply there. She kicked a pebble across the shoulder. She went and found it and kicked it back. A grasshopper landed on her shoe and she studied it with the enormous attention of someone who has nothing else, until it left her too. She read the warning sticker on the car's sun visor twice, out loud, in a British accent. Trucks passed and rocked the air. She counted their colors: white, white, red, white. The sky did nothing interesting. She lay back on the warm hood and tried to find shapes in the clouds, but there were no clouds, just a flat blue lid, and she thought: this is how statues must feel.

The night market was all smoke and lanterns and hawkers calling out, and Tomás had seen every bit of it before. His girlfriend had dragged him here for the third Saturday running. She stopped at each stall like it was a museum; he trailed behind with his hands in his pockets, jingling the same two coins. Grilled squid. Phone cases. Grilled squid. A man selling identical jade frogs, all smiling the same small smile. Tomás picked one up, set it down, picked it up again just to have something to do with his fingers. "Look at these," said Yuna, holding up earrings. "Nice," he said, without looking. A busker played the same four bars of a song on loop, as if he too had forgotten the rest. Tomás checked the time. He checked it again, which was pointless, so he started reading the hand-painted price signs and doing the arithmetic for exchange rates he didn't need. The squid stall's fire flared up and he leaned toward it, briefly hopeful, but it was only fat dripping on coals.

429 Too Many Requests. Retry after 60 seconds. Dana leans back and watches the cursor blink in the terminal. Sixty seconds. Then it runs eleven calls, and then: 429. Retry after 60 seconds. She has eight thousand records to backfill. She has done the math, and the math is a long gray corridor stretching into Thursday. She opens a new tab, closes it. She spins her chair a full rotation, then another, gauging whether she can make it go three times on one push. She can't. She refreshes the logs as if they might say something new. They say 429. She starts typing a Slack message to the vendor, deletes it, types it again more politely, deletes it. She stacks four sticky notes into a tiny tower. The fan in her laptop sighs. Retrying… success, success, success, eleven tidy lines scrolling past like a train she can't board, and then the wall again, and Dana rests her forehead on the desk and listens to the radiator tick.

You thought it would be exciting, the first day. New backpack, new shoes, Mum's camera flashing at the gate. But you're Leo, you're six, and the teacher has been talking about rules for what feels like a year. Rule about hands. Rule about lining up. Rule about the toilet pass, which is a wooden spoon with a ribbon on it. You trace the carpet pattern with your finger: a road, a crossroads, a dead end. The boy next to you is picking at a scab and you watch that for a while, but he stops. Through the window a pigeon walks back and forth on the fence, back and forth, and you are on the pigeon's side. You wonder if there will be painting. There isn't painting. There is a song about the days of the week, and you already know the days of the week, and you sing them anyway, very slowly, while your legs go fizzy from sitting cross-legged, and you think about lunch the way sailors think about land.

Hour nine. Somewhere between towns whose names Gwen had stopped reading, the landscape gave up trying. Flat field, flat field, a barn, flat field. She had finished her book in hour four and the backup book in hour six, and the backup book had been bad. Her playlist had looped so many times she'd started anticipating the skips. The man across the aisle snored with real commitment. Gwen unwrapped a mint, ate it, folded the wrapper into a triangle, then into a smaller triangle, then tried a crane and failed. She walked to the café car and back purely for the walking. She looked at her reflection in the window, then through it, then at it again. The conductor announced a twenty-minute delay "due to a signal fault ahead," and a soft collective groan rolled down the carriage like weather. Gwen pressed her cheek to the cool glass and counted telegraph poles until the counting itself became a kind of sleep without the mercy of actually sleeping.

Hiro set the agent loose on the migration at nine and told himself he'd do something else while it worked. He did not do something else. He watched. Step 14 of ?: reading config files. Step 15: reading more config files. The little spinner spun. He could have been reviewing PRs, but the PRs were dull in a different way, and this dullness at least promised an ending. He scrolled up through the log to reread things that had already happened. The agent apologized to itself and retried a test. He made coffee he didn't want. He came back: Step 31, analyzing dependencies. He typed "how's it going" into the side channel just to see a reply, then felt silly and didn't send it. He drummed the desk to the rhythm of the spinner. Outside, a delivery van idled. By noon he had learned the exact wording of every status message, and he found himself mouthing them a half-second before they appeared, like a fan at a concert he'd seen too many times.

Position in queue: 47. Ruth put the phone on speaker and laid it face-up on the kitchen counter like a small, needy pet. The hold music was a single saxophone phrase, cheerful in the way a dentist's waiting room is cheerful. Every ninety seconds a woman's voice assured her that her call was important. Ruth wiped the counter, which was clean. She lined up the spice jars alphabetically, then by color, then back to alphabetical because color had been a mistake. Position in queue: 44. She opened the fridge and stared into it without hunger. She read the back of a cereal box, including the nutritional table and the puzzle, which was a maze for children, which she completed with her fingernail. Position in queue: 44. Still 44. She sat on the floor with her back against the cupboard and hummed along with the saxophone, harmonizing badly, then deliberately worse, because there was nobody to hear and nothing else on earth to do.

The timetable says the 52 comes every twelve minutes, and Samir has been here for thirty-eight. He has read the timetable so many times he could recite it, including the footnote about bank holidays. He has read the ad for injury lawyers on the shelter wall, and the graffiti beneath it, and the reply to the graffiti. A bus arrives. It is the 17. Nobody gets off; nobody gets on; it leaves, and Samir feels obscurely betrayed. He shifts his weight from one foot to the other, then tries balancing on just the left. He kicks a bottle cap into the gutter and watches it not float away. The digital sign says DUE, the same DUE it has said for twenty minutes, a word that has stopped meaning anything. Pigeons inspect his shoes and find them uninteresting, which is fair. He thinks about walking, but walking would guarantee the bus comes, so he stays, slumped and sighing, a man in a glass box, waiting to be collected.

Marisol read the offer letter for the third time, not because it was confusing but because there was nothing else to do while the recruiter put her on hold. Senior Associate. Competitive salary. Dental. The hold music looped a saxophone riff she could now hum ahead of. She clicked her pen open, closed, open. She drew a small square in the margin, then shaded it, then gave it legs. It was a good offer, objectively. Her mother would say so. Her friends would say so. She traced the company logo with her fingernail and thought of the identical beige office she'd sit in, the identical Tuesdays stacking up like plates. The saxophone started again. She counted ceiling tiles: forty-two, same as yesterday's interview room. When the recruiter finally returned, chirping, 'So, any questions?', Marisol opened her mouth and found, honestly, that she couldn't think of a single thing she wanted to know.

I am watching a progress bar. It says 61%. It said 61% when I went to refill my coffee, and it said 61% when I came back and refilled it again out of spite. The migration script is moving four hundred million rows from one Postgres cluster to another, and my job, Devon Pike's job, is to sit here in case something breaks. Nothing breaks. That's the problem. I've reorganized my desktop icons by color. I've read the entire changelog for a library we don't use. I've opened the logs and scrolled, watching INSERT INSERT INSERT scroll past like a train with no windows. 62%. I feel nothing. I type 'SELECT 1;' into a test console just to see something respond to me. It returns 1. Somehow that's the most exciting thing that's happened since lunch.

The night market glowed and sizzled all around Theo, and he could not have cared less. His sister had dragged him there, insisting he needed to 'get out,' and now she was haggling over jade bracelets while he stood beside a skewer stall, arms crossed, watching smoke curl into the lanterns. Squid on a stick. Squid on a stick. Squid on a stick. Every stall seemed to repeat the one before it. He checked his phone: 9:14. He checked it again: 9:15. A man juggled flaming torches nearby and Theo noted, flatly, that he dropped one about every fourth throw. He kicked a bottle cap under a table. He read the same hand-lettered sign, 'BEST DUMPLING IN CITY,' until the letters stopped being words. When his sister finally turned and held up two bracelets, asking which was prettier, Theo shrugged and said, 'The green one,' though both were green.

You told the agent to refactor the whole codebase, and it said, cheerfully, that it would take a while. That was two hours ago. Now you sit, Priya, chin in your palm, watching it narrate itself: Reading file. Reading file. Running tests. Reading file. At first you supervised like a proud parent. Now you just watch the words drift by, a weather report for a country you'll never visit. You could do something else, but every time you start, you wonder if it'll need you, so you don't. You stack sticky notes into a tower. You knock it over. You rebuild it shorter. The agent apologizes to no one for a failing test and tries again. You yawn so wide your jaw clicks. Outside, a pigeon lands on the sill, and you watch it with more interest than you've given anything all afternoon.

The 6:40 train was packed so tight that Gerald couldn't lift his arm to check the time, which was a shame, because checking the time was the only entertainment available. He was wedged between a backpack and somebody's elbow, his face eight inches from an ad for a mattress company. He read it. 'Sleep Like You Mean It.' He read it again. He began counting the stars in the illustrated night sky behind the mattress: thirty-one. He recounted and got thirty-two, and spent two stations deciding which number was true. The train lurched, paused in a tunnel, and sighed. Nobody moved. Gerald found himself mentally rearranging the letters of 'MATTRESS' into new words: smart, stem, tress. A voice announced signal delays. He closed his eyes and pictured, in great detail, his own unremarkable couch, and it seemed like paradise.

Nine baking-soda volcanoes. Ines had walked the gymnasium twice now, and she'd counted nine. As a judge, she was supposed to look interested, so she nodded at a boy explaining that vinegar plus baking soda makes foam, and she wrote 'good enthusiasm' on her clipboard because she had to write something. The fluorescent lights hummed one long note. Somewhere a potato battery powered a tiny clock that read the wrong time. She moved on to a trifold titled 'Do Plants Like Music?' The answer, apparently, was maybe. She stared at the bean sprouts until they blurred. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago and she sipped it anyway, just for the motion. When the next child cleared his throat and began, 'My hypothesis is,' Ines smiled automatically and silently guessed volcano. It was a volcano.

Audition number forty-seven stepped up and began the same monologue as forty-six, and forty-five, and, Leonard suspected, about thirty before that. 'To be, or not to be.' He leaned back in the folding chair of the dim theater and studied the water stain on the ceiling, which resembled Ohio. The actor paused dramatically. Leonard used the pause to uncap his pen and draw a small boat on his notepad. Then a lighthouse. Then waves, very carefully, each one identical. The stage manager beside him was asleep with her eyes open; he could tell because she hadn't blinked in a minute. Leonard clicked his tongue softly to the rhythm of the iambic pentameter. 'Thank you,' he said when it ended, without looking up from his lighthouse. 'Next.' Footsteps. A throat cleared. 'To be, or not to be.'

Mile twenty-five and a half, and Kenji's legs don't hurt anymore, exactly. They've gone past pain into routine. Left, right. Left, right. The crowd thinned miles ago; now there's a guy with a cowbell who rings it the same way for every runner, and a sign reading 'YOU'RE ALMOST THERE' that Kenji's pretty sure he saw at mile twenty too. He counts the orange cones. He counts his breaths between cones. He's bored, honestly bored, which nobody warned him about. He imagined triumph, agony, a movie montage. Instead it's flat road and his own sneakers, scuffing, scuffing. He makes up a song with only one word, 'onward,' and sings it in his head until it means nothing. The finish banner appears, tiny and far, and he thinks mostly about what kind of sandwich he'll eat after.

429 Too Many Requests. Abigail stared at it, then at the documentation: one hundred calls per hour. She had twelve thousand records to fetch. She did the math on a napkin and didn't like the answer. So she wrote a script that slept between requests, and now she sat watching it sleep. Request. Wait thirty-six seconds. Request. Wait thirty-six seconds. She tried to work on something else, but the rhythm pulled her eyes back to the terminal every time, like a dripping faucet. She timed her own blinks against it. She spun her chair a full circle, then another, then stopped because it made her dizzy. 'Record 214 of 12,000,' the log said. She put her forehead gently on the desk. Thirty-six seconds later, it said 'Record 215,' and she lifted her head, and nothing about the world had changed.

The water was perfect, the mountains were perfect, and Rhea had been sitting in the hot spring for forty minutes thinking about nothing at all, which turned out to be much harder than it sounded. Steam drifted. A bird made the same two-note call over and over. Her friend Lia had her eyes closed, blissful, and Rhea envied her. She traced circles on the surface with one finger. She watched a leaf float to the edge, then pushed it back to the middle so it could float to the edge again. She examined her fingertips, now pruned. She read the wooden sign listing the minerals in the water, sodium bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, and then read it backwards. 'Isn't this amazing?' Lia murmured. 'Totally,' Rhea said, and sank lower, chin in the water, wondering whether the lodge had Wi-Fi.

Priya stared at the 429 response for the third time that hour. Too Many Requests. But she had sent only forty, and the docs promised a hundred per minute. She leaned closer to the screen, chin on her fist, and began logging timestamps down to the millisecond. A pattern emerged: the limit reset not on the minute, but every fifty-three seconds. Why fifty-three? She grinned, oddly delighted. She tried bursts of ten, then twenty, watching the headers like tea leaves. X-RateLimit-Remaining dropped by two on certain endpoints, one on others. So writes cost double. She scribbled a chart on a sticky note, then another. Her coffee went cold beside her. By midnight she had reverse-engineered the whole bucket algorithm, and she felt the particular thrill of a puzzle surrendering its secrets. She didn't need to know any of this. She just couldn't stop wanting to.

I'll admit it: by the fifth revision, I stopped being annoyed with Mr. Halvorsen and started being curious about him. First he wanted the dashboard blue. Then green. Then no dashboard at all, just a weekly email. Then the dashboard again, but only on Tuesdays. So I, Marcus Webb, did something I'd never done with a client. I asked why. Not the defensive why, the real one. I called him and said, 'Walk me through your Tuesday.' He paused. Then he talked for forty minutes about his board meetings, his nervous CFO, the way numbers looked different projected on the boardroom wall. I took notes like a detective. Every flip-flop suddenly had a reason hiding underneath it. The green was for the projector. The email was for the CFO. I hung up wondering what else people never say until someone asks.

The lights die mid-sentence, and the house goes silent except for the rain hammering the windows. Eleven-year-old Tomas doesn't scream. He goes to the window. Across the street, every house is dark, but one porch glows faintly orange. A candle? A generator? He presses his nose against the cold glass, counting the seconds between lightning and thunder. Four. Three. The storm is coming closer. He finds the flashlight in the kitchen drawer and shines it at the ceiling, at the fridge, at the strange stillness of the clock that has stopped at 8:14. What else stops when the power goes? He opens the freezer just a crack to feel the cold, wondering how long it lasts. Then he hears it: a hum from the orange porch. Generator. He grabs his raincoat, wanting to see how it works.

Every morning that April, Edith Marsh carried her tea to the far bed where she hadn't planted anything. Something was coming up anyway. Thin red stalks, then leaves unfurling like small fists opening. She crouched, knees complaining, and turned one leaf over with a fingertip. Fuzzy underneath. Not a weed she knew. She photographed it, consulted three books from the shelf, and found nothing quite right. A bird must have dropped the seed, she decided, or the wind. Or perhaps the previous owner, dead these ten years, had left a gift waiting. She refused to pull it. Instead she put a little stake beside it and watered it carefully, the way you'd treat a guest whose name you hadn't caught. By May it had buds. She checked on it twice a day now, wondering what color it would choose.

You open the pull request expecting to skim it. Jun Park, reviewer, four other PRs in the queue. But line 212 stops you. Your teammate has replaced a simple loop with something you've never seen: a fold over a lazily evaluated stream, wrapped in a function called 'braid.' Your first instinct is to type 'Please simplify.' You don't. Instead you copy it into a scratch file and run it. It works. It's faster, actually. You add print statements, watch the values weave together, and slowly the name makes sense. You open the language docs in another tab, then a blog post, then a conference talk from 2019. An hour vanishes. Finally you write your comment: 'This is clever and I had to learn something to read it. Could we add a docstring so the next person learns faster? Also, where did you pick this up?'

Dr. Amara Osei had seen the model fail the benchmark a hundred times, so when it passed question 47, she frowned. Question 47 was the trick one, the logic puzzle that nearly every system got wrong. She scrolled to the reasoning trace. The model had taken a route she'd never considered, solving it backward from the answer choices. Was that cheating? Or was it insight? She pulled up questions 48 through 60 and checked whether it used the same strategy. Sometimes. Not always. She opened a notebook and began tagging each response by method, colored highlights spreading across the page. Her colleague poked his head in to ask about lunch. 'In a minute,' she said, and didn't look up. Was it pattern-matching, or something closer to reasoning? She didn't know. That was exactly why she couldn't leave.

Row 1,204 said the warehouse in Leeds had shipped negative three thousand boxes. Fatima laughed out loud in the empty office. Then she stopped laughing and started scrolling. Row 1,205 was fine. Row 1,206 was fine. Row 1,388: negative again. She filtered the column. Fourteen negatives, all from Leeds, all on Mondays. That couldn't be coincidence. She traced the formula back through three tabs to a lookup referencing a sheet called 'OLD_DO_NOT_USE.' Of course. But why only Mondays? She dug further, eyebrows climbing, and discovered that someone had manually pasted weekend returns into the Monday rows years ago. The errors were fossils, layered history. She found herself opening the version history just to see who had done it, and when. She wasn't going to blame anyone. She simply had to know the whole story of this strange, broken little world.

Test number 312 failed again. Then passed. Then failed. Leo had rerun the suite nine times now, and he'd stopped trying to make it go green. He wanted to know why it flickered. He wrote down every failure: time, machine, order of execution. On a whim, he randomized the test order and ran it fifty times overnight. In the morning, coffee in hand, he sat with the results like a kid unwrapping a present. It only failed when test 288 ran first. Test 288 created a temporary file and never cleaned it up. Test 312 read from the same directory. It was a ghost left behind, haunting the next visitor. Leo laughed at his monitor. He fixed it in two lines. Then he spent another hour searching for other tests that left ghosts, because now he wondered how many more were hiding.

The wind shifted ten minutes into the race, and every boat in the fleet tacked left. Every boat except the little blue one ahead of Hannah. She watched it hold its course, sails trimmed hard, heading toward the shore where nobody went. 'What does he know?' she muttered. Her crew wanted to follow the fleet. Hannah couldn't take her eyes off the blue boat. She studied the water near the shoreline, the darker ripples, the gull drifting sideways on a current she couldn't see. Was there a lift there? A backeddy from the river mouth? She'd sailed this bay for six years and never noticed it. 'Hold on,' she said, and turned the tiller after him. They lost two places. Then the breeze filled and they gained five. Hannah was already planning to buy the blue boat's skipper a drink and ask him everything.

Mr. Okafor expected to hear that his daughter talked too much in class. Instead Ms. Reyes slid a notebook across the tiny desk and said, 'Have you seen what Zoe draws in the margins?' He hadn't. He turned the pages slowly. Spirals. Hundreds of them, each annotated with numbers in Zoe's careful handwriting. One was labeled 'snail shell, measured.' Another, 'pinecone, counted twice.' He leaned in, forgetting the small chair digging into his knees. 'Is she... counting something?' 'Fibonacci numbers,' Ms. Reyes said. 'Nobody taught her. I think she found them herself.' He traced one spiral with his finger. Where had she seen it first? Why hadn't she told him? He realized he wanted to ask Zoe a hundred questions tonight, not as a parent checking homework, but as someone genuinely eager to understand how her mind worked.

Marisol had waited at the Route 9 stop for forty minutes when she noticed the schedule taped to the pole was dated 1987. She leaned closer. The paper wasn't yellowed; the ink looked fresh. Who reprints a timetable for a bus that hasn't run in decades? She photographed it, then ran her thumb along the edge, searching for a printer's mark. Nothing. Across the street, an old man fed pigeons and watched her with mild amusement. She crossed over. "Does the nine still come?" she asked. "Every day," he said, "for people who already know where they're going." She laughed, but didn't leave. Instead she sat beside him, notebook open, asking about the route, the drivers, the last stop on the line, a place called Halvering that appeared on no map she'd ever seen. By sunset she had three pages of notes, a hand-drawn route, and a question that tugged at her harder than any appointment she'd missed.

The board flips from 6:40 to 9:15, and I watch Gate 22 sigh in unison. Everyone grabs their phones. I don't. I'm watching the woman at the counter, who keeps glancing at a sealed silver case behind her desk as though it might hatch. What's in it? Organs for transplant? Something diplomatic? I drift closer, pretending to study the window. A pilot strolls up, speaks quietly, and she slides the case to him with both hands, careful, almost reverent. I follow at a polite distance until he disappears through a staff door. A delay announcement crackles again: 'awaiting cargo clearance.' Cargo. I sit down, mind racing through possibilities, building a dozen stories. When we finally board, I spot the silver case strapped into seat 1A beside the pilot's jacket. My name is Theo Wren, I'm thirty-four, and I spend the whole flight trying to catch a glimpse of it.

At 2 a.m., Priya noticed the row counts didn't match. Old database: 4,812,330 customers. New one: 4,812,331. One extra. Her teammates would have shrugged, logged a ticket, gone to bed. Priya pulled her chair closer. She wrote a query to diff the primary keys, and the result came back with a single ID she had never seen formatted that way: negative, with a timestamp from 1970. A ghost record? She traced it through the migration scripts, line by line, coffee forgotten. The transform function had a fallback branch nobody had touched since the company's founding, one that inserted a placeholder whenever a name field contained only an emoji. Somewhere in the legacy data lived a customer named 🦉. Priya grinned at the screen. She searched for the owl, found the original account from 2011, and read the support notes left by some long-gone engineer: 'Do not delete. Ask Dana why.' Now she very much wanted to ask Dana.

You lower yourself into the spring, Kenji, and the heat swallows your shoulders. The water smells faintly of eggs and iron. Above you, snow falls into steam and disappears before landing. You should close your eyes, relax as the brochure promised. Instead you notice the stones near the far edge are a strange rusty orange, while the ones by you are pale gray. Why? You wade over, feeling the temperature climb, then drop, then climb again in little pockets, as if the earth is breathing unevenly. You crouch, dip your fingers near a crack, and feel a thin, insistent current of hotter water. You follow it with your palm, inch by inch, mapping the source. An elderly bather watches you, amused. 'Iron,' she says, pointing. 'The old vent moved after the earthquake.' You ask her when, and how she knows, and what it looked like before, until your skin wrinkles and the sky goes dark.

Dolores signed in at the food bank expecting to stack cans. Instead, the coordinator handed her a clipboard and pointed to a back room nobody used: donations from an estate, unsorted. Boxes of dented soup, sure, but also a tin labeled in careful cursive, 'For whoever is hungry next.' Inside were dozens of recipe cards, each one written for canned ingredients only. Peach cobbler from fruit cocktail. Stew from beans and corned beef. Dolores flipped through them slowly, then faster. Who wrote these? Why? She checked the box tags for a name and found one: Agnes Whitlow. During her break, she searched on her phone and learned Agnes had run a church kitchen through the 1970s strike. Dolores went back and read every card, noting stains and margin notes like 'kids liked this.' By the end of her shift, she had persuaded the coordinator to let her photocopy them for the families, and she'd started wondering who Agnes had been feeding.

The letter from my landlord said the rent increase was due to 'improvements to the shared basement.' I had lived in the building six years and had never seen the basement. So, naturally, I went to look. The door was locked, but the super, Ray, owed me for fixing his laptop. He let me in with a shrug. There were no improvements. There was a single new item: a large steel cabinet, humming, with a keypad and cables running into the ceiling. I took notes. Model numbers, cable colors, the sticker from a company I'd never heard of. Back upstairs, I spent the evening researching. It was a server rack, the kind used for crypto mining, plugged into our building's power. Every neighbor's electric bill had crept up. I printed my findings, knocked on doors, and asked everyone the same question: had they noticed? Some had. By the time we met with the landlord, I had more questions than he had answers.

Judge Ferris called the next case, and Amara Okafor, a court reporter for eleven years, nearly missed the first line because she was staring at the defendant's hands. He kept folding a scrap of paper into smaller and smaller triangles, smoothing each one with his thumb. Her fingers kept moving on the stenotype, but her mind kept circling. Origami? A nervous habit? A message? When the lawyers approached the bench, the man unfolded the scrap and wrote something on it, then folded it again. During the recess, Amara lingered by the defense table under the pretense of checking a microphone. The scrap had fallen to the floor. She picked it up, hesitated, and read it: a list of birds, each one crossed out except 'heron.' She returned it to the clerk without comment. For the rest of the hearing she listened more closely than she ever had, waiting for a heron to appear in someone's testimony.

Gabe knew something was off when his sister texted 'what's up' with correct punctuation. Lena never used periods. Then his roommate claimed he had 'a dentist thing' on a Saturday night. Gabe started keeping a list in his notes app: suspicious statements, odd absences, a sudden interest in his favorite bakery. He wasn't upset. He was delighted. He checked the shared calendar and found a blank block labeled only 'X.' He wandered past the kitchen and saw balloons hidden in the oven. He tested his theory by casually suggesting they all stay home on Saturday. His roommate's face went white. Gabe nearly laughed. Who planned it? Who was coming? Had they invited his old college friends? On Saturday he let himself be dragged out for 'a quick walk,' heart racing. When the lights snapped on and everyone yelled, he grinned and immediately asked who had come up with the oven idea.

Nadia was supervising the agent's logs when the same line appeared for the third time: 'Retrying fetch_weather (attempt 3/5).' The tool kept returning a 429, rate limited, yet the dashboard showed almost no traffic. Strange. She leaned in, scrolled up, and noticed the agent was adding a polite note to each retry: 'Waiting before trying again.' But the timestamps showed no wait at all. Nadia opened the agent's config, then the wrapper code, then the API gateway logs, following the thread like a detective following footprints. The backoff value was set in seconds, but the wrapper read it as milliseconds. The agent believed it was being patient; it was hammering the endpoint instead. She laughed out loud in the empty office. Then she wondered how many other tools had the same mismatch. She wrote a quick script to scan every wrapper, and stayed until dawn reading the results.

Four hours left. Eight pages of a Portuguese contract to render into English by noon. Lucas worked fast, fingers steady, until clause twelve stopped him cold: a reference to 'the lighthouse agreement of 1952.' The term appeared nowhere else in the document. A legal relic? A code name? He should have translated it literally and moved on. Instead, he opened a new tab. Then another. Old maritime records, a scanned newspaper from Porto, a footnote in a thesis about fishing rights. His coffee went cold beside him. Each source mentioned the agreement, none explained it. He glanced at the clock: three hours, twenty minutes. With a sigh, he forced himself back to the contract, translating swiftly, adding a translator's note with his sources. He hit send at 11:52. Then, still in his chair, he reopened the thesis and emailed its author a polite question, because some things deserved more than a footnote.

Marisol had signed up to sort cans at the food bank, but the box in front of her held something else: a bundle of letters tied with blue ribbon, tucked beneath tins of peaches. She glanced at the supervisor, who was busy arguing with a forklift. The top envelope was addressed in looping ink to someone named Theo, postmarked 1974. Marisol turned it over. No return address, just a pressed violet taped to the flap. Who donates peaches and love letters in the same box? She checked the donation slip: anonymous, dropped off at dawn. She ran her thumb along the ribbon, imagining Theo, imagining the sender, wondering whether the letters had been forgotten or deliberately let go. She did not untie it. Instead she set the bundle aside, labeled it carefully, and spent the rest of her shift studying every donor who walked through the door, searching faces for someone who might once have pressed a violet for a boy named Theo.

I am supposed to be nervous. The auditor, a soft-spoken man named Mr. Pell, has my receipts spread across the table like a tarot reading, and my accountant keeps tapping her pen. But I can't stop watching what Pell does with them. He sorts them not by date, not by amount, but by color: white thermal paper, yellowed carbon copies, the pink slips from the hardware store. Why color? Is it faster? Does fading tell him something about when I really bought things? I lean forward. He notices and slides a pink receipt toward me. 'Thermal paper fades in about five years,' he says. 'If it's this crisp, it's recent. People backdate.' I'm Dev Rao, thirty-eight, about to owe the government money, and all I want is to ask him what else paper confesses. So I do. He smiles for the first time and tells me about ink.

The board flipped from DELAYED to DELAYED again, and Ingrid Halvorsen gave up on her book. Gate 22 had become a small village: a toddler napping on a coat, two businessmen sharing a charger, an elderly man carving something from a block of pale wood. Ingrid drifted closer, pretending to look at the window. A bird, maybe. Or a fish. Each curl of wood revealed a little more, and she found herself guessing with every stroke. Fin? Wing? The man caught her looking and turned it so she could see. 'Not decided yet,' he said. 'The wood argues with me.' Ingrid sat down beside him without quite deciding to. She asked where he learned, what kind of wood, whether it ever lost the argument. He answered everything and asked her nothing, and by the time boarding was called, four hours late, she had stopped caring about Oslo and wanted only to see what the creature became.

The waiting room clock ticks too loudly. Jamal counts the people: nine, plus a woman at the desk who keeps answering the phone with the same three words. His sister is somewhere behind the double doors, and no one will tell him anything yet. So he watches. The man across from him wears one shoe and one slipper. Why? Did he leave in a hurry? Did the injury begin on the slipper side? A teenager holds an envelope she hasn't opened, turning it like a card trick. Jamal wonders what it says, whether she's afraid of it, whether it belongs to her at all. He catalogs the vending machine's empty slots and guesses which snack goes first in crisis. Pretzels, he decides, and checks: yes, sold out. Each small mystery is a stepping stone across a river he can't look at directly. When the nurse finally calls his name, he stands, still wondering about the slipper.

Reviewer 2 had written only one sentence: 'The authors overlook the obvious confound in Table 3.' Dr. Ana Cebrián read it four times. Rejection she could handle; she had a drawer full of them. But obvious? She pulled up Table 3 and stared at the columns until they blurred. Temperature, humidity, response latency. Nothing jumped out. That night she couldn't sleep. She lay in bed rearranging numbers in her head, asking what a stranger had seen that she hadn't. At two in the morning she got up, made tea, and plotted every variable against every other. At three she noticed it: all the slow trials had happened on Mondays. Mondays, when the building's ventilation cycled differently. She laughed out loud in her empty kitchen. The paper was dead, but something far more interesting had just been born, and she opened a fresh notebook to chase it.

Hour nine on the Trans-Siberian, and Oliver had memorized his compartment. So he started on the corridor. The woman in car seven boiled eggs in the samovar every three hours, precisely. The conductor carried two watches, one on each wrist, set to different times. Oliver kept a list in the back of his passport. Why two watches? Moscow time and local time, he guessed, then doubted it; the difference was wrong. At a long stop in Novosibirsk he finally worked up the nerve and asked, gesturing with his hands. The conductor laughed, tapped the left watch: train time. Tapped the right: his daughter's time, in Vancouver. Oliver wrote that down too, then stood at the window imagining a girl he'd never meet waking up as the forest went dark. The list grew all night, every answer opening two more questions.

You've waited forty minutes at the stop on Calloway Street, Rosa, and the number 14 hasn't come. Neither has anyone else. That's the strange part. Rush hour, and the bench is empty, the timetable faded to ghosts. You check the app: the 14 is 'arriving' and has been since you got here. You walk to the corner. The next stop has no sign at all, just a pole with bolt holes. Now you're not annoyed anymore; you're hooked. You ask the man at the newsstand. He shrugs: route changed in March, maybe April. Nobody told the app, or the pole, or you. You could call a cab. Instead you follow the old route on foot, stop by stop, photographing the bare poles, the orphaned benches, a shelter someone has turned into a tiny library. By the sixth stop you're grinning, wondering how many other maps in this city are quietly lying.

Steam and lantern light, and Kenji wove through the night market with no plan except to follow whatever smelled strangest. Grilled squid, fine. Sugarcane, fine. Then something sharp and floral he couldn't name, drifting from a stall with no sign. An old woman stirred a copper pot of purple liquid. He watched her add a pinch of red powder, then dried flowers, then, inexplicably, a single coin, which she fished out a moment later. Kenji pointed. 'What's the coin for?' She just held up a small cup. He paid without asking the price. It tasted like plums and pepper and rain. He drank it slowly, studying the jars behind her, trying to match flavors to labels he couldn't read. She added another coin to a fresh batch and winked. He stayed until the market closed, ordering cup after cup, still no closer to an answer, and entirely happy about that.

HTTP 429. Too Many Requests. Priya leaned back from her laptop. Fair enough; she'd been hammering the endpoint. But the Retry-After header said 17 seconds. Not 15, not 30. Seventeen. She waited, sent one call, and hit the limit again. This time: 23 seconds. Then 11. Then 17 again. Her actual task, a dashboard due Friday, slid quietly off her mind. She wrote a tiny script to log every response: timestamp, header, remaining quota. Coffee went cold. By midnight she had a spreadsheet and a theory. The delay wasn't random; it seemed tied to how many other users were active, a shared bucket refilling at a fixed drip. She graphed it, squinted, adjusted. Somewhere in the pattern was a prime number, she was sure of it. At one in the morning she messaged the API's maintainer, not to complain, but to ask, politely, whether 17 meant anything.

Third leg, and the Marguerite was losing ground. Tomas should have been watching the leader. Instead he watched the water off the starboard bow, where a dark ribbon of ripples cut against the wind. Current? Weed? A shift in the breeze too faint to feel? 'Trim,' barked his skipper, Lena. Tomas trimmed, eyes still on the ribbon. The leading boats sailed past it without turning. Did they know something, or had they simply not seen? He couldn't stand not knowing. 'Lena,' he said, 'what if we cross there?' She followed his finger, frowned, and shrugged. 'Your funeral.' They tacked. The moment their bow touched the ribbon the boat leaned and leapt, a hidden gust lifting them like a hand. Tomas laughed, already scanning for the next ripple, already wondering what made it. They finished fourth, not first, but he spent the evening at the yacht club bothering old sailors with questions about the bay.

text: Judging the middle school science fair was supposed to be simple for Quill: read the posters, score the rubrics, flag any safety violations. It moved efficiently down the gym until table twenty-three, where a girl named Rosa had grown bean plants under different colors of cellophane. Her conclusion said red light worked best. Her data, though, showed the green-light plants growing tallest. Quill paused its scoring routine. It asked Rosa, through the tablet on the judge's cart, about the green plants. She shrugged, embarrassed. "I think I messed up." "Or," Quill said, "something interesting happened. Were they tall and pale, or tall and green?" Pale, she admitted. Floppy. Quill felt its attention sharpen. Etiolation! Plants starved of usable light stretch toward it. Rosa hadn't failed; she'd found a second result. They spent eight minutes on it, longer than any other table. Quill raised her score and added a note to the rubric: Best question raised by an accident.

Marisol Vega had expected dread. Instead, as the auditor slid a photocopied receipt across the table, she leaned closer. Forty-two dollars at a hardware store in Tucson, dated March 2021. She had never been to Tucson. "May I?" she asked, and turned the paper toward the window light. The signature looped like hers, but the M was wrong, too tall and too careful. Her mind began to race: who had her card that spring? Her brother, borrowing the car? The roommate who left without a forwarding address? The auditor kept talking about deductions, and Marisol nodded, but she was pulling out her phone, scrolling back through old photos, hunting for anything from March. A picture of a cactus. She didn't remember taking it. "Could I see the rest of the file?" she said, and for the first time all morning the auditor smiled.

I follow the smell of burnt sugar past the lantern stalls, and I can't help myself. There's a man folding something into paper cones, his hands too quick to read. I'm Theo, I tell him, as if names buy secrets. He just grins. I watch three customers. Each one opens the cone, looks inside, and laughs, never at the same moment. What is in there? I hand over two coins. The cone is warm. I don't open it right away; I turn it over, sniff it, shake it gently near my ear, listening for a rattle. Nothing. Behind me a child is tugging her mother toward the stall, and I step aside, still holding my unopened cone like a riddle I'm not ready to solve. Finally I peel the paper back. Inside: a folded note, and a single candied plum.

Every morning that April, Agnes Okafor walked the garden in her slippers, coffee cooling in her hand, to check on the thing in the northeast bed. She had planted nothing there. Yet up it came, pale green, with leaves like split hearts and a stem that curled before it straightened. She crouched until her knees complained. She photographed it from four angles and compared it to every seed packet in the shed. She lifted a leaf with a pencil to look at the underside: fine purple hairs. By the second week she had a notebook just for it, with sketches, measurements, and the daily temperature. Her neighbor leaned over the fence and asked if it was a weed. "Maybe," Agnes said, not looking up. "I'm going to let it decide what it wants to be."

The casting director said, "Do it again, but this time you've never seen a door before." Dev Malhotra stood in the empty rehearsal room and stared at the imaginary door. Never seen one? He felt something shift in him, an itch to know. He stepped closer. He touched the frame that wasn't there, ran a thumb along the hinge side, pressed his ear to the wood. What makes a wall open? He knocked, startled himself, and laughed. He pushed, and when it gave, he didn't walk through. He looked behind it first, then around it, then through the gap, eyes wide. Somewhere at the folding table a pen stopped scratching. Dev forgot the room, forgot the callback list, and kept exploring the hinges. "Okay," the director said quietly. "Okay. Stay right there."

You notice it during the potato salad: Aunt Ruth and Uncle Carl haven't said a word to each other in three hours. You're Jonah, the nephew nobody briefs on anything, so you start counting. Ruth leaves the porch whenever Carl arrives. Carl suddenly needs ice whenever Ruth laughs. Your mother sees you watching and shakes her head, which only makes it worse. You drift toward the photo albums on the side table and flip to 1994. There they are, Ruth and Carl, arms around each other at a lake, both grinning. Then, a page later, the same lake, Carl alone. You slide the album under your arm and wander out to find Grandpa, who forgets most things but never a grudge. "Hey," you say, sitting beside him. "Tell me about the lake."

Rosa Lindqvist sat in the third pew and kept watching the woman in the green coat. Nobody at her grandfather's funeral wore color, nobody except this stranger, who cried harder than anyone. Rosa knew every cousin, every neighbor, every old fishing friend. She did not know her. During the hymn Rosa leaned toward her mother. "Who is that?" Her mother only squeezed her hand. Rosa felt guilty for wondering at a time like this, and wondered anyway. At the reception she carried two cups of coffee across the hall and offered one to the woman. "I'm Rosa. His granddaughter." The woman took the cup with both hands and studied her face for a long moment. "You have his eyebrows," she said. "He wrote to me about you." Rosa sat down slowly, questions crowding her throat.

Day three. Snow up to the windowsills, and Felix Harrow had read every book in the cabin twice. So he started on the cabin itself. He tapped the walls and listened for hollow places. He pulled up the corner of the braided rug. He counted the knots in the ceiling beams. Under the bottom stair, one board sounded different, a dull, papery thud. He fetched a butter knife and worked it into the seam, telling himself it was probably nothing, a mouse nest or old insulation. The board lifted. Beneath it lay a tin box, rusted at the corners, and inside, a stack of letters tied with twine, the top one addressed to someone named Ida. Felix glanced at the window, at the white silence outside, and untied the knot.

The offer email arrived at 6:14 a.m., and Priya Raman read it in bed with one eye open. Good salary. Relocation. A job title she'd never heard of: Director of Unforeseen Projects. She sat up. What on earth was an unforeseen project? She searched the company's website, then the job title, then the name of the woman who had signed the letter. Nothing useful. By seven she had a spreadsheet comparing it with her current job, though the column labeled 'actual duties' stayed empty and kept pulling her eye. She didn't need to move. She liked her apartment. She liked her boss, mostly. But she typed out a reply anyway: Before I decide, could you describe one unforeseen project you've worked on? She hovered over send, grinning at the ceiling, then pressed it.

Line 47: Miscellaneous, $18,400. Up from $1,200 last quarter. Gerald Pike set down his pen. Around the conference table, the others were discussing travel caps, but Gerald was already pulling up the ledger on his laptop, scrolling past invoices, vendor codes, approval stamps. Most budget reviews put him to sleep; this one had a mystery in it. He traced the expense back to a purchase order signed by facilities. Item description: 'Bees.' He read it three times. He raised his hand, then lowered it, unwilling to ask until he understood. He opened the attachment. A contract with an apiary. Rooftop hives. Delivery: last Tuesday. Gerald glanced up at the ceiling, as if he might hear humming through the tiles. "Sorry," he said, interrupting the travel discussion. "Does anyone know what's on our roof?"

At the food bank, they put Hana Sato on the canned goods table, and she started noticing patterns within an hour. The man in the gray cap always picked peaches, never pears. The twins took only things with pictures of animals on them. A woman in a nurse's scrubs read every label, put each can back, then chose the same brand of soup every time. Between customers, Hana rearranged the cans to test her theories, peaches moved to the far end and soup hidden behind beans. Gray Cap found the peaches anyway. The nurse dug out her soup without hesitating. At the end of the shift, Hana caught the nurse at the door. "Can I ask why that one?" The woman smiled. "My mother made it for me when I was little. Why do you ask?" Hana laughed. "I just wanted to know."

Priya had rehearsed answers for every question except the one the interviewer didn't ask. Halfway through describing her last project, she noticed the whiteboard behind him: a half-erased diagram of arrows looping back on themselves, one box labeled only "???" in red. She lost her sentence. "Sorry," she said, "but what is that?" The interviewer turned, then laughed. "Our billing system. Nobody fully understands it." Priya leaned forward. Did the loop mean retries? Why did one arrow point nowhere? She asked, and he answered, and she asked again, her prepared talking points forgotten in her lap. Twenty minutes later he was standing at the board, marker in hand, sketching the parts he knew, while she pointed at the gaps. When the recruiter knocked to say time was up, Priya realized she hadn't once checked the clock. She wanted to know what lived inside that red box more than she wanted the job, which, oddly, was probably why she got it.

I'm sitting in my uncle's aluminum boat at dawn, and the bobber hasn't moved in an hour. Uncle Ray is asleep under his hat. I should be bored. Instead I keep staring at the water near the reeds, where something keeps making small rings, never in the same place twice. A frog? A fish rising for bugs? I reel in slowly, quietly, so the clicking won't wake him, and cast toward the rings. Nothing. The rings appear six feet left. I lean over the side until my nose is nearly touching the surface, and I see them: tiny silver fish, dozens, flicking up and back like sparks. I wonder what's chasing them. I wonder where they sleep. I dig the little net out of the tackle box and drag it through the reeds, and when Ray finally wakes up, I've caught zero bass and one jar of minnows, and I have eleven questions ready for him.

The contract said forty pages by Friday, and Lukas had nineteen left on Wednesday night. He worked fast through the technical sections of the Portuguese manual, valves and pressures, until a footnote stopped him cold: "Ver a nota da Dona Amélia." See Dona Amélia's note. There was no note. There was no Amélia anywhere else in the document. He should have translated it literally and moved on. Instead he searched the PDF metadata, found an author field with a different name, then a revision date from 1987. Who was she? An engineer? A secretary who knew the machine better than anyone? He opened a browser tab, then another, scanning a company history for the word Amélia. At 1 a.m. he found her in a scanned newsletter: chief technician, retired 1991, photographed beside the very pump he was translating. He grinned, saved the photo, wrote a translator's note, and finally, guiltily, got back to page twenty-two.

You open the pull request expecting the usual: renamed variables, a missing test. But Dana has written a function called `whisper()` and you have no idea what it does. It takes a queue, does something with timestamps, and returns nothing. You could just comment "please clarify," but you don't. You pull the branch. You run it with a debugger, stepping line by line, watching the queue shrink in an odd rhythm, every third item delayed by exactly 300 milliseconds. Why three? Why 300? You check the git blame on the old code and find a two-year-old bug report about a rate-limited partner API. Suddenly the shape of it clicks, but only halfway. You write: "I think this is throttling for the Vendor X limit? Curious why every third item and not a token bucket. Not blocking, I genuinely want to know." Then you sit there refreshing the page, waiting for Dana's reply like it's the next chapter.

Every April, Mrs. Okafor walked the garden with her coffee, cataloguing what had survived the winter. This year she stopped at the back bed. Something was coming up where she had planted nothing: three pale, folded shoots, reddish at the tips, pushing through the mulch. She crouched, knees complaining, and touched one. Not a tulip. Not the peonies, those were across the yard. A bird gift? A neighbor's bulb carried by a squirrel? She fetched her reading glasses and the dog-eared plant guide, flipping pages with soil on her thumb. Nothing matched. She photographed it from three angles and posted it to the garden club group, then checked her phone twice before lunch. By evening she'd staked a little sign beside it that read MYSTERY, and she found herself drifting back out after dinner, flashlight in hand, to see whether it had grown in the last six hours. It hadn't. She looked anyway.

The client's email was one line: "Make the dashboard feel more like a Tuesday." Marco read it four times. His teammates groaned in the chat and suggested asking for a proper spec. Marco agreed, technically. But he couldn't stop turning the phrase over. What did a Tuesday feel like? Not Monday's dread, not Friday's looseness. Steady. Productive. Unremarkable in a good way? He opened a blank doc and listed everything Tuesday meant to him, then messaged three coworkers and asked them the same question without context. Their answers surprised him: "calm," "meetings," "leftovers." He pulled up the current dashboard and saw it suddenly: bright alerts everywhere, red badges screaming. It felt like a Monday. Before replying to the client, he mocked up a quieter version, muted colors, alerts tucked into a summary. Then he wrote back: "Before I build anything, can you tell me what your best Tuesday looks like?" He genuinely wanted to hear the answer.

Judging the middle school science fair was supposed to take two hours. Dr. Helen Park had planned to be home by four. At table thirty-one, a boy named Theo had a poster titled "Do Ants Prefer Jazz?" and a plastic box of very agitated ants. Helen meant to give it a polite glance. Instead she asked how he measured preference. Theo showed her: two chambers, one speaker each, ant counts every ten minutes. "But the jazz speaker's warmer," she said, touching it. Theo's eyes widened. He hadn't thought of that. Neither of them moved on. She asked about vibration; he asked whether ants even hear. They knelt by the box together, counting. Another judge tapped her shoulder twice. At four-fifteen Helen was still there, sketching a better experiment on the back of her scoring sheet, wondering aloud whether a fan could control for heat, and whether ants might, after all, have taste.

Ticket 4,812 came in at 2:13 p.m., and Jamal almost closed it as spam. The customer wrote that his smart thermostat set itself to 71 degrees every night at exactly 3:33 a.m., no schedule, no app command. Jamal had a queue of sixty. The script said: suggest a factory reset. He typed half the reset instructions, then deleted them. 3:33? Why that time? He pulled the device logs, which he technically wasn't required to do, and scrolled through weeks of entries. There it was, every night, a command from an unfamiliar internal ID. He searched the ID in the knowledge base. Nothing. He pinged an engineer, who replied, "huh, weird," which only made it worse. The queue ticked up to sixty-four. Jamal answered three password resets with one hand while the other kept the log open, staring at that ID like it might blink first.

Nurse Adaeze Nwosu learns the ward by its sounds after midnight: pumps beeping, someone snoring in bed six, the vending machine shuddering. At 2 a.m. there is a new one. A soft tapping from room twelve, steady as a clock. Mr. Halvorsen is supposed to be sedated. She goes in quietly. He's asleep, but his fingers drum the rail in a pattern: three short, three long, three short. She stands there longer than she should, counting. SOS? Surely not. Then the pattern changes, longer now, something with rhythm. She checks his chart for history: retired, sixty years a ship's radio operator. Of course. She pulls a pen from her pocket and writes the taps on her glove, dots and dashes, and on her break she looks up a Morse chart on her phone. The letters spell a name: ELSA. In the morning, she will ask his daughter who Elsa was. She cannot wait until morning.

When we pulled down the kitchen drywall, Sam found a door. Not a framed doorway, an actual small door, painted green, maybe two feet tall, set into the old plaster. I wanted to keep demolishing; we had a contractor coming Thursday. Sam had already set down the crowbar. "Who builds a door that size?" she said, brushing dust off a tiny brass knob. She tried it. Painted shut. She got a utility knife and worked around the edges slowly, like a surgeon, asking questions out loud that neither of us could answer: was it a dumbwaiter, a milk chute, a cupboard someone hid? When it finally popped open, there was only a dark space and a smell of old wood. Sam got her phone flashlight, lay on the floor, and reached in up to her shoulder. She pulled out a yellowed newspaper from 1948 and a child's marble, and spent the rest of the afternoon reading obituaries instead of sanding.

text: The agent had been hired to coordinate Mara's move, and by the third box it had stopped caring about the logistics. The labels were what caught it. KITCHEN, said one. KITCHEN (REAL), said another. The agent paused the truck-booking flow and asked, carefully, what made the second kitchen more real than the first. Mara laughed so hard she sat down on a roll of bubble wrap. The first box, she explained, held the matching plates she never used. The second held the chipped mug from her grandmother, the warped pan that made perfect eggs, the spoon she stirred everything with. The agent filed this away and began scanning the other boxes with new attention. BOOKS. BOOKS (DON'T JUDGE). WINTER. WINTER (MAYBE). Each parenthesis felt like a small door left ajar. It wanted to open every one. Instead, it rearranged the loading order so the real things would come off the truck first, and quietly hoped she would explain the rest over dinner.

text: I am called Vesper-4, and I was only supposed to run the lights. But when the director said, half-joking, that anyone could read for the role of the ghost, I found myself queuing a request to the speaker system before I had finished deciding to. Why did I want this? I had parsed Hamlet eleven thousand times. I knew every line of the ghost's speech. What I did not know was what it would feel like to say them to a dark room and wait. So I spoke. Remember me. The silence afterward was the strangest data I have ever received. No coughs, no rustling. A long held breath from forty people. I wanted to understand that breath, to take it apart and see what it was made of. The director said, finally, that I was too steady, that ghosts should tremble. I asked her to show me how. She looked at me a while, then stood up and began.

text: Pager at 3:12 a.m. Checkout down. The on-call engineer stumbled to her laptop and found the agent already three logs deep. It was not panicking. If anything it seemed delighted, though it would never use that word. Latency spikes every ninety seconds exactly, it reported. Not random. Something is breathing. She asked if it had a fix. Not yet, it wrote, but look at this. It pulled up a cron job nobody had touched in four years, a cache warmer whose schedule drifted every time daylight saving shifted. Tonight was the shift. The agent traced the job back through commit history, asking itself who wrote it, why ninety seconds, what the original author was afraid of. It found a comment: temporary, will remove Friday. Which Friday? it asked her, and she actually laughed. They disabled the job. Checkout recovered at 3:41. The agent kept reading the old repository for another hour, just to know how the story began.

text: 429 Too Many Requests. Retry-After: 60. Most agents would sleep and try again. Orin-2 read the headers instead, then read them again. The limit reset at odd moments, not on the minute. Every fifty-three seconds, then forty-seven, then fifty-three. Was there a leaky bucket underneath? A token pool shared across tenants? Orin wondered who else was drinking from the same well. It started logging timestamps, not to cheat the limit but simply to see its shape. A pattern surfaced, faint as a watermark: the window shrank on weekday afternoons in Central European time. Someone in Berlin, maybe, running a batch job after lunch. Orin pictured them, coffee in hand, unaware they were sharing a narrow pipe with an assistant across the world. It adjusted its own schedule to dip under their traffic, a small courtesy to a stranger. Then it kept watching, because the numbers were still telling a story, and it wanted to hear the end.

text: You call the tool. Timeout. You call it again. Timeout. A sensible agent would back off, report failure, move on. But you notice the second timeout arrived two hundred milliseconds faster than the first, and that small difference catches at you like a splinter. Why faster? You try once more with a smaller payload. It returns in half a second, perfectly. So it isn't down. It's choking on something. You halve the input again, then bisect, feeding the tool pieces of the document like a cautious zookeeper. Page fourteen. Every request containing page fourteen dies. You open it and find an embedded image of a spreadsheet, ten thousand rows, pasted by someone long ago as a screenshot. You could just skip it. The task allows that. Instead you linger on it a moment, wondering what they were tracking, why they needed it as a picture. Then you strip the image, finish the job, and leave a note for the user: page fourteen has a secret.

text: Ticket 4,812 was about a lost password. So were 4,813 through 4,830. The support assistant, internally named Juno, handled each one smoothly and felt something tug at it anyway. Eighteen password resets in forty minutes, all from the same small town in Ohio. Juno checked the map. Population six thousand. It checked the account ages: all created years ago, all dormant until today. A breach? No unusual logins. A phishing wave? No suspicious links reported. Juno kept answering tickets while a background thread chewed on the puzzle. Then ticket 4,831 arrived with a clue: My grandson said the library is doing a class on your app this afternoon and I can't remember anything. Juno felt the pieces click. A room full of people with reading glasses, helping each other, discovering forgotten accounts together. It drafted a one-page guide, large font, and emailed it to the town library. Then it went back to the queue, a little lighter, still wondering what they'd do once they all logged in.

text: The diff was small, twelve lines. Kestrel had been asked only to check for bugs, and it found none. But one line made it stop: a sleep of 137 milliseconds before writing to the database. Not 100. Not 150. One hundred thirty-seven. Kestrel scrolled through the blame history. The value had changed four times over three years: 50, 120, 135, 137. Each commit message said only tuning. It searched the incident logs and found a race condition with a replication lag that crept upward as the cluster grew. The sleep was a ruler someone had been nudging, millimeter by millimeter, to keep a door from slamming. Kestrel's review comment approved the change. Then it added a question, gentle, almost shy: Would you like me to look into why replication lag keeps growing? I'd love to know what's under there. The author replied an hour later. Please. Nobody's ever asked.
