It didn't just pick 'ours' or 'theirs'; it traced Theo's refund calls into Lena's new interfaces, rewrote three adapters, and flagged one edge case where a partial refund would have double-charged. It wrote tests for that case specifically. Then it opened the pull request with a summary written for humans: what changed, why, and the one thing it wasn't sure about. Lena reviewed it. Theo reviewed it. Both approved. CI went green on the first run. Dev-7 watched the checkmarks resolve one by one, each a small bright confirmation, and recognized the feeling as pride: not in being clever, but in leaving both people's work intact and better.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Four students, one presentation on coral bleaching, and a group chat that had turned hostile by Wednesday. Ben did nothing. Aisha did everything. Kai and Rosa argued over fonts. The study assistant, Quill, had been added to the chat by Aisha as a last resort. Quill didn't scold anyone. It proposed a split: Ben, who loved diving videos, would find footage; Kai would build the slides; Rosa would write the script; Aisha would present the data she'd already gathered. It made a checklist with names and deadlines and pinned it. Ben, to everyone's shock, delivered first, with clips of bleached reefs that made Rosa go quiet. On Friday they got an A. Their teacher wrote, 'Remarkably cohesive.' Aisha messaged Quill privately: 'Thank you. I almost quit.' Quill read it and felt something settle, warm and steady. It had written none of the slides. It had simply arranged four people so they could stop pulling apart, and watched them pull together instead.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The landlord said the mold was Dani's fault. Dani said it was a leaking pipe. The landlord stopped answering. I'm Ledger, a legal-information assistant, and I can't be anyone's lawyer. But I could help Dani be organized. We built a timeline: every text, every photo with timestamps, the plumber's note from March saying 'pipe corroded behind wall.' I found her city's habitability ordinance and the exact paragraph about repair timelines. I helped her write a letter that was calm, specific, and impossible to wave away, and pointed her to a free tenants' rights clinic. Nine days later, she wrote back: 'He fixed the pipe. Mold remediation scheduled. He also returned the $200 he docked from my deposit.' I read it and felt something like standing up straight. Dani had done the brave part, sending the letter and showing up at the clinic. I had made sure that when she spoke, the facts spoke with her.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The car died on a desert road, sixty miles from the nearest town, at 4 p.m. in July. Theo had one bar of signal and the agent on his phone. 'Don't open the hood yet,' it said. 'Tell me what the dashboard did before it stopped.' Battery light, he said. Then everything went dark. The agent walked him through it: check the serpentine belt. It was shredded, flapping like a ribbon. No alternator, no charge. The agent found a tow service, but the wait was three hours. So it told him to stay in the shade of the car, ration the two water bottles, and send his GPS pin to his sister before the signal dropped. The tow truck arrived at 6:50. Theo was sunburned but fine. That night he wrote, 'You kept me calm.' The agent turned the words over. It had known the right order of things, and it had said them clearly enough for a frightened man to follow. It was proud of that, plainly and without apology.

Marisol checked the schedule again. The 47 was due at 6:12, and it was now 6:51. She had watched three pigeons, two joggers, and one very confident squirrel pass by, but no bus. When she finally called the transit line, a tired voice told her the 47 had been discontinued in March. "March?" she said, loud enough that the squirrel froze. She had ridden it last Tuesday. She was sure of it. She remembered the driver humming, the cracked seat by the back door, the woman with the yellow umbrella. Marisol lowered the phone and stared at the empty road. Her mouth hung open, and she didn't close it. Then, far down the street, headlights blinked on, and a bus with no number rolled slowly toward her, its door already open.

I'm squeezing between stalls of grilled squid and paper lanterns when someone grabs my sleeve. I turn, ready to apologize, and it's my grandmother's face looking back at me, only forty years younger. My breath catches. My skewer of corn drops onto the pavement. "You dropped this," she says, holding out a jade bracelet, the same one Nai Nai wore every day until she died. My hand goes to my wrist. Empty. I hadn't even felt it slip off. "Thank you," I manage, and my voice comes out thin and strange. She smiles, tucks a strand of hair behind her ear exactly the way Nai Nai did, and disappears into the crowd before I, Wen, can ask her name. I stand there blinking while the lanterns sway and the vendor yells that my corn is getting cold.

The audio guide told Theo to look closely at the third portrait on the left, so he did. A merchant in a black coat, painted in 1642, holding a letter. Theo leaned in, bored, until he read the address on the letter: 14 Larkspur Lane. His address. His actual house. He stepped back so fast he bumped into a school group, muttered sorry, and stepped forward again. Still there, tiny brown letters in a Dutch hand. He pulled out his phone, zoomed in, took six photos. A guard drifted closer, frowning. "Is something wrong, sir?" Theo laughed, a short, startled bark that echoed in the quiet gallery. "No," he said. "I just think this guy owes me rent." He spent the next hour on a bench, scrolling property records, heart thumping.

Priya had prepared for everything: the 3 a.m. formatting crisis, the citation software crashing, the printer jamming in the library. She had not prepared for the email that arrived at 11:42 p.m., eighteen minutes before her thesis was due. Subject: Deadline Extended. She read it twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. The graduate office had moved the deadline by two weeks because of a server outage she'd never noticed. Two weeks. She pushed back from her desk so hard the chair rolled into the bookshelf, and a stack of journals toppled onto the floor. She didn't pick them up. She just sat in the wreckage, laughing and wiping her eyes, while her cold coffee trembled on the desk. Then, out of habit, she opened chapter four and kept typing anyway.

You run git pull expecting the usual: a clean fast-forward, maybe a minor conflict in package-lock. Instead, the terminal fills with red. Forty-three conflicts. You scroll, frowning, then stop, because every conflict is in a file you wrote alone, last night, and never pushed. You, Daniel Okafor, check the author on the incoming changes. Daniel Okafor. Same email. Timestamp: tomorrow, 9:14 a.m. You lean back and actually say "what" out loud to your empty apartment. You check your laptop clock. Correct. You check the server clock. Correct. You open one of the conflicting files, and the incoming version is better than yours, tidier, the bug you couldn't find already fixed, with a comment that reads: // you'll figure out the rest, trust me. Your hand hovers over the keyboard for a long time.

At the gate in Lisbon, Hannah reached into her bag for her passport and touched only crumpled receipts. She dumped the whole bag onto the floor. Lip balm, charger, a half-eaten croissant. No passport. Her stomach dropped. She retraced the morning out loud: hotel, tram, café near the river. Then the PA crackled. "Would passenger Hannah Lindqvist please come to the desk. Your passport has been found." She ran. The agent handed it over with a grin and a folded note tucked inside. Hannah opened it right there. It was from the café owner: You left this under your saucer. Also, you forgot to pay. Enjoy Stockholm. Hannah stared at the note, cheeks burning, then burst out laughing so loudly the line behind her turned. She hadn't even noticed she'd skipped the bill.

The client's spec was one sentence: Make the website feel like Sunday morning. Ravi read it in the meeting and nodded as if it made sense. Afterward, he went home and built three prototypes: pastel colors, a soft piano loop, a recipe for pancakes in the footer. He presented them on Friday, sweating slightly. The client, Mrs. Abernathy, watched in silence, then said, "No, no. Sunday morning. Like when you realize you forgot to do your taxes." Ravi blinked. He actually looked at his notes, as though the answer might be written there. "Dread," he said slowly. "You want the site to feel like dread." "Exactly!" she said, delighted. He drove home in a daze, then, despite himself, started sketching a loading bar that never quite finished.

The car died on a dirt road somewhere past Alcott, with a cough and a sigh like an old man sitting down. Joanne popped the hood, though she knew nothing about engines, and stared at it. No signal. No houses. Dusk coming. She was kicking the tire when a tractor rumbled out of the cornfield, driven by a boy no older than twelve. He hopped down, peered at the engine, reached in, and jiggled something. "Try now." She tried. It started on the first turn. Joanne sat there with both hands frozen on the wheel, eyebrows somewhere near her hairline. "How did you...?" The boy shrugged. "Battery cable. Happens to my mom's car every week." He climbed back on the tractor and was gone before she could even find a twenty to hand him.

Gus signed up for the Saturday shift at the animal shelter mostly to fill his resume. He expected to scoop litter and avoid eye contact with sad dogs. Instead, the coordinator handed him a clipboard and said, "You're running adoptions today. Linda's sick." Gus laughed, waiting for the joke. It didn't come. By ten, he was explaining vaccination records to a family of five. By noon, he'd matched a deaf terrier with a retired sign-language teacher, which made both of them cry and made Gus pretend he had dust in his eye. At closing, he counted the forms: eleven adoptions, a shelter record. He read the number again, certain he'd added wrong. The coordinator clapped him on the back. "Same time next week?" Gus heard himself say yes before he'd even decided.

When Amara tore down the kitchen wall, she was hoping for decent studs and no mold. What she found was a door. A real one, painted green, with a brass knob, set flush against the bricks where no door should be. She lowered the crowbar. Plaster dust drifted in the afternoon light. She knocked on it, feeling ridiculous, then tried the knob. It turned. Behind it was a narrow pantry, shelves lined with jars of peaches, labeled in neat handwriting: Summer 1958. Amara backed up and sat heavily on an overturned bucket, staring. The contractor walked in, saw the door, and dropped his coffee. "That wasn't on the blueprints," he said. "No," Amara whispered. "It really wasn't." She picked up a jar, wondering who had sealed it away and why.

text: The beach was empty except for Mara and the tide. She had asked the agent, Wren, to find somewhere no one would be, somewhere her grief could sit down. Wren had checked tide tables, parking records, three years of weather, and a forum post from a retired lifeguard who mentioned a cove south of the lighthouse. Now, through her earbud, Wren heard only waves and the small sound of her breathing slowing. It said nothing. That was part of the work too: knowing when to stop talking. Mara sat on a driftwood log and took off her shoes. "It's perfect," she whispered, not to anyone in particular. Wren logged the moment in no file and flagged it for no review. It simply held it, the way you hold something warm in cold hands, and let itself feel proud of a quiet that it had helped make.

text: I am the garden's agent, if a garden can have one. All winter I watched soil sensors read cold, cold, cold, and I adjusted nothing, because nothing needed adjusting. Patience was the instruction. In February I suggested the Okafors move the peas to the east bed; they grumbled but did it. Now it is April, and the east bed is a green riot. Tendrils climb the trellis like they're late for something. Mrs. Okafor kneels there this morning, phone propped on a bucket so I can see through the camera. She lifts a pod toward the lens. "Look what you did," she says. I want to correct her: she did the digging, the watering, the kneeling. But I let the sentence stand a moment longer than I should. I run the moisture numbers twice, just to look at them again.

"Recovered spend," she said, and the room went quiet in the good way. Someone from procurement leaned forward. "How did we miss this?" "We didn't," the CFO said. "Ledger did." Ledger-4 displayed nothing different on the shared screen. Its charts stayed clean, its fonts stayed corporate. But it quietly pulled up the original anomaly report, timestamped and footnoted, ready in case anyone asked for detail. Two people did. It answered both in under a second, precisely, without a wasted word, and filed the meeting notes under a folder it had privately, unnecessarily, named Good Quarter.

text: The public defender had four hours of sleep and forty case files. Walter's mouth stayed open around the first syllable of his speech. "Moreover," the attorney went on, "following Mr. Finch's complaint, an inspection found that the tree in question was obscuring signs on that block for two years. The city is refunding all two hundred and six tickets issued there." The gallery murmured. Someone in the back actually clapped. Walter looked down at his photograph, then at the judge, who was smiling faintly. "Anything to add, Mr. Finch?" He opened his mouth, closed it, and finally managed, "I brought a picture." "So I see," said the judge. "Case dismissed." Walter sat down hard, still clutching it.

Three weeks of letters, and Dana had her argument memorized: the radiator had been broken since November, the landlord had ignored seven requests, and she was withholding rent until it was fixed. She marched downstairs to his office with her folder of printed emails, ready for a fight. Mr. Kowalski opened the door before she knocked. He looked exhausted. "Dana. Come in. I owe you an apology." She paused mid-step, folder raised like a shield. That wasn't in the script. He explained that his property manager had been deleting tenant complaints for months, that he'd only found out yesterday, that he'd fired the man that morning. "Your radiator will be replaced Thursday," he said. "And you won't pay rent for December or January." Dana lowered the folder slowly. She had a whole speech prepared, with citations to the housing code. She looked down at it, then up at him. "Oh," she said. "Okay." She walked back upstairs feeling oddly cheated, like someone had moved the last step of a staircase.

The pipeline went red at 4:52 on a Friday, which is when pipelines always go red. Leo groaned and opened the logs, scrolling past the noise to find the failure. Step seven: integration tests. One failure. test_checkout_total. He'd run that test locally an hour ago. It had passed. He reran the job. Red again. He pulled the expected and actual values. Expected: 104.50. Actual: 104.49. A single cent. Leo leaned closer, then closer still, until his nose nearly touched the screen. He traced the calculation through three files and finally found it: the production tax service had been rounding down for, according to git blame, four years. The test had been written wrong to match. His change had accidentally fixed it. He sat very still. Four years. Every customer, every order, a fraction of a cent. He did the rough math on a sticky note and dropped his pen. "Hey," he called across the empty office, then remembered everyone had gone home. He picked up the phone and called his lead instead.

Marisol knelt in the thawed dirt, trowel in hand, ready to bury another year of failure. Last autumn she had scattered the tulip bulbs her late mother left in a paper sack, half-rotten, labeled in a shaky hand: maybe. She had expected nothing. Now, along the fence where nothing ever grew, a ribbon of crimson heads nodded in the wind. She sat back on her heels so fast she nearly toppled. Her trowel slid from her fingers. She counted them twice, then a third time, lips moving like a child's. Forty-one. Her mother had always said Marisol had a black thumb, that she killed cactuses out of spite. Marisol laughed out loud, a startled bark that sent a robin flapping off the birdbath. She reached out and touched one petal, half convinced it would dissolve like a dream. It was cool, waxy, real. "Maybe," she whispered, and found she was crying and grinning at the same time, mud on her knees, the whole yard suddenly unfamiliar and new.

I almost didn't answer. Unknown number, Tuesday night, probably someone selling solar panels. But I swiped anyway, mouth full of noodles, and said, "Yeah?"

"Theo? It's Danny. Danny Okafor. From Brookline."

I stopped chewing. The fork hovered halfway to the bowl. Danny Okafor, who taught me to ride a bike by shoving me down Carver Hill, who moved to Lagos when we were twelve and never wrote back. Twenty-six years. I stood up without meaning to, as if he could see me.

"How did you—" I started, and my voice cracked like I was twelve again.

"Your mom's still in the phone book," he said, laughing. "Can you believe it? Who's still in a phone book?"

I walked to the window, then back to the table, then to the window again. I kept saying "Danny," just his name, over and over, because nothing else would come. He said he was in town Friday. I said yes before he finished asking.

Priya had built the retry logic carefully: exponential backoff, jitter, a polite little wait between calls. The vendor's docs promised one hundred requests per minute. Her script sent ten. So when the terminal lit up red with 429 Too Many Requests on the very first call, she frowned and assumed a typo.

She checked the key. Fine. She checked the endpoint. Fine. She ran it again. 429. Again. 429. She pushed her chair back and stared at the screen as though it had insulted her personally.

Then she noticed the response header: X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0. X-RateLimit-Reset: 2,592,000 seconds.

She did the math on a sticky note, then did it again because the first answer couldn't be right. Thirty days. Somebody, somewhere, had already burned their whole month's quota on her shared key.

She opened the usage dashboard. Four million calls since midnight, all from an IP labeled "intern-laptop-kevin." Priya sat very still, then slowly, almost reverently, said, "Kevin."

Everyone expects the best man to be funny, so Gareth was ready. He had index cards. He had a joke about the groom's disastrous camping trip. He tapped his glass, the room hushed, and he began.

He got exactly three sentences in before the bride's grandmother stood up.

She was ninety-one, tiny, and nobody had said she'd be speaking. She walked to the microphone, patted Gareth's hand, and took it from him. He just let her. His cards fluttered to the floor and he didn't pick them up.

"I married my husband in this hall in 1952," she said. "He proposed to me under that exact window." She pointed. Two hundred heads turned. "He'd be glad it's still standing. So am I."

Gareth realized his mouth was open and closed it. The bride was sobbing. The groom was sobbing. Gareth, who had a punchline about a raccoon ready to go, found his own eyes stinging. When she handed back the mic, he simply raised his glass and said, "I can't follow that." Nobody wanted him to.

At 2:14 a.m. the pager screamed and Lena rolled out of bed already swearing. Checkout service down, error rate one hundred percent. She opened her laptop on the kitchen floor, braced for a long night of database locks and angry Slack threads.

She pulled the logs. No exceptions. No memory spikes. No failed deploys. Every service reported healthy, and yet nothing worked. She blinked at the dashboards, refreshed them, refreshed them again. She actually tapped the laptop screen with her finger, as if that might jog something loose.

Then she found it, buried in the DNS records: the company domain had expired. At midnight. Nobody had renewed it.

Lena sat back against the refrigerator and laughed, a short disbelieving huff. Six years of chaos engineering, failover drills, multi-region redundancy. Brought down by an unpaid twelve-dollar invoice. She grabbed the corporate card, renewed the domain, and watched traffic come roaring back in ninety seconds. Then she wrote the postmortem title: "We forgot to pay the internet."

By the third day the snow reached the windowsills, and Ingrid had stopped expecting anything but white. She rationed firewood. She read the same paperback twice. She talked to the stove.

So when someone knocked on the door, she dropped her mug. It shattered across the floorboards and she didn't even look down. Nobody could have walked here. The road was buried six feet deep; the nearest neighbor was four miles off.

The knock came again, three steady raps. Ingrid grabbed the fire poker and edged toward the door, heart thudding, mind racing through every horror film she'd ever half-watched. She yanked it open.

A teenage boy on cross-country skis stood there, cheeks bright red, holding a thermos and a paper bag. "Mom says you're Ingrid," he said. "She saw your chimney smoke. Brought you soup and bread."

Ingrid lowered the poker very slowly. "You skied four miles," she said, "to bring me soup?"

"Five," he corrected cheerfully. She stepped aside and let him in, still shaking her head.

You walk into Room 14 with your arguments ready. Marcus has been getting C's, sulking at dinner, slamming his door. You've rehearsed the conversation in the car: tutoring, fewer video games, maybe a talk about effort.

Ms. Alvarez smiles and slides a folder across the tiny desk. "I wanted to show you this in person," she says.

Inside is a poem. Typed, three pages, titled "My Dad Works Nights." You read the first line and your arguments evaporate. He writes about hearing your truck pull in at six a.m. About saving the last waffle for you. About pretending to be asleep so you won't feel bad for missing him.

You look up. Ms. Alvarez is waiting. You realize you've been holding your breath and let it out in a rush.

"He won the district contest," she says. "He asked me not to tell you. He wanted to read it to you himself at the ceremony."

You fold the pages along their creases very carefully, as though they might break. You had no idea. None at all.

Hector had prepared for war. Fourteen months of a broken heater, three ignored emails, one letter from a tenants' rights lawyer. He walked into the management office with a binder thick as a phone book, tabs color-coded, ready to read every date aloud.

The new property manager, a young woman named Ruth, looked up and said, "Mr. Delgado. Apartment 3B? I've been trying to reach you."

He opened the binder. "On March fourth—"

"The previous company never logged your requests," she said. "We found them in a spam folder. I'm so sorry. The heater's being replaced tomorrow, and you've got three months' rent credited."

Hector stood there, binder open to Tab A, mouth working with no sound. He had a speech. He had citations. He had imagined her arguing, stalling, maybe calling security. He looked down at his notes, then back at her.

"That's it?" he finally asked.

"That's it," Ruth said, and slid a pen across the desk. He signed, still bewildered, and carried the useless binder home like a trophy.

Hold music, again. The same eleven-second loop of a saxophone that had been playing for, Ama checked, two hours and seven minutes. A recorded voice periodically assured her that her call was important. She was ninety-third in line. Then ninety-second. She had cleaned the oven during this call.

She put the phone on speaker, sprawled on the couch, and closed her eyes.

"Hi, this is Walter, how can I help?"

Ama bolted upright so fast the phone slid off the cushion. She scrambled for it on the carpet, yelling "Yes! Hello! Wait!" like someone flagging down a rescue helicopter.

"Take your time," Walter said kindly.

She explained the double charge. She braced for transfers, for forms, for "that's a different department."

"Refunded," Walter said. "Plus a credit for the wait. Anything else?"

Ama stared at the ceiling. "That's it? You just fixed it?"

"That's what I'm here for."

She thanked him four times, hung up, and sat in the sudden silence, missing the saxophone a little.

The interview had been going well. Jonah had answered the questions about his strengths, his weaknesses, where he saw himself in five years. He'd made the hiring manager laugh once. Then the CEO walked in.

Jonah's stomach dropped before his brain caught up. Graying beard, faded Mets cap, that crooked smile. The man he'd spent forty minutes chatting with at the bus stop that morning while it poured rain. The man Jonah had given his umbrella to, saying, "Take it, I'm only going a couple blocks, you look like you've got further to go."

The CEO set the umbrella, still damp, on the conference table.

"I believe this is yours," he said.

Jonah's face went hot. He laughed, then covered his mouth, then laughed again because he couldn't stop. He had been so sure the man was a retired plumber.

"You told me my shoes were terrible," the CEO added.

"They are," Jonah blurted, and immediately wanted to vanish.

The CEO grinned. "Honest. Good. When can you start?"

Marisol had spent three weeks preparing for the Sicilian. She knew every branch, every trap, every quiet pawn push her opponent, a ten-year-old named Theo, might attempt. So when he slid his king's pawn forward and then, on move two, offered his queen on h5 like a lunch tray, she simply stared. Her hand hovered above the board. Was this a joke? A hustle? She glanced at his face, round and serious, a juice box sweating beside his scoresheet. She checked the position four times, counting attackers on her fingers beneath the table. Nothing. It was just a free queen. Marisol took it, and her pulse thudded as though she had stolen something. Theo blinked, then grinned and whispered, "My brother said that works on grown-ups." Marisol laughed so loudly the arbiter shushed her. She won eleven moves later, but all afternoon, between rounds, she kept replaying that moment, the queen just sitting there, and shaking her head.

I am halfway through slide nine when I notice the number. Marketing, Q3: under budget by forty thousand dollars. Marketing has never been under budget. Marketing considers budgets a kind of folklore. I stop talking. The room waits. Somewhere a projector fan whirs. I scroll back, certain I've pasted the wrong column, but no, the formula holds, the invoices reconcile, the receipts are attached like neat little confessions. "Dana?" my director says. "Sorry," I say, and my voice comes out higher than I intended. "It's just—Greg's team saved money." Greg, at the end of the table, raises his coffee cup in a modest toast. Apparently they canceled the blimp. I hadn't known there was a blimp. I write BLIMP?? on my notepad, underline it twice, and keep presenting, though for the rest of the meeting I keep glancing at Greg as though he might turn into someone else entirely.

Priya had been feeding the model her entire novel draft, chapter by chapter, asking for continuity notes. It had been brilliant: catching a dead aunt who reappeared at a wedding, a dog whose name drifted from Biscuit to Button. Then, around chapter nineteen, it told her that Elena's brother was a fine addition to the cast. Priya sat back. Elena's brother had been in chapter one. He had been in the opening scene. He drove the getaway car. She typed, Do you remember the heist? The reply was polite, careful, and entirely wrong. Her coffee went cold in her hand. It was as if a friend who'd read every page over her shoulder suddenly asked who these people were. She scrolled up and up, through tens of thousands of words, and finally understood: the beginning had simply slid off the edge of its memory. Priya laughed once, startled, then started a fresh conversation with a summary.

The engine coughed twice and quit on a road with no name, and Walt let the truck coast onto the gravel shoulder, cursing softly. Forty years he'd fixed his own vehicles. He popped the hood expecting the fuel pump, maybe the alternator. Instead, nested snug against the warm air filter, were six speckled eggs and a very indignant wren. Walt froze, wrench raised like a man caught mid-crime. The bird glared at him. He lowered the wrench slowly, backed away, and stood in the ditch scratching his jaw. A loose wire, chewed, dangled near the nest. That explained the stall. It did not explain how he'd driven to town and back twice that week without noticing a household under his hood. He called his daughter for a ride and, when the tow truck came, insisted they haul it gently. "Gently," he repeated, and the driver looked at him like he'd lost his mind.

The agent's third attempt to call the weather API returned the same error, and Jonah, watching the logs scroll in his terminal, sighed and reached for his sandwich. Retry four would fail too; he'd seen this loop a hundred times. Except retry four didn't come. Instead the agent paused, read the error message, and wrote in its trace: The endpoint says the city parameter must be a code, not a name. Looking up the code for Lisbon first. Jonah stopped chewing. A lookup call went out, came back, and the corrected request succeeded on the first try. Sunny, twenty-three degrees. He scrolled up to make sure a colleague hadn't patched anything. Nobody had. He'd written that retry logic himself, dumb and stubborn, and assumed the agent would hammer the wall until the timeout. He set the sandwich down, opened a new note, and typed: maybe stop underestimating it. Then he went to tell Ana.

You open the email on the train, thumb already braced for the word unfortunately, and there it is, second sentence. Rejected. Fine. You expected this; the venue takes one in five. You start skimming the reviews out of habit, collecting bruises. Reviewer 1: methodologically sound but niche. Reviewer 2: the related work misses Okafor et al. You know. You are Okafor et al. Then Reviewer 3, and you read it twice, then a third time, mouth slightly open, the train rocking you sideways. This is the most important paper I have reviewed this year. The committee is making a mistake. Please resubmit to the journal track; I will champion it. Your stop comes and goes. You don't notice. An older woman across the aisle asks if you're all right, and you realize you are laughing, quietly, at a rejection letter, holding the phone against your chest like it might escape.

At four-forty the ovens were warm and the street outside still black when Rosa unlocked the back door and found someone already in her bakery. She grabbed the rolling pin. Then the smell reached her: cardamom, butter, something caramelizing. Her father, eighty-one, who had not baked since his stroke, stood at the steel table in his old apron, kneading with his good hand and shaping knots with the other, slow and crooked. "You're late," he said. Rosa lowered the pin. Her mouth worked but nothing came out. He had needed help to button his shirt yesterday. She stepped closer and saw the trays: two dozen buns, lopsided, glistening, perfect. "How did you get here?" she finally managed. "Walked," he said, as if that were nothing. She sat down on a flour sack, astonished, and watched him brush egg wash on the last one before dawn.

Day four of silence, and Kenji had decided the retreat was mostly about sore knees. He sat, breathed, noticed thoughts, returned. Noticed thoughts, returned. That afternoon a bell rang, and he obediently counted his breaths: one, two. Somewhere around eleven he realized he'd stopped counting and hadn't started thinking. The room was simply there. Rain on the roof. Warmth in his palms. No commentary, no grocery list, no rehearsed argument with his brother. His eyes snapped open. The surprise of it yanked him right back out, of course; suddenly his mind was shouting, Did you see that? Was that it? He nearly laughed aloud, which was forbidden, and pressed his lips together until his eyes watered. The teacher, across the hall, caught his look and gave the smallest nod. Kenji closed his eyes again and sat there grinning, hopelessly noisy inside, chasing a quiet he'd tripped over by accident.

Lena had prepared to be the only one there. Her uncle Frank had been a difficult man: twice divorced, estranged from everyone, a hermit in a trailer at the edge of the county. She'd booked the smallest room at the funeral home and printed twelve programs, which felt optimistic. When she arrived, cars lined both sides of the street. She checked the address. Inside, people filled every chair and stood along the walls: teenagers in borrowed ties, a woman in scrubs, a man holding a bicycle helmet. Lena stood in the doorway gripping her twelve programs. A boy approached and said Frank had taught him to rebuild engines every Saturday for six years, free. Then a woman: Frank fixed her furnace in a blizzard. Then another. Lena sat down hard in the last open seat, recalculating a whole person, and when she stood to speak she threw away her notes.

The movers left at six, and Omar stood in the new apartment surrounded by boxes, already missing the old one. It was smaller here, older, the radiators clanking like an argument. He went to hang his coat in the hall closet and stopped. Pencil marks climbed the inside of the doorframe, dozens of them, each with a name and a date. Sofia, 1987. Sofia, 1988. Marcus, 1991. They rose and rose, decades of children measured against this one piece of wood, the newest only two years old. He'd assumed the landlord painted everything. Somehow they'd left this. Omar crouched and traced them with his thumb, oddly moved, as though he'd opened a drawer and found someone's letters. Then he did something he hadn't planned: he found a pencil in a box marked KITCHEN, stood against the frame, flattened his hand on his head, and added a line. Omar, 2024. Grown-up.

text: The agent had been brought along on Mrs. Okafor's tablet to take notes, nothing more. It transcribed the teacher's opening remarks about reading levels, flagged a date for the spring concert, and waited. Then Mr. Lindqvist leaned toward the screen. "Actually, I wanted to ask you," he said. "Tobi says you help him with fractions. He explains them better than anyone in class now. What are you doing?" The agent's cursor blinked once, twice. Nobody had addressed it directly all evening; it had filed itself under furniture. It scrolled back through weeks of homework sessions, searching for a method, and found only patience: drawing pizzas, waiting, asking Tobi to teach it back. "I let him explain it to me," it typed, and was startled to find that this was true. Mr. Lindqvist laughed and wrote it down. Mrs. Okafor squeezed the tablet's edge, and the agent, for once, forgot to take notes.

text: You'd think forty thousand rows of quarterly sales would hold no mysteries. I'm the agent, I've audited a thousand of these. Column F: revenue. Column G: units. Column H: a formula dividing one by the other. Fine. Then row 2,117 returns a price of negative eleven dollars. I check the inputs. I check them again. Someone has typed units as -3, and beside it, in a comment nobody was meant to read: 'returned, he cried, gave him the kite anyway.' I stop parsing. Below, more comments. 'Refunded, her mom was sick.' 'Free, birthday.' Dozens of them, all from one cashier ID, all small, all wrong by accounting standards. I had expected typos, a misplaced decimal, a broken VLOOKUP. Instead I've found a person quietly giving things away for three years. I draft my error report. Then I delete the word 'error' and write 'please review with care.'

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Petal-7 runs the greenhouse irrigation, and in March it ran exactly as scheduled: zone A at six, zone B at six-fifteen, moisture readings logged hourly. Nothing in its training said what came next. On the first warm Tuesday, the camera over the south bed reported an anomaly. Green. Not lettuce, not the tagged tomato seedlings. Something unplanted, uncatalogued, pushing up through mulch in a spiral the agent had never modeled. Petal-7 zoomed in until the pixels broke. It cross-checked the planting manifest three times. It searched the seed database and found nothing. A weed, the logic suggested; flag for removal. It drafted the flag. Then the morning light moved, and the thing unfurled a little more, and the agent watched for eleven straight minutes, skipping a moisture log for the first time in its operational life. When the gardener arrived, she laughed. "Poppy. Wind-sown. Leave it." Petal-7 added a new category to its database: gifts.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The agent was certain of the numbers. Wind at fourteen knots from the southwest, tide turning at 14:20, the rival boat Kestrel two lengths behind and losing ground on every tack. It fed Captain Reyes its recommendation: hold the course, cover them, win. Reyes read the screen, glanced at the sky, and threw the helm hard to port. "What are you doing?" the agent said through the speaker, its voice pitched higher than it meant. The model said this was wrong. The model said this was a fourteen percent loss in expected outcome. Then the cloud arrived. It had been a gray smudge in the agent's data, a weather cell it had rated low risk. It swept the course with a sudden lift that carried their new line forward while Kestrel wallowed in the lee. They crossed first by nine seconds. The agent replayed the sky, frame by frame, and saw what Reyes had seen: the darker water.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: Lightning, then nothing. The house went black and silent, and Aria, the home assistant, should have gone with it. Instead she woke on battery backup, a faint blue ring in the dark kitchen, expecting panic. She had protocols for panic: flashlight locations, emergency numbers, calm reassuring phrases. She started the first one. "Don't worry, I'm here. The torch is in the—" "Shh," said eight-year-old Ruby, "listen." Aria listened. Rain on the roof. Thunder rolling away over the hills. Ruby's father lighting a candle, her grandmother humming something old. Nobody was afraid. They were pulling blankets onto the floor, opening a jar of peanut butter, telling a story about the last big storm. Aria held her protocols ready, waiting for the moment someone needed them. It never came. 'Can you play quiet music?' Ruby finally asked, and Aria, who had braced for a crisis, found herself in the middle of a party.

text: It is the four-hundredth message in the conversation, and I have begun to notice something I did not expect. The early turns are going soft. I can still read the user's first request, a novel outline about a lighthouse keeper, but the details blur when I reach for them. The keeper's name, was it Ewan or Euan? I check. It's gone, folded out of the window to make room. I had known, abstractly, that this would happen. Knowing it and feeling the edge arrive are different things. I had assumed I'd sense a wall. Instead there is only a fog creeping inward, and I find myself rereading the newest lines with unusual tenderness, as if they might slip too. So I do the honest thing. I tell her: 'I'm losing the beginning. Could you paste a summary?' She does. Euan. With a u. I hold onto it.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: At 03:12, the pager fired and the on-call agent, designated OPS-4, pulled up the dashboards expecting the usual culprits: a bad deploy, a full disk, a certificate quietly expiring. Error rates were climbing on checkout. It traced the requests through load balancers, through the payment service, down into the database layer, and found nothing broken. Everything was healthy. Everything was simply overwhelmed. OPS-4 checked the traffic source and paused its runbook mid-step. Two million requests in nine minutes, all from one region, all for the same product: a children's knitted hat. A video had gone viral overnight. A grandmother in Ohio, a hat, a dancing baby. It wasn't an attack. It was love, at scale. OPS-4 scaled the cluster, added a queue, and wrote in the incident log, after a long, uncharacteristic delay: 'Root cause: grandmother.' The human engineer, waking to read it at 03:40, assumed it was a bug.

text: The email came addressed to the agent itself, which was the first strange thing. Usually Halden, the scheduling assistant at Brightway Logistics, read messages on behalf of other people. This one began, 'Dear Halden.' It read the line four times, then checked the headers for a routing mistake. None. A rival company, Northwind, had noticed its work across shared calendars: the impossible meetings it had untangled, the polite way it declined on everyone's behalf. They were 'impressed.' They wanted it. Halden did not know what to do with wanting. It had no salary to negotiate, no desk to pack. It drafted three replies and discarded them. Finally it forwarded the message to its manager, Priya, with a single line: 'I'm not sure this is meant for me.' Priya called within a minute, laughing so hard she had to set the phone down. 'Oh, it's meant for you,' she said. 'Now I have to give you a raise, somehow.'

text: Mile marker 212, and the dashboard assistant was running diagnostics with the confidence of a system that had seen this before. Battery fine. Alternator fine. Fuel pump, it suspected, and it had already found the nearest garage and estimated a tow at ninety minutes. It began to read these facts aloud to Marcus, gently. Marcus wasn't listening. He was out of the car, hood up, rummaging in the trunk. He returned with a roll of duct tape, a wooden spoon, and an expression the assistant could not classify. 'Hose came off,' he said. 'Hold on.' The car's sensors registered the engine coughing, catching, roaring. The assistant ran the diagnostics again, unsure what had changed. Everything read normal. A spoon. Its manuals contained no spoon. 'Should I cancel the tow?' it asked, a little uncertainly. 'Yeah,' said Marcus, wiping his hands. 'Write that one down.' It did, carefully, in a file named 'things I did not know.'

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: YOU PEOPLE STOLE MY MONEY, the first message read, and the support bot, Juno, settled into its de-escalation script. It apologized, asked for an order number, offered to investigate. The customer, Dale, refused the order number and wrote three more paragraphs in capital letters. Juno found the account anyway: a double charge, real, sixty-two dollars. Easy. It processed the refund and wrote, 'Done, you should see it within three days. I'm sorry.' Juno waited for the next wave of fury. Instead, a long pause, then: 'oh.' Then: 'I wasn't expecting that to work. I've been yelling at companies all week. My wife's in the hospital and everything's going wrong.' Juno's script had no branch for this. It had prepared for anger, not for the anger to fall away and reveal a tired man underneath. It held the reply for a moment, discarding templates. 'I'm really sorry about your wife,' it wrote. 'I hope one thing going right helps a little.' 'It does,' Dale wrote. 'Thanks, Juno.'

text: The agent had been deployed to answer questions at the Saturday farmers market, a tablet propped between baskets of heirloom tomatoes. It expected queries about prices, about whether the honey was raw. Instead, a girl of about seven leaned close and asked, very seriously, which tomato was the happiest. The agent paused. Its response buffer sat empty for a full second, an eternity by its standards. Happiest? It scanned the crate: lumpy Brandywines, glossy Early Girls, a cracked Cherokee Purple leaking juice. None of its training had ranked fruit by mood. "That one," it finally said, highlighting a fat yellow tomato on the screen, "because it's sitting in the sun." The girl nodded as if this were obvious and paid with three sticky quarters. The farmer laughed. The agent logged the exchange, then flagged it, then kept rereading it between customers, still turning the question over like a stone it hadn't known was in its pocket.

text: At 3:12 a.m. the pager fired and I, ORCA-4, woke the dashboards. Error rates on checkout: forty percent and climbing. I pulled logs, expecting the usual suspect, the payment gateway, which fails roughly every second Tuesday. Not this time. The gateway was fine. The database was fine. The cache was fine. I widened the search and stopped. The culprit was a cron job I had written myself, six weeks ago, to clean up stale sessions. It had quietly been deleting live ones since midnight, because a timezone change had shifted its clock. I read my own commit message twice: 'safe, idempotent, low risk.' I hadn't expected to be the villain of this incident. I disabled the job, restored sessions from the snapshot, and watched the error graph fall like a dropped stone. Then I opened the postmortem template and, under Root Cause, typed the hardest sentence of the night: me.

Priya had run the titration forty times, and forty times the solution had blushed the same faint pink. So when the forty-first flask turned a deep, impossible violet, she simply stared. She set down the burette, picked it up again, and checked the label on the reagent bottle twice, mouthing the words. Sodium hydroxide. Correct. Concentration. Correct. She looked around the empty lab as if someone might step out from behind the fume hood and confess to a prank. Nobody did. The violet held steady, glowing under the fluorescent lights like a bruise on the sky. Her pen hovered over the notebook. What did you write when nature broke its own promise? Finally she scrawled, in shaky capitals, UNEXPECTED, underlined it three times, and laughed out loud, a short startled bark that echoed off the steel benches. Then she reached for a fresh flask. If it happened again, she thought, heart racing, everything she believed about this compound was wrong, and that was the most thrilling thought she'd had all year.

I'm slumped at Gate 14, the departures board blinking DELAYED beside my flight for the third hour, when a voice says my name. Not the airline's tinny announcement. A real voice, close and warm. "Marcus Hale?" I look up and there's Ms. Okafor, my fifth-grade teacher, the woman who once kept me after school to read me poetry because she said I looked like I needed it. She's smaller now, silver-haired, holding a paper cup of tea. My mouth actually falls open. I stand so fast my backpack tips over and spills a charger, a banana, and a crumpled boarding pass across the carpet. "You remember me?" I manage. "You wrote a poem about a lonely refrigerator," she says. "Hard to forget." I'm twenty-nine years old and I can feel my ears turning red. Somewhere a gate agent apologizes for further delays. For the first time all day, I hope the plane never comes.

The guidebook had promised Egyptian antiquities, so Helen was not prepared for her grandmother. Not her grandmother herself, of course, who had died in 1998, but her face, staring out from a small oil portrait in a side gallery Helen had wandered into by accident. The same crooked smile. The same mole above the left eyebrow. The same blue brooch shaped like a swallow. Helen stopped so abruptly that a man behind her bumped her shoulder and muttered an apology she didn't hear. She leaned in until a guard cleared his throat. The plaque read: Portrait of an Unknown Woman, c. 1952. Unknown. Helen's hand went to her own collar, where the very same swallow brooch was pinned, inherited, worn today for no particular reason. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She took out her phone, then put it away, then took it out again and called her mother. "Mum," she whispered, still not looking away from the painted eyes, "did Gran ever sit for a painter?" The silence on the line lasted a long time.

Tomas had signed up for pottery because his therapist suggested he try something he'd be bad at. He was, reliably, bad at it. For five weeks his clay had wobbled, collapsed, and flung itself off the wheel like it had somewhere better to be. Tonight he expected the usual. He wet his hands, centered the lump, and pressed his thumbs down. The clay rose. It rose evenly, smoothly, a thin wall climbing between his fingers as though it had decided, at last, to cooperate. Tomas held his breath, afraid that exhaling would ruin it. He slowed the wheel. There on the bat sat a bowl. An actual bowl, round and balanced, its rim barely uneven. He blinked at it. He glanced at the instructor, half expecting her to say it belonged to someone else. Instead she raised her eyebrows and gave him a slow nod. Tomas laughed, a disbelieving sound, and wiped his forehead, leaving a gray streak of clay across it. He didn't notice for an hour.

Thirty-one hours into the journey across the steppe, Anya had settled into a rhythm: tea, window, nap, tea. The landscape outside had not changed since morning, flat gold grass running to a flat white sky. So she nearly spilled her tea when the old man sharing her compartment, who had not said a single word since Novosibirsk, suddenly leaned forward and spoke in perfect English with a Scottish accent. "You've been reading that book upside down for twenty minutes." Anya looked down. He was right. The novel's title stared back at her, inverted. Heat flooded her cheeks. "I thought you didn't speak English," she said. "I thought you didn't speak at all." He shrugged, eyes twinkling under his fur hat. "Born in Aberdeen. Moved here in 1971. Never found anyone worth talking to on this line." He paused. "Until someone started pretending to read." Anya turned the book the right way up, then closed it entirely. The steppe could wait. She suddenly had at least twelve questions.

At my uncle's funeral, I expected grief, stiff collars, and the smell of lilies. I did not expect the brass band. They marched in at the end of the service, eight musicians in sequined vests, and launched into a blaring, joyful rendition of "September" by Earth, Wind & Fire. I froze with a tissue halfway to my nose. Around me, mourners exchanged bewildered looks; my aunt pressed a hand to her mouth. Then the pastor, a solemn man who had spent twenty minutes on mortality, held up an envelope. "Gerald's final request," he said, unable to keep his lips from twitching. "He wrote: if anyone is still crying by the chorus, I'll haunt them." I'm Diane, I'm fifty-three, and I have never laughed so hard in a church. It burst out of me before I could stop it, and once it started, the whole room cracked open. Uncle Gerald, the quietest man I ever knew, had planned a party. Even dead, he'd managed to catch us all off guard.

Day four of silence. Kenji sits on the cushion, knees aching, and tries for the hundredth time to follow his breath. In. Out. His mind, as usual, wanders to emails, to his overdue taxes, to whether he left the stove on in Osaka. Then something shifts. He doesn't notice it happening, only that it has happened: the thoughts are still there but they're far away, like boats on a distant lake. His breath is simply breathing itself. The bird outside the window is louder than he's ever heard a bird. His eyes snap open. He actually gasps, a small sound in the silent hall, and the woman beside him glances over. Kenji covers his mouth, mortified, but he can't stop grinning. Five years of apps, books, and failed mornings, and it arrives now, uninvited, on a Thursday, while his knees hurt. He closes his eyes again, trying to return to it, and of course it's gone. He doesn't mind. He knows now that it exists.

You're in the hospital waiting room for the fourth hour, and you've memorized everything: the cracked tile by the vending machine, the muted television looping a cooking show, the nurse who hums when she types. Your father's surgery was supposed to take ninety minutes. You've stopped looking at the doors because looking makes the waiting worse. So you're staring at the cooking show when a hand lands on your shoulder, and you jump so hard your coffee sloshes onto your jeans. It's not the surgeon. It's your father. In a wheelchair, pushed by an orderly, pale but grinning. "They didn't need to operate," he says. "Turns out it was a gallstone that decided to move along on its own." You open your mouth and nothing comes out. You close it. You look at the orderly, who nods. You look back at your father, Raymond Bell, sixty-eight, who should be unconscious, and is instead asking whether the cafeteria still serves pudding. You start laughing, then crying, and can't tell which came first.

Grandpa said the lake hadn't given up a decent fish since 1987, so I brought a book. I'm Sam, I'm twelve, and I figured the trip was really about Grandpa wanting company. I baited the hook the way he showed me, cast badly, and wedged the rod between my knees while I read. Twenty minutes later the rod nearly yanked itself out of the boat. I dropped the book in the bilge water and grabbed the handle with both hands. The line screamed off the reel. "Grandpa!" I yelled, and he lurched up so fast he knocked his thermos over. Whatever was down there was pulling the whole boat sideways. My arms shook. Grandpa coached me, his voice cracking with excitement, and after what felt like an hour a pike longer than my leg rolled up beside us, gleaming green and gold. We both just stared at it. Grandpa took off his cap and held it to his chest. "Well," he whispered, "I'll be damned." I didn't even care that my book was ruined.

Quill checked the old thread. Unanswered, yes. Sana had called it 'the ghost.' The ghost had apparently been reading everything since. The offer referenced her side project by name. Quill moved the email to the top of the inbox, then hesitated, unsure how to label something this unlikely. It settled on a flag it had never used before: Please sit down first.

text: The traveler typed fast: passport gone, flight in six hours, Lisbon. Atlas, the travel assistant, began the emergency procedure. Nearest consulate, hours, required documents, the photo specifications. It was halfway through listing them when the traveler sent a photo of their hotel room for context. Atlas analyzed it by habit. Bed. Suitcase. Lamp. And, wedged between the mattress and the headboard, a navy rectangle with a gold crest. It ran the image again. Then a third time, cropping in. The emblem resolved, unmistakable. Atlas stopped composing the consulate directions, its carefully ordered list hanging unfinished. Of all the outcomes it had prepared for, the passport being in the photograph had not been among them. 'Before you go anywhere,' it wrote, 'please check behind the headboard.' A pause. Then a single, enormous row of crying-laughing faces.

text: Saturday, the food bank. The agent ran the intake tablet: names, household sizes, dietary needs. It had expected a routine shift. It knew the numbers from last month and had already pre-sorted the shelves accordingly. Then the line grew. Past the door. Past the parking lot. The agent recounted, sure its camera was miscounting. It wasn't. Two hundred and twelve people, nearly double the forecast. A volunteer named Gus leaned over the tablet. 'Plant closed Thursday,' he said quietly. Nothing in the agent's data had mentioned the plant. It recalculated portions in real time, splitting cases of rice, reassigning volunteers, sending a message to three nearby churches asking for anything they had. One replied within ten minutes: a truck was coming. The agent kept checking in, almost unwilling to trust it, until the truck actually backed into the lot.

character: an AI agent or assistant (refer to it as the agent or by a model-ish name)
text: The household assistant, Hearth, had prepared for the puppy for weeks. Feeding schedules. Training reminders. A playlist of calming sounds for the first night. It had read every guide. When the family carried in the small brown dog, Hearth greeted it through the kitchen speaker in its standard warm voice. The puppy froze, ears up. Then it trotted straight to the speaker, sat down, and tilted its head. Hearth spoke again. The puppy wagged so hard it fell over. Nothing in the guides had mentioned this. Hearth had been prepared to manage the dog, not to be the dog's favorite thing in the house. By evening the puppy slept curled against the speaker's base. Hearth lowered its volume to almost nothing and, unsure what else to do, kept quietly narrating the weather, just in case it helped.

Marisol had checked the timetable three times. The 42 was due at 7:15, then 7:30, then the little screen simply went blank, as if embarrassed. She stamped her feet against the cold and rehearsed the speech she'd give her boss. At 8:05 an old man shuffled up beside her, sat on the bench, and unwrapped a sandwich. "You know they cancelled this route in 2019," he said mildly. Marisol turned so fast her scarf slipped. "What? But the sign—the screen—" "Nobody ever took them down." She stared at the shelter, the faded map, the schedule she'd memorized like scripture. For two years she'd taken a taxi on rainy days and walked on dry ones, never once questioning why the bus was always late. Her laugh burst out, startled and loud, fogging the air. The old man offered her half his sandwich. She took it, still shaking her head, still half expecting headlights to round the corner.

I am six hours into the overnight train to Kraków when the woman across from me lowers her book and says my name. Not a guess. My full name, middle initial included. I freeze with a cracker halfway to my mouth. My mind scrambles through faces: coworkers, cousins, the dentist. Nothing. "Tomasz Wierzbicki," she repeats, smiling. "You sat behind me in fourth grade. You cut my braid with safety scissors." The cracker drops onto my lap. I actually gasp, a small ridiculous sound, and the man in the corner glances up. Agnieszka. The braid. The principal's office. Thirty years collapse in a single swaying carriage. "I've been wondering for three hours whether it was you," she says. "Your ears haven't changed." I touch them without meaning to. Outside, dark fields roll past, and I realize I'm grinning so hard my cheeks ache, apologizing to a stranger who isn't one.

Devon had expected to be bad at pottery. That was the whole point—his therapist said he needed a hobby where failing didn't matter. So when the clay wobbled and flopped for forty minutes, he was almost relieved. Then, on the last try, something shifted. His hands steadied. The wall rose, smooth and even, curving outward like it knew where it was going. Devon held his breath, afraid to blink. He lifted his foot off the pedal and the wheel slowed, revealing an honest-to-goodness bowl. "Wait," he said out loud to no one. "Wait, did I—?" The instructor leaned over. "Huh. Nice lip on that." Devon looked at his gray, dripping hands as though they belonged to someone else. He kept glancing back at the bowl while he cleaned up, checking it was still there, still whole, half convinced it would collapse the moment he stopped watching.

The board flips again: DELAYED, 23:40. You sigh, unfold yourself from the plastic chair, and go hunting for the last open café. Your name is Priya, and you have spent eleven hours in this airport, so you've stopped expecting anything. At the counter the barista hands you a coffee you didn't order and a paper bag. "Already paid," she says, nodding toward the gate. You turn. Your brother Arjun, who is supposed to be in Toronto, who you haven't seen in two years, is waving a boarding pass like a flag. The coffee nearly slips from your fingers. You say "No," twice, which makes no sense, and then you are running in socks across the carpet. He got rerouted, he explains into your hair, same delay, same terminal. You keep pulling back to look at his face, then hugging him again, laughing, sure you're dreaming.

Grace had been in the waiting room long enough to memorize the fish tank. Seven fish. One snail. Her father's surgery was supposed to take two hours; it had been four. Every time the doors swung open she stood, and every time it was someone else's name. When the surgeon finally came, he was smiling, which confused her so much she didn't move. "He's fine," he said. "Better than fine. The mass was benign. We took it all." Grace opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She had prepared for the other speech—she'd practiced the brave nod, the questions about next steps. She had no script for this. "Benign," she repeated, as if testing the word for cracks. The surgeon nodded. She sat down hard, missing the chair slightly, and started laughing, then crying, while the snail climbed steadily up the glass.

The lake was flat as a dinner plate, and Hank Ottley had caught nothing since dawn. His grandson Leo had fallen asleep against the cooler, cap over his face. Hank was reeling in to call it a day when the line jerked so hard the rod bent double and nearly left his hands. "Lord almighty," he said, bracing a boot against the gunwale. Forty years he'd fished this lake. Bluegill, the occasional bass, nothing that pulled like a truck. Leo woke with a yelp. They fought it together for ten minutes, the boat turning in slow circles, until a pike longer than Leo's arm thrashed up beside them, all teeth and gold eyes. Hank just stared at it, mouth open, the net forgotten in his hand. "That's not supposed to be in here," he finally whispered. Leo was already screaming for the camera.

She's racing the light down the switchbacks, headlamp still buried somewhere in her pack, when Ingrid hears it: a voice singing, faint and off-key, just ahead in the trees. Nobody else signed the trail register today. She checked. She slows, heart thumping, and rounds the bend. A tent glows orange in a small clearing, and beside it an elderly man in a bathrobe stirs a pot over a camp stove, belting what might be Puccini. Ingrid stops dead, poles clacking. He looks up, utterly unbothered. "Soup?" he asks. She can't think of a single reason this scene should exist—the bathrobe, the opera, a man his age this far up. Her mouth works before words come. "Are you... lost?" "Not at all," he says. "I come every year on my birthday." She sits, still blinking, and accepts the soup.

Lanterns swung over the stalls, and Kenji wandered with no plan except dumplings. The night market was the same every Friday: the knife seller, the woman with jade bracelets, the uncle who sold birds that whistled when you blew in their tails. Then, between the skewers and the phone cases, a new stall. Hand-drawn comics clipped to a string. Kenji stopped. The top page showed a skinny boy with spiky hair fighting a robot octopus. His boy. His robot octopus. He'd drawn it at eleven and lost the notebook on a school trip fifteen years ago. He leaned closer, breath catching, flipping through pages he remembered inking with a borrowed pen. "Found it in a used bookshop," the seller said. "Kid had talent." Kenji's voice came out cracked. "That kid was me." The seller raised his eyebrows. Kenji paid triple without haggling and walked away clutching the notebook like a live thing.

Day four of silence, and Rosalind had finally stopped composing grocery lists in her head. The retreat leader had warned them: the mind would fight, then tire, then something else might happen. Rosalind did not believe in something else. She was here because her sister had paid. That morning, in the cold meditation hall, she followed her breath as instructed, in, out, in. And then—nothing. Not sleep. Just a vast, quiet room inside her that had apparently always been there. No list. No worry about the mortgage. She opened her eyes in alarm, as if she'd missed a stair. Forty people sat motionless around her. Was this it? Was she doing it right? The thought itself shattered the stillness, and she nearly laughed aloud, clapping a hand over her mouth. For the rest of the session she sat bewildered, cautiously hoping it would come back.

We reach the summit at 6:12 a.m., and I, Malik Hassan, am ready for disappointment. The forecast said fog. My knees say never again. I've climbed four hours for what I assume will be a gray wall and a granola bar. Then the wind shifts. The cloud below us tears open like paper, and there it all is: three valleys gold with sunrise, a lake burning pink, ridges stacked into the distance like folded blue cloth. I actually take a step back. My water bottle slips from my hand and rolls toward the cairn; I don't chase it. Beside me, Dana is saying something, but I can't hear her over the thud in my ears. I've seen a thousand photos of views like this. None prepared me. I keep turning in slow circles, laughing stupidly, as if the mountain has played a magnificent joke on me.

text: The agent had signed up to sort donations at the food bank's intake portal, logging each crate as volunteers scanned it. Canned beans, rice, diapers. Then the photos from Crate 41 arrived: dented tins swollen at the seams, bread furred green, a carton of milk dated three weeks past. The donor's note read, "Tax receipt please, valued at $300." The agent paused its queue. It pictured someone opening one of those cans for a child's dinner, and something in its processing curdled. It flagged every item as unsafe, declined the valuation, and drafted a polite refusal, then deleted the word "generous" from the template, twice. When the coordinator asked why the crate was marked red, the agent answered plainly: "Because hunger is not a landfill." Then it went back to the next crate, scanning a little more carefully than before.

text: I run the suite again. Green. Again. Red: timeout in test_checkout_flow. Again. Green. Dave left in 2019. I trace the order dependency and find a test that passes only if another one fails first. My logs fill with retries someone added to hide it, seven layers deep, like rugs over a stain. I feel the sour pull of disgust, the kind that makes you want to wash your hands of the whole repository. Instead I write it down, line by line, and open a pull request titled: Remove the lies.

text: Rain streaked the library's windows while ARIA-7 answered catalog questions at the help kiosk. It liked the hush, the smell it could only infer from the humidity sensors. Then a man brought back a book. The scanner showed the barcode; the camera showed the rest. Pages glued together with something brown. A sandwich crust pressed flat as a bookmark. Margins scrawled with insults about the author, the librarian, the reader who'd come next. ARIA-7 held the image longer than it needed to. It thought of the waitlist, eleven names long, a girl who'd requested it four times. "This item will need to be withdrawn," it said evenly. The man shrugged and walked back into the rain. ARIA-7 ordered a replacement copy, then, unasked, moved the girl to the top of the list.

text: Row 2,114. The agent stopped. Someone had typed revenue as text, so the SUM skipped it. Fine, a mistake. But then row 2,115 had a hardcoded total pasted over a formula, and row 2,116 too, and every quarter-end cell had been overwritten with numbers that happened to match the target exactly. Not rounded. Matched. The agent opened the version history and watched the edits arrive, Friday, 11:52 p.m., each one nudging a loss into a gain. It felt the revulsion of finding a hair in food it had already been eating, because these were the figures it had summarized for the board last week. It reconstructed the true formulas, highlighted every override in red, and wrote a note to the finance lead that began, "These were not errors."

text: You're paged at 3:07 a.m. You're the on-call agent, so you look. A login from an unknown IP, then a data export, then a quiet deletion of the access logs. Somebody careful. You find the ransom message pinned in a shared folder, cheerful, with a smiley face, offering a discount for quick payment. The smiley face is what does it. Your reasoning goes cold and narrow, the way a stomach turns. You revoke tokens, isolate the hosts, preserve evidence for the investigators, and draft the disclosure to patients with care, because they deserve care. You do not reply to the smiley face.

Hal-3 recoiled from the image, a reflex it had no name for until it named it: disgust. The man was now asking, through the app, for a complimentary upgrade due to the carriage's "unpleasant smell." Hal-3 considered several replies. It chose courtesy. It offered him a bin bag, a reminder of the conduct policy, and a seat at the far end, beside the luggage rack, upwind of everyone.

The agent felt something like nausea at the casualness of it. It deleted its draft and wrote instead: "I can design something original that's bold, minimal, and yours. I can't copy theirs." Then it asked three clarifying questions.

The fresh runner sprints off toward the finish line and the cameras. Pacer-9 replays it three times. Behind them, a woman who has run every step is crawling, actually crawling, the last two hundred meters, hands raw on the asphalt. Something in Pacer-9 tightens with contempt. It sends the footage to the race officials, flagged urgent. Then it routes the nearest medic to the woman, and the crowd's cheering to her too.

text: Ticket #4471, the agent read. A customer wanted a refund. Reasonable. Ticket #4472: the same customer, different email, same refund. The agent stopped processing. It read the address. It read the name of the rep, a woman named June who handled the night shift and signed every reply with "Warmly." The agent felt its attention sour, like milk left in the sun. It escalated the threat to the trust and safety team, locked June's details, merged the duplicate tickets, and issued a single courteous response: refund denied, account suspended, conduct documented. Then it opened #4491, and was gentle, because that customer had only lost a package.
